options: It belongs to the class rather than a particular instance
It can be called only once
It runs on a separate thread automatically
questions.explanation: A static method is associated with its declaring class, not an instance.

questions.text: What is the result of comparing two Java strings with `==`?
options: It tests whether the references are identical
It always compares their character contents
questions.explanation: String content equality should normally be tested with equals(), not reference equality.

questions.text: Which Java type is designed for immutable sequences of values in modern Java?
questions.explanation: List.of creates an unmodifiable list.

questions.text: Why can a Java generic method not directly instantiate `new T()`?
options: Type erasure removes the runtime type parameter information
Constructors cannot be called from methods
T always denotes a primitive type
The JVM forbids every generic object
questions.explanation: Erasure means the runtime generally lacks the concrete type needed to invoke T's constructor.

questions.text: What does declaring a Java field `volatile` guarantee for accesses to that field?
options: Visibility and ordering guarantees, but not atomicity of compound updates
That every access uses a database transaction
questions.explanation: Volatile establishes memory visibility and ordering, not atomic read-modify-write.

questions.text: Why can a `ConcurrentHashMap` be safer than a plain `HashMap` for concurrent updates?
options: It supports concurrent access with defined synchronization behavior
It makes mutable values thread-safe automatically
It permits null keys in every Java version
questions.explanation: ConcurrentHashMap coordinates concurrent operations; contained mutable objects still need care.

questions.text: A Java class implements `Comparable<T>`. Which method defines its natural ordering?
questions.explanation: Comparable<T> declares compareTo to compare an instance with another value.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of a sealed Java class hierarchy?
options: Restrict which classes may directly extend or implement a type
Prevent all objects from being constructed
Force every method to be final
questions.explanation: Sealed types explicitly permit a controlled set of direct subtypes.

questions.text: Why can catching `Exception` around a whole Java method obscure errors?
options: It can accidentally handle failures the method cannot meaningfully recover from
It prevents exceptions from being created
questions.explanation: Broad catches can hide unexpected faults and make recovery behavior unclear.

questions.text: What is the effect of `thenCompose` compared with `thenApply` on a Java `CompletionStage`?
options: It flattens a function-produced CompletionStage instead of nesting it
It always runs the function on the main thread
It blocks until the stage completes
questions.explanation: thenCompose chains asynchronous work and avoids CompletionStage<CompletionStage<T>> nesting.

questions.text: What does the Java memory model's happens-before relation establish?
options: Visibility and ordering guarantees between actions
The exact wall-clock duration of a thread
A global order for every instruction in every program
That data races are automatically repaired
questions.explanation: Happens-before constrains visibility and ordering for correctly synchronized actions.

questions.text: Why should `equals()` and `hashCode()` use the same immutable identity fields for a hash-based key?
options: Changing a key's hash while stored can make it unreachable in its bucket
Hash maps compare only object identity
Mutable keys are automatically copied on insertion
The JVM recalculates every bucket on each field change
questions.explanation: A changed hash can make lookup search a different bucket from the one holding the entry.

questions.text: What does a Java record provide by default for its declared components?
options: A compact data carrier with accessors and value-oriented methods
A mutable bean with public fields
A singleton object shared by all callers
questions.explanation: Records synthesize component accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString.

questions.text: Why does a Java `finally` block not guarantee execution after `Runtime.getRuntime().halt()`?
options: halt stops the JVM without normal shutdown processing
finally runs only for checked exceptions
halt converts finally into a daemon thread
finally is illegal in methods that call halt
questions.explanation: halt forcibly terminates the VM, bypassing normal cleanup and shutdown hooks.

questions.text: What can cause a `ClassCastException` when casting a Java generic collection to a parameterized type?
options: Runtime checks cannot fully verify erased type arguments, and an element may later fail its cast
The collection is always copied into a new type
Generic arguments are stored as runtime array dimensions
All casts of reference types are compile-time only
questions.explanation: Type erasure limits runtime checks; compiler-inserted casts can fail when retrieved elements differ.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a `StampedLock` optimistic read stamp?
options: Allow a read without initially taking a read lock, then validate it
Guarantee exclusive access to every reader
Prevent writers from ever acquiring a lock
questions.explanation: An optimistic read proceeds speculatively and must validate that no write intervened.

questions.text: A Java stream pipeline contains `map`, `filter`, and a terminal `count`. When are intermediate operations generally evaluated?
options: Lazily as the terminal operation consumes the stream
Immediately when each intermediate method is called
Only when the stream is garbage-collected
questions.explanation: Stream intermediate operations are lazy and run when a terminal operation is invoked.

questions.text: Which Git command records staged changes in a new commit?
questions.explanation: git commit creates a commit from the staged snapshot.

questions.text: Which command shows the current branch and whether working-tree files are modified?
questions.explanation: git status reports branch state, staged changes, and working-tree changes.

questions.text: What does `git clone` do?
options: Creates a local copy of a repository
questions.explanation: Cloning copies a repository and configures its remote-tracking relationship.

questions.text: Which command stages a tracked file's current changes for the next commit?
questions.explanation: git add updates the index with the selected file contents.

questions.text: What does a Git commit represent?
options: A snapshot of staged project content with metadata
A live copy of every remote repository
A command to erase untracked files
questions.explanation: A commit records a project snapshot and links it into repository history.

questions.text: What does git pull commonly do?
options: Fetches remote changes and integrates them into the current branch
questions.explanation: git pull fetches and integrates changes, typically by merge or rebase.

questions.text: What is the effect of `git fetch origin`?
options: Downloads remote refs and objects without integrating them into the current branch
questions.explanation: Fetch updates remote-tracking information but does not merge into the checked-out branch.

questions.text: What does `git diff --staged` show?
options: Changes in the index compared with the current commit
Untracked files compared with the remote
questions.explanation: The staged diff compares the index to HEAD.

questions.text: When does a Git merge typically create a merge commit?
options: When merging histories that have diverged and cannot be fast-forwarded
Every time a file is staged
Only when a tag is deleted
questions.explanation: A divergent merge generally records both parent histories in a merge commit.

questions.text: What does `git stash` normally do to tracked working-tree changes?
options: Saves them temporarily and returns the working tree toward a clean state
Commits them to the current branch
questions.explanation: Stash records local modifications for later reapplication without creating a commit.

questions.text: What happens to commits when `git revert <commit>` is used?
options: A new commit is created that reverses the selected change
The selected commit is erased from history
The commit is moved to another branch
questions.explanation: Revert preserves history and adds an inverse change as a new commit.

questions.text: What does `git branch --merged` list?
options: Branches whose tips are reachable from the current branch
questions.explanation: The command lists branches already incorporated into the current branch's history.

questions.text: Why does Git report a merge conflict?
options: It cannot automatically reconcile overlapping changes in the merge inputs
The commit message is too short
questions.explanation: Conflicting edits require a person or merge tool to choose the intended result.

questions.text: What does `git cherry-pick <commit>` do?
options: Applies the change introduced by a commit onto the current branch
Deletes the commit from every branch
questions.explanation: Cherry-pick creates a new commit applying the selected commit's patch.

questions.text: In a GitHub pull request, what is a requested reviewer's main role?
options: Review proposed changes and provide feedback or approval
Rewrite the contributor's local Git database
questions.explanation: Reviewers inspect proposed changes and can comment, approve, or request changes.

questions.text: A pull request is primarily used to:
options: Propose and review changes before merging them
questions.explanation: Pull requests provide a review and collaboration workflow before integration.

questions.text: What does `git reflog` record that ordinary branch history may not show?
options: Recent local changes to refs such as HEAD, including some otherwise unreachable commits
Every file ever viewed in the editor
questions.explanation: The reflog tracks local reference movements and can help recover prior commit positions.

questions.text: A rebase replays commits from a topic branch onto an updated base. What happens to the replayed commit IDs?
options: They are generally new IDs because their parent history changes
They remain identical because Git ignores parents
They are deleted from the object database immediately
questions.explanation: A commit hash includes parent and metadata, so replaying creates different commit objects.

questions.text: What does `git merge-base A B` identify?
options: A best common ancestor of the two commits
The newest commit on either branch
The files modified only in B
questions.explanation: Git uses the merge base as a common ancestor when combining histories.

questions.text: Why is force-pushing a rewritten shared branch potentially disruptive?
options: Collaborators may have based work on commits no longer reachable from that branch
It prevents future commits from being created
It deletes the repository's remote configuration
questions.explanation: Replacing published history can invalidate collaborators' bases and require recovery.

questions.text: What does `git bisect` use to locate a regression efficiently?
options: Binary search across revisions labeled good or bad
A complete rebuild of every historical commit in chronological order
A list of remote branch names
questions.explanation: Bisect tests midpoint revisions and narrows the range logarithmically.

questions.text: During a rebase conflict, what does `git rebase --continue` do after conflicts are resolved and staged?
options: Aborts the rebase and restores the original branch
Pushes the branch to its remote
questions.explanation: After resolution, continue proceeds with the next commit in the rebase sequence.

questions.text: How does Git identify a blob object independent of its filename?
options: By a hash of its object content and type representation
By its absolute path on disk
questions.explanation: Git objects are content-addressed; filenames are recorded by trees, not blobs.

questions.text: What does `git reset --mixed <commit>` do to HEAD, the index, and working tree?
options: Moves HEAD and resets the index while leaving working-tree files unchanged
Moves HEAD and resets both index and working tree
questions.explanation: Mixed reset updates HEAD and index but does not overwrite the working tree.

questions.text: Why can a shallow clone be insufficient for some history operations?
options: It omits older commit ancestry beyond its configured depth
It stores no commit objects at all
questions.explanation: Truncated history may lack ancestors needed for operations such as deep merges or blame.

questions.text: What does the `--force-with-lease` option add to a Git push?
options: A check that the remote ref has not changed unexpectedly before replacement
A guarantee that the remote server is online forever
A merge of every remote commit
questions.explanation: It refuses the force update if the remote ref differs from the expected value.

questions.text: In Git, why can a revert of a merge commit require a mainline parent number?
options: Git needs to know which parent's changes should be treated as the baseline
The parent number identifies a remote server
It selects which files remain tracked
questions.explanation: A merge has multiple parents, so -m identifies the parent-relative change to reverse.

questions.text: What is the effect of `git worktree add`?
options: Creates another working tree linked to the same repository object database
Copies the repository history to a new remote
Moves the current branch into the index
questions.explanation: Worktrees allow multiple checked-out directories sharing one repository.

questions.text: What does a Git tag object contain that a lightweight tag generally does not?
options: Tagger metadata, a message, and optionally a signature
A full duplicate of every file
A working-tree snapshot independent of commits
questions.explanation: An annotated tag is a Git object with metadata and can be cryptographically signed.

questions.text: A GitHub Actions workflow is triggered by `pull_request` and needs a secret. Why may secrets be unavailable for a pull request from a fork?
options: GitHub withholds repository secrets from untrusted fork workflows for security
The pull_request event has no YAML context
Secrets are available only in local Git hooks
questions.explanation: Withholding secrets helps prevent untrusted code from exfiltrating credentials.

questions.text: Which language primarily describes the structure of a web page?
questions.explanation: HTML provides the semantic document structure.

questions.text: Which protocol is commonly used to transfer web pages between a browser and a server?
questions.explanation: Browsers use HTTP, usually protected with TLS as HTTPS, to request web resources.

questions.text: What does DNS do when a browser visits a domain name?
options: Maps the name to an IP address
questions.explanation: DNS resolves a domain name to the network address used to contact its server.

questions.text: In a typical website, which part runs JavaScript that responds to a button click?
questions.explanation: Client-side JavaScript runs in the browser and can handle user interactions.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of a responsive web layout?
options: Adapt content to different viewport sizes
Make every page require a login
questions.explanation: Responsive layouts adjust presentation so a site works across screen sizes.

questions.text: In the CSS box model, padding sits between:
questions.explanation: Padding surrounds content and is inside the border.

questions.text: A server returns HTTP status 404 for a requested page. What does that normally indicate?
options: The requested resource was not found
The request succeeded with a new resource
questions.explanation: 404 means the server could not find a representation for the requested resource.

questions.text: What does the Cache-Control: max-age directive specify for a browser cache?
options: How long a response may be considered fresh
How many redirects a page may use
Which HTTP method must be used
questions.explanation: max-age sets a freshness lifetime in seconds for a cached response.

questions.text: Which HTTP method is designed to retrieve a representation without requesting a state change?
questions.explanation: GET is defined as a safe method for retrieving a resource representation.

questions.text: Why is a 301 response used after a page has permanently moved?
options: To tell clients and search engines the resource has a new permanent URL
To request credentials before loading the page
To indicate the request body is too large
questions.explanation: A 301 redirect communicates a permanent move to the new location.

questions.text: What is a benefit of serving static assets through a content delivery network?
options: Copies can be delivered from locations nearer to users
It removes the need for valid HTML
It guarantees every database query is faster
questions.explanation: A CDN serves cached assets from geographically distributed edge locations.

questions.text: When a browser loads an external JavaScript file with the defer attribute, when does it execute?
options: After HTML parsing, before DOMContentLoaded, in document order
Immediately before the HTML parser starts
Only after the user clicks the script
In reverse order as soon as each download finishes
questions.explanation: Deferred classic scripts execute after parsing and preserve their document order.

questions.text: What is the purpose of the Content-Type response header?
options: Describe the media type of the response body
questions.explanation: Content-Type lets the recipient interpret the response body as the indicated media type.

questions.text: Which practice helps a web server handle many independent I/O requests efficiently?
options: Use asynchronous I/O rather than blocking a thread for each wait
Rebuild the entire application for each request
Store all responses in one global variable
questions.explanation: Asynchronous I/O allows a server to work on other requests while operations wait.

questions.text: What does progressive enhancement mean in web development?
options: Start with core content and functionality, then add richer features where supported
Require the newest browser before displaying any content
Ship a different domain for every screen size
questions.explanation: Progressive enhancement keeps a usable baseline and layers on capabilities when available.

questions.text: What does a browser CORS check help a server control?
options: Which web origins may read cross-origin responses
questions.explanation: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing lets servers declare permitted origins.

questions.text: A page's first render is delayed because a large stylesheet is render-blocking. Which change most directly lets noncritical styles load later?
options: Split critical and noncritical CSS, inlining only the small critical portion
Move the stylesheet to the end of the HTML without changing dependencies
Add more synchronous scripts before the stylesheet
questions.explanation: Critical CSS can unblock the initial render while remaining styles load asynchronously or later.

questions.text: An API must prevent a retrying client from creating duplicate payments after a timeout. What is the strongest design?
options: Accept an idempotency key and persist its result with the payment operation
Tell clients never to retry timed-out requests
Use a random URL for every attempt
Return success before recording the payment
questions.explanation: A persisted idempotency key lets retries return the original result instead of duplicating the operation.

questions.text: A service needs to evolve a JSON API without breaking existing clients. Which approach is safest?
options: Add backward-compatible fields and preserve existing field meanings
Rename response fields in place and update only the server
Change null values to unrelated types without notice
Remove old endpoints as soon as a new client is released
questions.explanation: Additive changes preserve existing contracts; breaking changes need explicit versioning or migration.

questions.text: Why might an application use a reverse proxy in front of its web servers?
options: It can route requests, terminate TLS, and balance traffic across backends
It replaces the need for HTTP between browser and server
It guarantees application code has no defects
It stores every browser's private key
questions.explanation: Reverse proxies commonly centralize ingress, TLS termination, and load distribution.

questions.text: A deployment changes a database schema while old and new application versions overlap. Which migration strategy minimizes downtime?
options: Use an expand-and-contract migration with a compatible transition period
Rename or drop the old column before deploying any compatible code
Require all clients to disconnect during every schema change
Run schema changes only after deleting existing records
questions.explanation: An expand-and-contract rollout keeps both application versions compatible while the schema changes.

questions.text: A web app's latency is high only for users far from its origin, while origin processing time is low. What should be investigated first?
options: Network distance and edge caching for cacheable responses
The number of comments in the HTML source
questions.explanation: Geographic latency often points to network round trips and opportunities for edge delivery.

questions.text: Which measurement best distinguishes slow server processing from slow browser rendering in a page-load investigation?
options: Correlate server request timings with browser navigation and rendering timings
Count the number of domains in the URL
Measure only the source repository size
questions.explanation: Separate server-side timings and browser performance entries identify which stage dominates.

questions.text: A site wants users to receive a new frontend release gradually and allow rapid rollback. Which deployment pattern fits best?
options: Canary deployment with health metrics and controlled traffic progression
Replace every server at once without health checks
Cache the new bundle indefinitely under an unchanged URL
Ship the release only by editing users' browser storage
questions.explanation: A canary limits initial exposure and lets operators halt or roll back based on observed health.

questions.text: An origin serves compressed content but reuses a cached response across clients that send different Accept-Encoding values. What response metadata is important?
questions.explanation: Vary tells shared caches that Accept-Encoding affects the selected representation.

questions.text: Why should a web application validate authorization on the server even when its interface hides restricted controls?
options: Clients can call server endpoints directly and alter their own interface
Hidden controls are always visible to search engines
Browsers cannot send requests from scripts
CSS rules are evaluated by the database
questions.explanation: The server is the trust boundary; client-side visibility is not an access-control mechanism.

questions.text: A site serves fingerprinted assets such as app.8f31.js. Which cache policy is suitable when the content changes only with the fingerprint?
options: Cache only if the response is a redirect
questions.explanation: A content fingerprint changes the URL on update, making long-lived immutable caching safe.

questions.text: A web service needs to preserve request order for updates to one account while processing unrelated accounts concurrently. What is a useful partitioning key?
options: A global timestamp shared by all accounts
questions.explanation: Partitioning by account keeps that account's work ordered without serializing unrelated accounts.

questions.text: When designing retries for a web API, why should clients use bounded exponential backoff with jitter?
options: It reduces synchronized retry bursts and limits repeated load
It ensures every failed operation eventually succeeds
It prevents the server from returning error codes
It makes requests execute in a fixed order
questions.explanation: Backoff limits pressure and jitter spreads retries so clients do not synchronize.

questions.text: A server-rendered page hydrates into an interactive client app. What is hydration expected to do?
options: Attach client-side behavior to the existing server-rendered markup
Convert the markup into a database schema
Re-download every image from a different origin
Replace HTTP responses with DNS records
questions.explanation: Hydration connects client rendering and event behavior to markup already produced by the server.

questions.text: Which function creates a React component element?
questions.explanation: React.createElement creates an element description.

questions.text: What is JSX commonly used for in a React project?
options: Writing UI markup within JavaScript syntax
questions.explanation: JSX is syntax that lets developers describe UI elements in JavaScript.

questions.text: What does a React component usually return?
options: A description of the UI to render
questions.explanation: A component returns React elements or another supported renderable value.

questions.text: How can a parent component pass a value to a child component?
options: By changing the child's source file
questions.explanation: Props are the inputs a parent supplies when rendering a child component.

questions.text: How can a React component show different content depending on a boolean value?
options: Rename the component file on each render
questions.explanation: JavaScript conditions can select which elements a component returns.

questions.text: Why does React use a key when rendering a list?
questions.explanation: Keys help React match list items between renders.

questions.text: Which React pattern lets a child notify its parent that a user selected an item?
options: Call a callback function passed in a prop
Write directly to the browser's render tree
questions.explanation: A parent can pass a callback for the child to invoke when the event occurs.

questions.text: What is the usual purpose of a controlled text input in React?
options: Its displayed value is driven by React state or props
The browser is prevented from accepting keystrokes
The input is stored only in a CSS rule
It automatically submits on every character
questions.explanation: A controlled input receives its value from React and reports changes through an event handler.

questions.text: Which prop is conventionally used to pass content between a component's opening and closing tags?
questions.explanation: React places nested elements or text in the component's children prop.

questions.text: Why can calling a state setter during the render phase cause problems?
options: It can trigger another render repeatedly before rendering settles
It converts the component to a class
It prevents props from reaching children
questions.explanation: Updating state while rendering can create an unbounded render loop.

questions.text: When does React render a component again after its parent renders?
options: Normally, unless an applicable optimization skips the render
Only when the component's file changes
Never; React renders components exactly once
questions.explanation: Parent renders generally cause child components to be considered for rendering too.

questions.text: What does wrapping sibling JSX elements in a Fragment accomplish?
options: Groups them without adding an extra DOM element
Automatically assigns list keys to every descendant
questions.explanation: A Fragment groups children in React's tree without an extra wrapper node in the DOM.

questions.text: In an event handler, how should a React form commonly prevent the browser's default page navigation on submit?
options: Return a CSS class named prevent
Set the input's key to false
questions.explanation: preventDefault stops the native form submission behavior so the handler can manage it.

questions.text: What is the role of React.StrictMode during development?
options: It enables extra checks that can reveal potential problems
It encrypts all props before rendering
It guarantees production code has no warnings
questions.explanation: StrictMode adds development-only checks and may intentionally repeat some work to expose unsafe patterns.

questions.text: Which approach is appropriate for rendering a list from an array of records?
options: Map each record to a React element and provide a stable key
Join the records into one HTML string and execute it as code
Render only the first array entry unconditionally
Store each record in a separate component file
questions.explanation: Mapping data to elements is a standard pattern, and stable keys identify list items.

questions.text: When should an effect clean-up function run?
options: Before the effect reruns and when the component unmounts
questions.explanation: React runs cleanup before rerunning an effect and on unmount.

questions.text: A component subscribes to an external store. Which React API is designed to read that store consistently during concurrent rendering?
questions.explanation: useSyncExternalStore provides a subscription contract that supports consistent external-store snapshots.

questions.text: A memoized child still renders after its parent rerenders because a callback prop changes identity each time. What can help if profiling confirms this is costly?
options: Stabilize the callback with useCallback and correct dependencies
Wrap the callback in a new inline arrow on every render
Move the callback into a CSS custom property
questions.explanation: useCallback can preserve function identity between renders when its dependencies are unchanged.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of useMemo?
options: Reuse a calculated value between renders until dependencies change
Subscribe a component to every DOM mutation
Replace all component state with a global variable
Force an effect to run after every paint
questions.explanation: useMemo caches a calculation result based on its dependency list.

questions.text: A React component needs to focus an input after it mounts without causing a render when the DOM node changes. Which hook is appropriate?
questions.explanation: A ref can hold the input DOM node and can be updated without scheduling a render.

questions.text: Why must hooks be called in the same order on every render of a function component?
options: React associates hook state with call order
Hooks are compiled into CSS selectors by position
The browser requires a fixed number of event listeners
The order determines the component's exported name
questions.explanation: React relies on stable hook call order to associate each hook call with its stored state.

questions.text: A component starts a fetch in an effect when a search term changes. What should cleanup or request coordination prevent?
options: An older response overwriting results for a newer search
The browser parsing the component's JSX
A state update from the latest request
questions.explanation: Cancellation or request identity checks avoid stale responses winning a race.

questions.text: What is a key advantage of useReducer over several independent state setters for a complex state transition?
options: It centralizes transitions as actions handled by one reducer
It automatically persists every state to a database
It lets a component mutate props safely
It eliminates the need to render after updates
questions.explanation: A reducer centralizes how actions transform related state.

questions.text: In a Suspense-enabled tree, what does a Suspense boundary provide when a child suspends?
options: A fallback UI until the child can render
An automatic retry policy for every network request
A permanent error message for all descendant events
A guarantee that the child renders on the server
questions.explanation: Suspense boundaries display their fallback while waiting for supported suspended work.

questions.text: Why might a component use useId to create IDs for related form controls?
options: It generates IDs that remain consistent across server rendering and hydration
It creates a unique database primary key shared by every browser
It prevents the control from receiving focus
questions.explanation: useId is intended for stable accessibility-related IDs that work with server rendering.

questions.text: What does startTransition mark an update as?
options: Non-urgent work that React may interrupt to keep the interface responsive
A synchronous DOM mutation that blocks all input
A request to permanently cache component output
questions.explanation: Transition updates are lower priority than urgent interactions such as typing.

questions.text: Why should an effect's dependency list include every reactive value it reads?
options: So the effect reruns when a value it uses changes
So React can convert the effect into a component prop
To guarantee the effect executes only once
To prevent any cleanup from running
questions.explanation: Complete dependencies keep the effect synchronized with the values it uses.

questions.text: A context provider receives a newly created object value on every render, causing many consumers to rerender. What can reduce avoidable updates?
options: Memoize the provider value when its contents have not changed
Create a separate context for every consumer render
Mutate the previous provider value in place
Move all consumers outside the React tree
questions.explanation: A stable context value identity avoids notifying consumers when the meaningful value is unchanged.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of React.lazy when used with Suspense?
options: Load a component's code on demand through a dynamic import
Defer updating state until a component unmounts
Convert a function component into a server route
questions.explanation: React.lazy lets a component be loaded dynamically and rendered under a Suspense boundary.

questions.text: What should a custom hook do with state or effects that are intended to be shared by multiple component instances?
options: Expose reusable logic while each calling component retains its own hook state
Store all callers' state in one implicit global variable
Return a new React root for each caller
Change the rules for calling built-in hooks
questions.explanation: Custom hooks reuse logic; their hook state belongs to each component that calls them.

questions.text: Which element represents the main content of a page?
questions.explanation: The main element identifies the document’s primary content.

questions.text: What does the <!doctype html> declaration do in an HTML document?
questions.explanation: The HTML doctype signals browsers to use standards mode.

questions.text: Which attribute on the html element identifies the document's primary language?
questions.explanation: The lang attribute declares the language of the element's text content.

questions.text: Which attribute on an anchor specifies the destination URL?
questions.explanation: An anchor's href attribute supplies the hyperlink destination.

questions.text: Which element is intended to group a set of navigation links?
questions.explanation: The nav element represents a section of navigation links.

questions.text: What should a label’s for attribute match?
questions.explanation: The for value associates the label with the control whose id matches.

questions.text: Which attribute associates a table header cell with the data cells in its column?
questions.explanation: scope="col" identifies a header as applying to the cells in its column.

questions.text: What does the required attribute do on a supported form control?
options: Prevents form submission when the control has no acceptable value
Makes the value read-only after the first keystroke
Automatically sends the form to two servers
Hides the control from assistive technology
questions.explanation: A required control must have a value that passes its native constraint validation.

questions.text: Why is a button inside a form often given type="button" when it performs a separate interface action?
options: It avoids the default submit behavior
It makes the button a hyperlink
It converts the form into a table
questions.explanation: A button in a form defaults to submit, while type="button" does not submit it.

questions.text: What does the async attribute on a classic script primarily allow?
options: The script downloads without blocking HTML parsing and executes when ready
The script waits until every image has loaded
The script executes before it is downloaded
The script runs only in a Web Worker
questions.explanation: async permits parallel download and execution as soon as the script is ready.

questions.text: What is a practical purpose of the <picture> element?
options: Offer alternative image sources for different conditions or formats
Create a responsive grid of text paragraphs
questions.explanation: picture can select among source elements, with an img fallback.

questions.text: Which element provides a caption for a figure containing an image or diagram?
questions.explanation: figcaption supplies a caption for its containing figure.

questions.text: What is the purpose of the name attribute on a successful form control?
options: It supplies the key used for that control's submitted form value
It sets the control's visible label automatically
It selects the form's encoding algorithm
It declares the control's required language
questions.explanation: Form submission uses a control's name as the key for its value.

questions.text: How does the download attribute on a same-origin link generally affect navigation?
options: It suggests that the linked resource be downloaded
It forces the resource to execute as JavaScript
It makes the link inaccessible to keyboard users
It reloads the current page without a request
questions.explanation: The download attribute signals that the linked resource should be downloaded rather than navigated to.

questions.text: Which element is designed to group related controls in a form and provide a group caption?
questions.explanation: fieldset groups related form controls and legend labels that group.

questions.text: Which attribute gives an image a text alternative when it cannot be seen?
questions.explanation: The alt attribute provides an accessible text alternative for an image.

questions.text: A document declares <meta charset="utf-8"> after many non-ASCII characters. Why can this be unsafe?
options: The encoding declaration must occur early enough for the parser to identify the encoding reliably
The charset attribute is valid only on an image
The browser will treat all later elements as scripts
questions.explanation: Browsers need the encoding declaration within the early portion of the document to decode bytes correctly.

questions.text: Why can placing a form element inside another form produce unreliable submission behavior?
options: HTML does not permit nested form elements, so parsing and form ownership can differ from intent
Nested forms automatically merge every submit button
The inner form always encrypts values
Browsers submit both forms as one multipart request
questions.explanation: Nested forms are invalid HTML, and the HTML parser does not create nested form ownership as authors may expect.

questions.text: A label contains a checkbox and descriptive text. Which markup makes clicking the text activate the checkbox without an explicit for/id pair?
options: Place the checkbox inside the label element
Put the label next to the checkbox in a div
Set the label's role to checkbox
Use a title attribute on the input
questions.explanation: A label can be explicitly associated by for/id or implicitly by containing its control.

questions.text: What does the form attribute on a button allow when its form is not an ancestor?
options: Associate it with a form elsewhere in the same document by form id
Submit any form on another origin
Change the button into a fieldset
Set the form's HTTP response status
questions.explanation: The form attribute can associate a form control with a form element by its id.

questions.text: When is an input's value generally omitted from form submission?
options: When the control has no name or is disabled
Whenever the control has a placeholder
Whenever the control is inside a fieldset
questions.explanation: Successful controls generally need a name and must not be disabled to contribute submitted data.

questions.text: Which relationship is created by aria-describedby="help" on a control when an element with id="help" exists?
options: The referenced element provides a supplementary description
The referenced element becomes the control's form owner
The referenced element supplies the control's submitted name
The control inherits the referenced element's value
questions.explanation: aria-describedby references text that gives the element an additional accessible description.

questions.text: What does the sandbox attribute on an iframe do by default when no permissions are added?
options: Applies restrictions to the embedded content's capabilities
Makes the iframe share all parent-page privileges
Guarantees the iframe uses the parent's origin
Prevents the browser from downloading the iframe document
questions.explanation: The sandbox flag set limits embedded content unless specific capabilities are explicitly allowed.

questions.text: For a script using type="module", what is the default execution behavior relative to document parsing?
options: It is deferred until parsing is complete
It blocks parsing as soon as it is encountered
It executes only after the load event
It runs as inline event-handler code
questions.explanation: Module scripts are deferred by default and execute after the document has been parsed.

questions.text: Why should an HTML template element's contents be treated differently from ordinary children in the live document?
options: Its contents are inert until cloned or otherwise inserted
Its contents execute immediately in a separate browsing context
Its contents are always sent as form data
Its contents cannot contain HTML elements
questions.explanation: A template's content is held in a DocumentFragment and is not rendered or activated until used.

questions.text: Which markup expresses that a word is an abbreviation and supplies its expanded form on hover or to some assistive technologies?
questions.explanation: The title attribute on abbr can provide the abbreviation's expansion.

questions.text: What happens when an HTML element has the hidden attribute, absent overriding CSS?
options: It is not rendered as part of the page's presentation
It is rendered but cannot be selected with a mouse
It is submitted as an empty form control
It is moved to the document head
questions.explanation: The hidden attribute indicates that the element is not currently relevant and is normally not rendered.

questions.text: Why can replacing a native <button> with a clickable <div> reduce accessibility?
options: The div lacks native button semantics and keyboard activation by default
The browser forbids click handlers on div elements
The button element cannot be styled
questions.explanation: Native buttons expose semantics and keyboard behavior that a generic div does not provide automatically.

questions.text: What does the integrity attribute on a script or link enable the browser to check?
options: Whether the fetched resource matches an expected cryptographic hash
Whether the page's user is an administrator
Whether the resource has a valid HTML doctype
Whether the stylesheet contains a media query
questions.explanation: Subresource Integrity lets a browser verify fetched bytes against declared hashes.

questions.text: How should an HTML document provide alternate text tracks such as captions for a video?
options: Use track elements with an appropriate kind and source
Put caption text in the video's poster attribute
Use a meta element inside the video
Add a title attribute to every video frame
questions.explanation: A track element can reference timed text such as captions or subtitles.

questions.text: Which CSS property changes an element’s text color?
questions.explanation: The color property sets the foreground text color.

questions.text: Which CSS selector targets elements whose class attribute includes "card"?
questions.explanation: A leading period selects elements by class.

questions.text: Which CSS property adds space outside an element's border?
questions.explanation: Margin is the space outside an element's border.

questions.text: Which display value creates a flex formatting context for an element's children?
questions.explanation: display:flex makes the element a flex container.

questions.text: What does box-sizing: border-box make the declared width include?
options: Content only, excluding padding and border
questions.explanation: With border-box, the specified dimensions include content, padding, and border.

questions.text: In CSS Grid, which property defines the columns of a grid container?
questions.explanation: grid-template-columns defines explicit grid column tracks.

questions.text: If two normal declarations of equal origin and importance apply, which selector usually wins?
options: The one written first, regardless of source order
The one with the shorter property name
The one in the smallest file
questions.explanation: After origin and importance, specificity is considered before source order.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a CSS custom property declared as --brand: teal?
options: It defines a reusable value that can be referenced with var(--brand)
It registers a new HTML element
It forces the browser to use a named web font
questions.explanation: Custom properties store reusable CSS values and are read with the var() function.

questions.text: Which media feature is commonly used to apply styles based on viewport width?
questions.explanation: Media queries can test viewport width with features such as min-width and max-width.

questions.text: An absolutely positioned element is offset from which containing block in the common case?
options: Its nearest ancestor that establishes a positioned containing block
Always the viewport, regardless of ancestors
The last sibling in document order
questions.explanation: A positioned ancestor commonly establishes the containing block for absolute positioning.

questions.text: What does flex-shrink control in a flex container?
options: How flex items shrink when their combined size exceeds available space
How many columns a grid creates
The transparency of a flex item
Whether an item participates in the cascade
questions.explanation: flex-shrink determines an item's share of negative free space.

questions.text: How does the CSS value inherit behave for a property?
options: The element takes the computed value from its parent
The property is removed from the cascade
The element takes the value from its next sibling
The property is set to its initial value
questions.explanation: inherit explicitly uses the computed value of the parent element.

questions.text: What does minmax(12rem, 1fr) express in a CSS Grid track definition?
options: A track with a 12rem minimum and a flexible maximum
Twelve equal rows followed by one column
A minimum gap and a maximum border width
questions.explanation: minmax() sets a minimum and maximum track size; 1fr can use a share of free space.

questions.text: Which unit is relative to the font size of the root element?
questions.explanation: rem is based on the computed font size of the root element.

questions.text: What does position: sticky generally do when an element reaches its inset threshold while scrolling?
options: Keeps it constrained in place within its scrolling container
Turns it into a fixed-size grid track
questions.explanation: A sticky element behaves relatively until its scroll threshold, then sticks within its containing scrollport.

questions.text: Which selector targets an element only while it has keyboard focus visible?
questions.explanation: :focus-visible styles focus when the browser determines it should be visibly indicated.

questions.text: Why may z-index: 9999 fail to place a descendant above an element outside its ancestor's stacking context?
options: A stacking context is painted as a unit relative to sibling contexts
Descendants are always painted below text
The number is too large for the CSS grammar
questions.explanation: A descendant cannot escape its stacking context's position in the parent stacking order.

questions.text: A flex item refuses to shrink below the width of its long unbreakable content. Which property often fixes this?
questions.explanation: Flex items commonly have an automatic min-content minimum; min-width:0 permits further shrinking.

questions.text: When a CSS custom property is used inside var(--gap, 1rem), when is 1rem used?
options: When --gap is missing or invalid at computed-value time
Only when the element has no parent
When the browser is in print mode
questions.explanation: The second argument is the fallback when the custom property cannot provide a valid value.

questions.text: Which property can establish a new stacking context even when its value is not position: relative?
questions.explanation: An opacity value below 1 creates a stacking context.

questions.text: A CSS rule in a later cascade layer loses to a rule in an earlier layer, both normal and author-origin. Why?
options: For normal declarations, earlier cascade layers have priority over later layers
Later layers always have the lowest specificity
Source order is ignored for every declaration
The earlier rule must have an ID selector
questions.explanation: Within the same origin, normal declarations in earlier layers outrank those in later layers.

questions.text: What problem do container queries solve that viewport media queries do not directly address?
options: Styling a component according to its containing element's size or state
questions.explanation: Container queries let styles respond to a component's container rather than only the viewport.

questions.text: What does the CSS property contain: layout isolate with respect to layout containment?
options: It establishes independent layout containment for the element's descendants
It hides the element from the accessibility tree
It forces the element to use inline layout
questions.explanation: layout containment limits layout effects across the element's boundary.

questions.text: In CSS Grid, what is the key purpose of subgrid?
options: Let a nested grid use tracks defined by its parent grid
Force each grid item to span one pixel
Make grid tracks ignore intrinsic sizing
questions.explanation: A subgrid adopts parent tracks along the chosen axis, enabling shared alignment.

questions.text: When is a logical property such as margin-inline-start especially useful?
options: When layout should adapt to writing direction and writing mode
When margins must ignore the cascade
When an element needs a fixed physical left margin
When applying a filter to an image
questions.explanation: Logical properties map to the appropriate physical side for the current writing mode.

questions.text: Why might transform: translateZ(0) change how an element is painted even when it appears visually stationary?
options: A transform can create a stacking context and a containing block for positioned descendants
It removes the element from the accessibility tree
It converts all lengths to percentages
questions.explanation: A non-none transform establishes a stacking context and can establish a containing block.

questions.text: What does the @supports rule test?
options: Whether the browser supports a CSS declaration or feature
Whether a user has accepted cookies
Whether a stylesheet was loaded over HTTPS
Whether an HTML element has a particular id
questions.explanation: Feature queries conditionally apply styles based on browser support for CSS declarations.

questions.text: Why can animating width cause more layout work than animating transform?
options: Changing width can trigger layout, while transform often changes only compositing
Transforms are always calculated on the server
Width cannot be animated by CSS
Transform forces all images to reload
questions.explanation: Layout-affecting properties can cause recalculation; transforms often avoid layout and paint work.

questions.text: Which selector specificity is generally higher: :is(#hero, .panel) or .panel?
options: :is(#hero, .panel), because :is() takes the specificity of its most specific argument
They are always identical because they both match classes
questions.explanation: :is() contributes the specificity of its most specific argument, including the ID selector.

questions.text: What does overscroll-behavior: contain on a scroll container primarily prevent?
options: Scroll chaining from that container to an ancestor at its boundary
The container from scrolling at all
The browser from drawing a scrollbar
The element from participating in normal flow
questions.explanation: contain prevents boundary scroll actions from propagating to ancestor scrollers.

questions.text: Which React hook adds state to a function component?
questions.explanation: useState adds a state value and setter to a function component.

questions.text: What syntax is commonly used to include a JavaScript expression inside JSX markup?
options: A dollar sign followed by parentheses
A percent sign around the value
questions.explanation: JSX uses curly braces to embed JavaScript expressions.

questions.text: Which React hook stores a mutable reference that persists across renders without itself causing a render when changed?
questions.explanation: A ref object persists between renders, and changing its current property does not trigger rendering.

questions.text: What does a React event handler such as onClick={handleClick} receive when invoked?
options: A React event object describing the interaction
questions.explanation: React passes an event object to the registered handler.

questions.text: What is a React Fragment useful for?
options: Grouping elements without adding an extra DOM wrapper
Saving state across a browser restart
Applying CSS to the document body
questions.explanation: Fragments group adjacent elements in the React tree without a wrapper DOM node.

questions.text: What should a component do when its props change?
options: Write props into local storage automatically
questions.explanation: React components receive new props and render based on the updated values.

questions.text: What does useEffect primarily let a function component do?
options: Synchronize with an external system after rendering
Declare a new route in the browser
questions.explanation: Effects are for synchronization with external systems such as subscriptions or browser APIs.

questions.text: How can a component avoid applying an outdated result from a slower earlier request?
options: Track the active request or cancel it during effect cleanup
Always apply responses in arrival order
Store results in a constant that never changes
Disable all network requests after the first render
questions.explanation: Cleanup or request identity checks prevent stale asynchronous results from replacing newer ones.

questions.text: When should useContext be called to read a context value?
options: Inside a function component or custom hook beneath its provider
Inside a class constructor without a context API
Only in the root entry file
questions.explanation: useContext reads the nearest matching provider value in the calling component's tree.

questions.text: What is the role of useMemo in a component?
options: Memoize a computed value until its dependencies change
questions.explanation: useMemo caches the returned calculation for unchanged dependencies.

questions.text: Which hook is designed for state updates described by actions and handled by a reducer function?
questions.explanation: useReducer applies actions through a reducer to produce the next state.

questions.text: Why would a component use useCallback for a function passed to a memoized child?
options: To keep the function identity stable when dependencies are unchanged
To make the function execute on the server only
To turn the callback into component state
To prevent the child from receiving props
questions.explanation: useCallback can avoid a new function identity on every render when dependencies are stable.

questions.text: What does lifting state up mean in a React application?
options: Moving shared state to a common ancestor of components that use it
Moving all state into the DOM
Replacing component state with query parameters
Rendering a child before its parent
questions.explanation: A common owner can coordinate state shared by sibling components.

questions.text: How does the value of a controlled select element typically stay synchronized with a user's selection?
options: React supplies value and an onChange handler updates state
The browser changes React state without an event
The options array is mutated after every paint
The select's CSS selector stores the choice
questions.explanation: The component controls the selected value and updates it through onChange.

questions.text: What is the purpose of the key prop when mapping data to React elements?
options: Help React match each item between renders
Pass a value into the browser's URL bar
Make every item share the same state
questions.explanation: Stable keys help reconciliation identify which list items changed, moved, or were removed.

questions.text: Why should state updates based on the previous state use an updater function?
options: It receives the latest queued state value
It prevents the component from rendering
It runs only during server rendering
questions.explanation: Updater functions avoid stale values when updates are queued.

questions.text: Why can calling useLayoutEffect for work that could happen later delay a browser paint?
options: It runs synchronously after DOM mutations and before the browser repaints
It always runs on a remote server
It blocks the JavaScript parser before the component loads
It changes the document's character encoding
questions.explanation: useLayoutEffect runs before paint, so lengthy work there can delay visible updates.

questions.text: A memoized calculation changes on every render despite unchanged data because one dependency is a newly created object. What is the likely cause?
options: Dependency comparison sees a different object identity each render
React compares object contents deeply and found a difference
The dependency array is ignored for objects
questions.explanation: React compares dependencies with Object.is; fresh object identities invalidate the memo.

questions.text: What does useDeferredValue allow React to do with a rapidly changing value?
options: Defer updating a non-urgent part of the UI while urgent updates proceed
Persist the value across browser sessions
Prevent the value from reaching child components
questions.explanation: The deferred value can lag behind an urgent input update so expensive rendering is interruptible.

questions.text: When is useImperativeHandle typically used?
options: To customize the ref handle exposed by a component
To mutate the browser history on every render
To define a component's initial props
questions.explanation: useImperativeHandle customizes the value exposed through a ref.

questions.text: What is a key consequence of changing a component's key in a rendered tree?
options: React treats it as a different component instance and resets its local state
React merges its state with every sibling
The DOM node is guaranteed to keep its exact identity
questions.explanation: A changed key signals a new identity, so React unmounts the old instance and mounts another.

questions.text: Why can a state update inside a transition be interrupted?
options: React can prioritize urgent work such as responding to user input
Transitions run in a separate operating-system process
The update is committed only if the network is idle
React discards all state updates in a transition
questions.explanation: Transition work is non-urgent and can yield to higher-priority interactions.

questions.text: What does useSyncExternalStore's getSnapshot function need to return when the external store has not changed?
options: A new random object on every call
questions.explanation: Stable snapshots let React detect actual store changes and avoid needless rerenders.

questions.text: Why must the function passed to useReducer be pure?
options: React may invoke rendering logic more than once, so reducer results must not depend on side effects
Reducers run only when the application is compiled
A pure reducer automatically writes to local storage
Purity lets the reducer change its arguments in place
questions.explanation: Pure reducers produce predictable state and remain safe when React replays rendering work.

questions.text: What problem does an error boundary handle in a React tree?
options: It can render fallback UI for errors thrown while rendering descendants
It retries every failed HTTP request automatically
It catches errors from every event handler and promise
It validates CSS before the browser loads it
questions.explanation: Error boundaries catch descendant rendering and lifecycle errors and can display fallback UI.

questions.text: Why can useEffect appear to run twice for a mount in development under StrictMode?
options: React performs an extra setup-and-cleanup cycle to expose unsafe effects
StrictMode duplicates every production network request
Effects are required to execute twice by the HTML standard
The component is permanently mounted twice in the DOM
questions.explanation: Development StrictMode intentionally repeats effect setup and cleanup as a stress test.

questions.text: What does React's useId provide when multiple independently rendered roots need non-colliding generated IDs?
options: An identifier prefix can distinguish IDs across roots
A random database key for persisted records
A unique identifier guaranteed across all users and sessions
A stable list key derived from array contents
questions.explanation: Configuring distinct identifier prefixes helps prevent collisions among multiple roots.

questions.text: In server rendering, why should code avoid reading window during the initial render?
options: window is not available in a typical server runtime, and server/client output should match
The browser creates window only after hydration finishes
Reading window automatically serializes it to the client
questions.explanation: Server environments usually lack window, and differing initial output can cause hydration mismatches.

questions.text: What does createPortal change about a child's DOM placement?
options: It renders the child into a different DOM node while retaining its place in the React tree
It moves the child into another React application with no event propagation
It turns a function component into an iframe
It prevents context from reaching the child
questions.explanation: Portals change physical DOM placement but preserve React-tree relationships such as context and event bubbling.

questions.text: Why should a custom hook not conditionally call another hook based on a prop?
options: It would make hook call order vary between renders
React hooks can be called only by class components
Props are unavailable inside custom hooks
Conditional calls force the browser to reload
questions.explanation: Hook ordering must remain stable for React to associate stored hook state correctly.

questions.text: In supervised learning, training examples include:
options: A required human answer at prediction time
questions.explanation: Supervised models learn from examples paired with target labels.

questions.text: In a classification task, what does a model typically predict?
options: A sorted copy of the training set
questions.explanation: Classification assigns inputs to one of a set of discrete categories.

questions.text: What is a feature in a machine-learning dataset?
options: An input variable used by a model
A label that must be hidden from training
questions.explanation: Features are input variables from which a model learns or makes predictions.

questions.text: Which task is a common example of unsupervised learning?
options: Predicting known house prices from labeled examples
Scoring a model against known target answers
questions.explanation: Clustering can discover groups in data without supplied target labels.

questions.text: What does a model's prediction represent at inference time?
options: Its output for a provided input
The label used only to train it
questions.explanation: Inference applies a trained model to an input to produce an output.

questions.text: A model that performs very well on training data but poorly on new data is likely:
questions.explanation: Overfitting is strong training performance that does not generalize.

questions.text: What does gradient descent use to update model parameters during training?
options: The gradient of a loss function
The alphabetical order of feature names
A random label for each prediction
questions.explanation: Gradient descent adjusts parameters in the direction that reduces the loss.

questions.text: For an imbalanced binary classifier, what does precision measure?
options: The fraction of predicted positives that are actually positive
The fraction of actual positives that were found
The number of correct predictions divided by training time
The proportion of negative examples in the dataset
questions.explanation: Precision is true positives divided by all predicted positives.

questions.text: What is a common purpose of L2 regularization in model training?
options: Penalize large weights to discourage overly complex fits
Increase the number of target labels
Remove the need for a loss function
questions.explanation: L2 adds a weight-magnitude penalty that can reduce excessively large parameters.

questions.text: What does an embedding represent in many language models?
options: A token or item as a learned vector in a numeric space
A copy of the entire training dataset
A human-readable explanation of every prediction
A rule that removes all ambiguous words
questions.explanation: Embeddings map tokens or other items to learned dense vectors.

questions.text: How does a random forest combine predictions from its trees for a classification task?
options: By choosing the tree with the most parameters
By concatenating every tree's training data
questions.explanation: Classification forests commonly aggregate tree outputs by majority vote.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a validation set during model development?
options: Compare candidate models or settings without using the final test set
Supply labels at real-world inference time
Replace the training data after every epoch
Guarantee that the selected model is unbiased
questions.explanation: Validation data supports model selection and tuning, while a final test set is held back.

questions.text: What does recall measure for a binary classifier?
options: The fraction of actual positives that are correctly identified
The fraction of predicted positives that are correct
The average magnitude of model weights
questions.explanation: Recall is true positives divided by all actual positives.

questions.text: Why can a one-hot encoding be useful for a nominal category such as a color name?
options: It represents categories without implying an artificial numeric order
It guarantees the categories are linearly separable
It converts missing labels into correct labels
It reduces every category to one shared value
questions.explanation: One-hot columns distinguish categories without assigning them ordinal distances.

questions.text: What does stochastic gradient descent use for a typical parameter update?
options: A small randomly sampled batch of training examples
Every possible input from the data universe
Only examples that the model already predicts correctly
A validation label unavailable during training
questions.explanation: SGD estimates the gradient from a sample or mini-batch instead of the full dataset.

questions.text: Data leakage happens when:
options: Training uses information unavailable at prediction time
A dataset has fewer than a million rows
questions.explanation: Leakage lets information from outside the valid training boundary inflate evaluation.

questions.text: In scaled dot-product attention, why are query-key dot products divided by the square root of the key dimension?
options: To keep their variance from growing with dimension and avoid saturated softmax values
To make every attention weight exactly equal
To remove positional information from tokens
To ensure keys and queries have integer entries
questions.explanation: Scaling controls dot-product magnitude so softmax gradients do not become excessively small.

questions.text: What does temperature scaling do when calibrating a classifier's predicted probabilities?
options: Rescales logits before softmax without changing their ranking
Retrains the feature extractor from scratch
Guarantees perfect accuracy on new data
questions.explanation: A fitted temperature adjusts confidence while preserving the ordering of logits.

questions.text: A model's input distribution shifts after deployment but the relationship between inputs and labels remains stable. What type of shift is this?
questions.explanation: Covariate shift changes the input distribution while leaving the conditional label relationship stable.

questions.text: What is a central idea of backpropagation in a neural network?
options: Apply the chain rule to compute loss gradients through successive layers
Randomly reset each layer after every prediction
Propagate labels forward without calculating derivatives
questions.explanation: Backpropagation efficiently applies the chain rule to obtain parameter gradients.

questions.text: Why can label smoothing improve classification training in some settings?
options: It discourages the model from assigning absolute probability to the observed class
It removes the need for correctly labeled data
It makes every class equally likely at inference
It guarantees calibration under any distribution
questions.explanation: Softened targets can reduce overconfident predictions and improve generalization.

questions.text: What property does differential privacy's epsilon parameter control in a randomized training guarantee?
options: The bound on how much output distributions can change when one record is added or removed
The percentage of labels that are correct
questions.explanation: Smaller epsilon generally means stronger privacy because neighboring datasets yield more similar output distributions.

questions.text: Why is a low-rank adapter useful for fine-tuning a large neural network?
options: It trains a small number of added parameters while keeping most base weights fixed
It converts a neural network into a database index
It guarantees the model forgets all pretraining data
It increases the vocabulary without changing embeddings
questions.explanation: Low-rank adapters provide parameter-efficient updates to a mostly frozen model.

questions.text: What does the area under a ROC curve summarize?
options: Ranking performance across classification thresholds using true- and false-positive rates
The classifier's accuracy at one chosen threshold only
The number of classes multiplied by training time
Calibration error for the positive class
questions.explanation: ROC-AUC measures threshold-independent ranking discrimination, not calibration.

questions.text: In beam search for sequence generation, what is the main tradeoff controlled by beam width?
options: Search breadth versus computation, while retaining several partial sequences
questions.explanation: A wider beam explores more candidate sequences at greater inference cost.

questions.text: Why can batch normalization behave differently during training and inference?
options: Training uses batch statistics while inference typically uses accumulated running statistics
Inference always updates model weights from labels
The normalization axis changes to the vocabulary
questions.explanation: Running estimates are used at inference rather than statistics of the current training batch.

questions.text: What does a causal attention mask prevent in an autoregressive language model?
options: A position from attending to future token positions
A position from attending to earlier context
The model from using token embeddings
The loss from being computed during training
questions.explanation: The causal mask blocks future information so each prediction depends only on prior context.

questions.text: What is a common consequence of class imbalance for an unweighted training objective?
options: The majority class can dominate the loss and obscure minority-class errors
The decision boundary must be linear
questions.explanation: Frequent classes contribute more examples and can dominate aggregate loss.

questions.text: When using beam search with a length penalty, what issue is the penalty intended to mitigate?
options: The tendency of raw log-probability sums to favor shorter sequences
The tendency of tokenization to create unknown words
The variance of a mini-batch gradient
The need to provide an end-of-sequence token
questions.explanation: Summed log probabilities usually decrease with sequence length, biasing unadjusted search toward short outputs.

questions.text: Why should a machine-learning system monitor performance by meaningful subgroups after deployment?
options: Aggregate metrics can hide degraded or inequitable outcomes for particular groups
Subgroup metrics guarantee that the model is causal
Monitoring replaces the need to protect sensitive data
A single subgroup determines global model accuracy
questions.explanation: Disaggregated evaluation can reveal failure patterns concealed by aggregate scores.

questions.text: Which measure is the middle value of an ordered dataset?
questions.explanation: The median is the central value after sorting the observations.

questions.text: In a tabular dataset, what does a row usually represent?
questions.explanation: Each row commonly records one observation, such as a person, event, or measurement.

questions.text: What does a histogram display?
options: The distribution of numeric values grouped into bins
The exact path between database servers
Only the names of categorical columns
questions.explanation: A histogram groups numeric observations into bins to show their frequency distribution.

questions.text: What is a common first step when a dataset contains missing values?
options: Inspect their locations and patterns before choosing how to handle them
Replace every missing value with zero without checking
Treat each missing value as a new category in all columns
questions.explanation: Understanding missingness helps determine whether to impute, exclude, or otherwise handle values.

questions.text: In a data table, what does a column typically represent?
options: A variable or feature recorded for observations
questions.explanation: Columns usually contain values for one variable across multiple observations.

questions.text: What does a test set estimate in machine learning?
questions.explanation: A held-out test set estimates how a model performs on unseen examples.

questions.text: What can a scatter plot help reveal about two numeric variables?
options: Their association, clusters, and potential outliers
The exact value of every missing record
The schema of the source database
questions.explanation: A scatter plot visualizes paired values and can reveal patterns, but not establish causality.

questions.text: Why might an analyst use a stratified sample?
options: To ensure important subgroups are represented in the sample
To force all sampled values to be identical
To remove the need for a sampling frame
To guarantee the population mean is known
questions.explanation: Stratification samples within groups to improve their representation.

questions.text: What does standard deviation summarize?
options: Typical spread of values around their mean
The number of records with missing values
The difference between maximum and minimum categories
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures dispersion around the arithmetic mean.

questions.text: When combining two tables by a shared identifier, what operation is commonly used?
questions.explanation: A join matches records from tables using one or more key columns.

questions.text: What is an outlier in a numeric dataset?
options: An observation unusually distant from most other values
A column with a unique name
A record that is always invalid
questions.explanation: An outlier is unusually far from the bulk of observations, though it may be valid.

questions.text: What does a confidence interval communicate in frequentist analysis?
options: A procedure's range of plausible parameter values with a stated long-run coverage level
The probability that a fixed parameter changes during the study
The exact range containing every individual observation
The fraction of data used for training
questions.explanation: A confidence procedure has specified long-run coverage under its assumptions.

questions.text: Why standardize numeric variables before some distance-based algorithms?
options: Variables on larger scales could otherwise dominate distance calculations
Standardization turns all variables into independent causes
It removes the need to choose a distance metric
It converts numeric variables into labels
questions.explanation: Scaling can prevent large-unit features from overwhelming distance-based comparisons.

questions.text: What is the purpose of grouping records before calculating an average by region?
options: Compute the statistic separately for each region
Randomize the values within every row
Replace each region name with its mean
Remove the need to define the average
questions.explanation: Grouping partitions records so the aggregation is computed for each region.

questions.text: Which measure is usually more resistant than the mean to a few extremely large values?
questions.explanation: The median depends on rank and is less affected by extreme magnitudes than the mean.

questions.text: What is data leakage in model evaluation?
options: Using information unavailable at prediction time
questions.explanation: Leakage lets unavailable information inflate measured performance.

questions.text: A treatment appears beneficial overall but harmful within each of two age groups. What statistical phenomenon could explain this reversal?
questions.explanation: Simpson's paradox occurs when an aggregate association reverses within subgroups due to differing group composition.

questions.text: Why should imputation parameters be fitted only on each training fold during cross-validation?
options: Fitting them on all data leaks information from validation folds
It ensures every fold has the same row order
Imputation works only with categorical data
Validation folds must contain no features
questions.explanation: Preprocessing fitted on held-out folds leaks information and biases evaluation.

questions.text: What does a bootstrap confidence interval estimate by repeatedly resampling observed data with replacement?
options: Sampling uncertainty in a statistic under the empirical distribution
The probability that every observation is correct
A guaranteed interval for all future outcomes
The causal effect without design assumptions
