questions.explanation: Bootstrap resampling approximates the sampling distribution of a statistic.

questions.text: If many hypotheses are tested, what does controlling the false discovery rate aim to limit?
options: The expected proportion of false rejections among rejected hypotheses
The probability of any false rejection at all
The size of the original dataset
The chance that all null hypotheses are true
questions.explanation: FDR control limits the expected false-discovery share among declared discoveries.

questions.text: A study reports a small p-value but a tiny estimated effect. What is the best interpretation?
options: The result may be statistically detectable but its practical importance needs separate assessment
The effect must be large in the population
The null hypothesis is proven impossible
questions.explanation: Statistical evidence and practical effect size answer different questions.

questions.text: What does a permutation test construct under a null hypothesis of exchangeability?
options: A reference distribution by rearranging labels or observations
A confidence interval by adding synthetic rows
A causal graph from variable names
A model that memorizes the observed outcomes
questions.explanation: Permuting exchangeable assignments simulates outcomes expected under the null.

questions.text: Why can principal component analysis be sensitive to feature scaling?
options: High-variance units can dominate the covariance structure
Scaling changes the number of observations
PCA always removes the mean before fitting
questions.explanation: Unscaled features with large units may dominate principal directions.

questions.text: In a causal analysis, what is a confounder?
options: A common cause of both the exposure and outcome that can distort their association
A random error in a chart label
An outcome measured after treatment only
A variable unrelated to every study variable
questions.explanation: A confounder influences exposure and outcome and can create a misleading association.

questions.text: What does a difference-in-differences estimator compare?
options: The before-after change in a treated group against the change in a comparison group
The treated group's final mean against a national median only
Two outcome variances within the treated group
Random assignment against a regression coefficient
questions.explanation: It subtracts the comparison group's change from the treated group's change.

questions.text: Why is a log transform often applied to a strongly right-skewed positive variable?
options: It compresses large values and can make multiplicative patterns easier to model
It guarantees that the data become normally distributed
It preserves all pairwise distances exactly
It converts missing values into zeros
questions.explanation: The logarithm reduces scale at the high end, though it does not guarantee normality.

questions.text: What does a data lineage record help an analyst determine?
options: Where data came from and how it was transformed
Whether a model's predictions are causal
The number of pixels in a visualization
questions.explanation: Lineage documents data sources and transformation steps for traceability.

questions.text: When is a robust statistic especially useful?
options: When estimates should be less sensitive to outliers or assumption violations
When the sample must contain no variation
When all measured variables are perfectly normal
When a result needs to prove causation
questions.explanation: Robust methods reduce sensitivity to departures such as extreme observations.

questions.text: What is a key reason to pre-register a statistical analysis plan?
options: Reduce undisclosed analytic flexibility after seeing outcomes
Guarantee that the study will find a significant result
Replace the need to collect data carefully
questions.explanation: Pre-registration makes planned analyses transparent and helps distinguish confirmatory from exploratory work.

questions.text: For a time series, why should evaluation often use a chronological split rather than a random split?
options: Random splitting can train on future observations relative to the test period
Chronological splits always produce equal class counts
Random splitting changes the units of time
questions.explanation: A temporal split better mimics forecasting from past data into the future.

questions.text: What does a primary key identify?
options: A row uniquely within a table
questions.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies each table row.

questions.text: What is a database schema?
options: A definition of the database's structure, such as tables and columns
A copy of every user password
A chart of query execution time
questions.explanation: A schema describes how database data is organized and constrained.

questions.text: What does a foreign key commonly reference?
options: A key in another table, enforcing a relationship
questions.explanation: A foreign key links values to a referenced key and can enforce referential integrity.

questions.text: In a relational database, what does NULL generally represent?
options: The number zero in every data type
An empty string in every database
questions.explanation: NULL denotes an absent or unknown value and is distinct from zero or an empty string.

questions.text: What does a database transaction group together?
options: Operations treated as one logical unit of work
A set of unrelated user accounts
questions.explanation: A transaction groups related operations so the database can apply defined transaction behavior.

questions.text: What is a common benefit of a database index?
questions.explanation: Indexes speed up lookups but require storage and maintenance on writes.

questions.text: What is the main goal of normalizing relational tables?
options: Reduce undesirable redundancy and update anomalies
Make every query use more joins
Guarantee that no index is needed
questions.explanation: Normalization organizes dependencies to limit duplication and modification anomalies.

questions.text: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do for a foreign-key relationship?
options: Deletes referencing rows when the referenced row is deleted
Copies the deleted row into every table
Prevents all deletions in the database
questions.explanation: CASCADE propagates the referenced-row deletion to dependent rows.

questions.text: What is a database view in the common relational sense?
options: A named query that presents data as a virtual table
A physical backup of the server screen
A command that permanently sorts a table
A lock that prevents all reads
questions.explanation: A view exposes a query result through a reusable virtual-table interface.

questions.text: Why might a database administrator create a composite index on (customer_id, created_at)?
options: To support queries filtering or ordering by the leading customer_id key and possibly created_at
To guarantee faster inserts for every table
To enforce that created_at is unique globally
To compress every value into one column
questions.explanation: Composite-index usefulness depends on its column order and query predicates.

questions.text: In a relational database, what does a CHECK constraint enforce?
options: A Boolean condition on inserted or updated row values
That a table is always stored in memory
That a query returns a fixed number of rows
That every column has a foreign key
questions.explanation: A CHECK constraint rejects row values that do not satisfy its condition.

questions.text: Which isolation level generally permits nonrepeatable reads but prevents dirty reads?
questions.explanation: Read committed prevents reading uncommitted changes but may observe later committed updates.

questions.text: What does a materialized view typically store compared with a regular view?
options: A persisted result that must be refreshed to reflect source changes
Only the SQL text and no query definition
A copy of the database's transaction log
A list of client IP addresses
questions.explanation: Materialized views store query results and can become stale until refreshed.

questions.text: What is a common tradeoff of adding an index to a table?
options: Reads may improve, while storage and write-maintenance costs increase
Writes become free and storage decreases
The table no longer needs constraints
questions.explanation: Indexes can accelerate lookups but consume space and must be maintained on data changes.

questions.text: Why is a connection pool used by many database applications?
options: Reuse a limited set of database connections instead of opening one per operation
Allow a single connection to belong to two transactions at once
questions.explanation: Pooling reduces connection setup overhead and controls concurrent connection usage.

questions.text: In ACID transactions, atomicity means:
options: All transaction changes happen or none do
questions.explanation: Atomicity makes a transaction an all-or-nothing unit.

questions.text: How can a database detect a deadlock involving transactions that hold locks while waiting for each other?
options: Build a wait-for graph and identify a cycle
Count the number of columns in each transaction
questions.explanation: A cycle in a wait-for graph indicates transactions are mutually blocked.

questions.text: What does multi-version concurrency control commonly allow a database to do?
options: Let readers observe a consistent version while writers create newer versions
Eliminate the need to store transaction metadata
Guarantee every transaction runs serially on one CPU
Convert every isolation level to read uncommitted
questions.explanation: MVCC maintains versions so reads can proceed against an appropriate snapshot.

questions.text: In a write-ahead logging system, what must generally happen before a changed data page is written to disk?
options: The log record describing the change is made durable first
The entire database is exported to CSV
Every index is dropped and rebuilt
The client acknowledges a query it never sent
questions.explanation: WAL requires the relevant log record to reach durable storage before the data page.

questions.text: What anomaly does serializable isolation aim to prevent beyond ordinary repeatable reads in systems that use predicate locking?
options: Phantom rows from a repeated predicate query
A client sending a malformed SQL keyword
A table having two different indexes
questions.explanation: Serializable execution prevents interleavings such as new rows appearing within a previously read predicate.

questions.text: Why can a covering index improve a query?
options: The index contains all columns needed by the query, avoiding a table-row lookup
It removes the need for a query predicate
It makes every update atomic across databases
It converts a heap table into a view
questions.explanation: A covering index can satisfy a query directly from index entries.

questions.text: What is a key concern when a distributed database uses synchronous replication for commits?
options: Commit latency can include waiting for replicas to acknowledge durable writes
It always allows writes during every network partition
It makes replica data immediately independent
It removes the need for conflict handling
questions.explanation: Synchronous acknowledgment improves durability guarantees but adds replica round-trip latency.

questions.text: What does a database checkpoint generally accomplish?
options: Flushes or marks a bounded set of changes so recovery need not replay the entire log
Makes every query result permanently cached
questions.explanation: Checkpoints establish a recovery point that limits how much log must be replayed.

questions.text: Why might a query planner choose a sequential scan even when an index exists?
options: The predicate matches a large share of rows, making a table scan cheaper
An index always prevents reading table pages
The SQL contains a SELECT keyword
The table has a primary key
questions.explanation: For low selectivity, sequentially reading the table can cost less than many index lookups.

questions.text: What does a transaction's write skew anomaly involve?
options: Concurrent transactions read overlapping state and make disjoint writes that jointly violate an invariant
One transaction writes the same byte twice
A query returns rows in an unexpected sort order
A backup contains fewer indexes than its source
questions.explanation: Write skew can occur when each transaction's writes do not conflict despite violating a cross-row constraint together.

questions.text: How does a B-tree index support ordered range queries?
options: Its balanced search structure keeps keys ordered and permits traversal across a key interval
It hashes all values so neighboring keys are adjacent
It stores only the first row of each table
It sorts data only when the database shuts down
questions.explanation: B-tree key order supports efficient seeks and scans across ranges.

questions.text: What is the purpose of two-phase commit in a distributed transaction?
options: Coordinate participants so they prepare and then commit or abort together
Split every row into exactly two columns
Replicate each query to only two clients
Guarantee that a network never partitions
questions.explanation: Two-phase commit coordinates a prepare decision followed by a shared commit or abort outcome.

questions.text: What does a database's redo log support after a crash?
options: Reapply logged changes that should be durable but were not yet reflected in data pages
Reconstruct SQL comments from query plans
questions.explanation: Redo applies durable logged operations during recovery.

questions.text: Why can a long-running transaction cause problems for an MVCC database?
options: It may prevent old row versions from being reclaimed
It guarantees a deadlock on commit
questions.explanation: Long snapshots can keep obsolete versions visible and delay vacuum or garbage collection.

questions.text: In a distributed database, what does quorum replication require in a common read/write protocol?
options: Operations contact enough replicas to satisfy configured read and write quorums
Every operation reaches every replica synchronously
A primary key is generated by each client
The database has exactly three nodes
questions.explanation: Quorum thresholds govern how many replica responses are needed for reads and writes.

questions.text: MongoDB stores records primarily as which format?
questions.explanation: MongoDB stores BSON documents in collections.

questions.text: In MongoDB, what is a collection most similar to in a relational database?
questions.explanation: A collection groups documents and is broadly analogous to a relational table.

questions.text: Which field is automatically present as a unique identifier in a MongoDB document when one is not supplied?
questions.explanation: MongoDB assigns an _id value to documents that do not provide one.

questions.text: Which MongoDB query operator matches a field equal to one specified value?
questions.explanation: $eq explicitly matches values equal to its operand.

questions.text: What does the MongoDB shell command show dbs display?
options: Databases visible to the current connection
All indexes in the current collection
questions.explanation: show dbs lists databases available to the connected MongoDB deployment.

questions.text: Which MongoDB operation adds a document to a collection?
questions.explanation: insertOne inserts a single document into a collection.

questions.text: What does a projection in a MongoDB find query control?
options: Which fields are returned for each matched document
Whether BSON is converted to SQL
questions.explanation: A projection includes or excludes fields from returned documents.

questions.text: Which aggregation stage groups documents and can compute values such as a count?
questions.explanation: $group collects documents by an _id expression and can calculate accumulators.

questions.text: What does the $unwind aggregation stage do to an array field?
options: Outputs a document for each array element
Converts every element to an index
questions.explanation: $unwind deconstructs an array field into separate pipeline documents.

questions.text: What is the role of a MongoDB validator configured for a collection?
options: Reject or warn on inserts and updates that do not meet its document rules
Encrypt all stored documents with a client password
Choose a replica set's primary node
questions.explanation: Collection validation checks documents against configured rules, often using JSON Schema.

questions.text: What does the $set update operator do?
options: Sets specified field values, creating fields when needed
questions.explanation: $set assigns values to specified fields in matching documents.

questions.text: What is a capped collection designed to do?
options: Maintain a fixed-size collection that preserves insertion order and overwrites older data when full
Reject every insert after its first document
Store only documents with a numeric _id
questions.explanation: Capped collections have fixed capacity and overwrite oldest entries when space is needed.

questions.text: What does the $in query operator match?
options: A field whose value equals any value in a specified array
A field that contains every value in an array
Only fields whose type is an array
questions.explanation: $in matches a field against any listed candidate value.

questions.text: When does a MongoDB TTL index remove an expired document?
options: Asynchronously, after the background TTL monitor processes it
Immediately within the same insert operation
Only when a client runs deleteMany
questions.explanation: TTL deletion is performed by a background process and is not exact to the expiration instant.

questions.text: What is the purpose of the $match stage near the start of an aggregation pipeline?
options: Filter documents passing into later stages
Join every document to all collections
questions.explanation: $match selects documents that satisfy a query predicate.

questions.text: Which SQL command reads rows from a table?
questions.explanation: SELECT retrieves data from one or more tables.

questions.text: Which SQL statement creates a new table definition?
questions.explanation: CREATE TABLE defines a table and its columns.

questions.text: Which SQL clause sorts returned rows by a column?
questions.explanation: ORDER BY specifies the ordering of result rows.

questions.text: Which SQL command adds a row to a table?
questions.explanation: INSERT adds one or more rows to a table.

questions.text: What does the SQL keyword DISTINCT do in a query result?
options: Deletes duplicate rows from the source table
questions.explanation: SELECT DISTINCT returns unique rows for the selected expressions.

questions.text: Which clause filters rows before grouping?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters source rows before grouping and aggregation.

questions.text: Which SQL clause filters groups after aggregate calculations?
questions.explanation: HAVING filters grouped results, commonly using aggregate expressions.

questions.text: What does COUNT(*) count in a SQL query?
options: Rows in the result group, including rows with NULL columns
Only rows where every column is non-NULL
Distinct values in the first column
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of whether individual fields contain NULL.

questions.text: How does SQL's UNION operator treat duplicate rows by default?
options: It sorts only the first query
It rejects results with matching values
questions.explanation: UNION eliminates duplicate result rows; UNION ALL preserves them.

questions.text: Which SQL expression replaces a NULL value with a fallback value in many SQL dialects?
questions.explanation: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL expression from its arguments.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a common table expression introduced with WITH?
options: Name a query result for use within the following statement
Persist a new table after the query ends
Create an index on every referenced column
Lock all rows in the database
questions.explanation: A CTE names a temporary result set scoped to one statement.

questions.text: Which constraint prevents duplicate values in a SQL column or column combination?
questions.explanation: A UNIQUE constraint disallows duplicate key values under the database's NULL rules.

questions.text: What does the CASE expression provide in a SQL SELECT list?
options: A way to create a new database
A lock on the current row
questions.explanation: CASE returns a value based on the first matching WHEN condition.

questions.text: What does an INNER JOIN return when rows are matched using its join condition?
options: Only row combinations satisfying the condition
All left rows regardless of a match
All right rows regardless of a match
Only rows with NULL join keys
questions.explanation: An inner join returns combinations for which the join predicate is true.

questions.text: In SQL three-valued logic, what is the result of NULL = 5?
options: A syntax error in every SQL dialect
questions.explanation: Comparisons involving NULL generally evaluate to UNKNOWN; use IS NULL to test nullness.

questions.text: What does a LEFT JOIN preserve from its left input?
options: All left-side rows, with matching right-side values when available
Only rows that match on both sides
questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every left row and fills unmatched right columns with nulls.

questions.text: What does ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) assign?
options: A sequential rank within each department, with ties receiving different numbers
A shared rank for equal salaries across all departments
A count of rows in the entire table
A persistent primary key stored in the table
questions.explanation: ROW_NUMBER assigns consecutive values within each partition using the specified order.

questions.text: In a window frame, what does ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW include?
options: The current row and up to two preceding physical rows in the window order
Every row with a value within two units
The current row and two following rows
Exactly two rows from the entire query
questions.explanation: ROWS defines the frame by row positions relative to the current row.

questions.text: Why can NOT IN (subquery) produce unexpected results if the subquery returns NULL?
options: Three-valued logic can make the predicate UNKNOWN for otherwise unmatched values
NULL values are automatically converted to zero
NOT IN always ignores all subquery rows
The query is parsed as an outer join
questions.explanation: A NULL in the set can make comparisons unknown; NOT EXISTS is often safer for anti-joins.

questions.text: What does a recursive common table expression typically require to terminate?
options: A base case and a recursive step that eventually produces no further rows
A unique index on every output column
A COMMIT after each recursive level
An ORDER BY in the base case
questions.explanation: Recursion stops when the recursive member produces no additional rows or a limit is reached.

questions.text: What is the key difference between RANK() and DENSE_RANK() for tied values?
options: RANK leaves gaps after ties, while DENSE_RANK does not
DENSE_RANK assigns a unique number to every row
RANK ignores ORDER BY while DENSE_RANK requires it
They differ only in how NULL is stored
questions.explanation: RANK skips rank numbers after peer groups; DENSE_RANK assigns consecutive group ranks.

questions.text: In SQL, why is placing a predicate on the nullable side of a LEFT JOIN in WHERE sometimes equivalent to an inner join?
options: The WHERE predicate can reject the NULL-extended unmatched rows
WHERE executes before the join in every query
LEFT JOIN ignores predicates on the right table
The predicate converts NULL into a matching value
questions.explanation: A WHERE condition that is not true for NULL-extended rows removes those rows.

questions.text: What does a deferred constraint allow a transaction to do?
options: Delay checking the constraint until a later point, often transaction commit
Change a foreign key into an index
questions.explanation: Deferrable constraints can postpone validation until the configured check time.

questions.text: What does a covering index provide to a query plan?
options: All required columns from the index so base-table access may be avoided
A guarantee that the query uses no predicates
A way to serialize concurrent transactions
A copy of the result saved permanently
questions.explanation: If index entries contain every needed value, the engine may satisfy the query without fetching table rows.

questions.text: Why can an expression such as WHERE DATE(created_at) = DATE '2026-01-01' prevent use of a plain index on created_at in some databases?
options: Applying a function to the indexed column may not match the index's stored key order
DATE is not a valid SQL type
The equality operator cannot compare dates
Indexes are never usable in WHERE clauses
questions.explanation: A function on the column may require a matching expression index or a range predicate on the raw column.

questions.text: What is the usual purpose of SAVEPOINT within a SQL transaction?
options: Mark a point to which part of the transaction can be rolled back
Create a backup of every database file
questions.explanation: A savepoint permits a partial rollback while keeping the transaction active.

questions.text: What does a correlated subquery do that an independent subquery does not?
options: References a value from the current row of its outer query
Runs only before the outer query begins
questions.explanation: A correlated subquery depends on columns from the outer query.

questions.text: When a query uses GROUPING SETS, what does the feature provide?
options: Multiple grouping levels in one grouped query result
A guarantee that all groups have the same number of rows
A way to update groups concurrently
A substitute for every aggregate function
questions.explanation: GROUPING SETS computes several specified groupings in one query.

questions.text: What is a likely effect of using SELECT FOR UPDATE in a transaction?
options: Lock selected rows against conflicting updates until the transaction ends
Permanently mark the rows as read-only
Create a unique index for the selected columns
Return only rows modified by another session
questions.explanation: FOR UPDATE commonly obtains row locks to coordinate concurrent modifications.

questions.text: Why can an anti-join written with NOT EXISTS be more robust than NOT IN when nullable values are possible?
options: NOT EXISTS tests for matching rows without NULL poisoning the predicate
NOT EXISTS always forces a hash join
NOT IN cannot compare non-null integers
NOT EXISTS changes the transaction isolation level
questions.explanation: NOT EXISTS checks whether a matching row exists; a NULL elsewhere does not make it unknown.

questions.text: What does multi-factor authentication require?
options: More than one type of proof of identity
Two copies of the same password
questions.explanation: MFA combines different factor types such as knowledge and possession.

questions.text: What does the principle of least privilege recommend?
options: Give each user only the access needed for their task
Share one account among a whole team
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits the impact of mistakes or compromised accounts.

questions.text: Why should software security updates be installed promptly?
options: They can fix known vulnerabilities attackers may exploit
They guarantee a device cannot be infected
They replace the need for backups
questions.explanation: Updates often patch publicly known weaknesses that otherwise remain exploitable.

questions.text: What does HTTPS help protect while data travels between a browser and website?
options: Confidentiality and integrity of the connection, with server authentication
The website from every coding flaw
The user's files from hardware failure
The accuracy of every page's claims
questions.explanation: TLS in HTTPS encrypts and authenticates data in transit and authenticates the server.

questions.text: What is a firewall commonly used to do?
options: Allow or block network traffic according to rules
Generate secure passwords for every user
Prove an email's sender is honest
questions.explanation: Firewalls enforce traffic policies between networks or hosts.

questions.text: A message that tricks someone into revealing a password is an example of:
questions.explanation: Phishing uses deceptive messages to steal information or trigger unsafe actions.

questions.text: What is a common defense against SQL injection in an application?
options: Use parameterized queries for untrusted values
Hide the database hostname in a CSS file
Reject every request containing a digit
Escape output only after executing the query
questions.explanation: Prepared statements keep input data separate from SQL syntax.

questions.text: What does a secure, HttpOnly cookie attribute help prevent?
options: Client-side scripts from reading the cookie value
The cookie from being sent over HTTPS
The server from setting an expiration
The browser from storing any cookie
questions.explanation: HttpOnly prevents access through script APIs such as document.cookie.

questions.text: Why should an application verify a TLS certificate chain?
options: To authenticate that the peer's certificate chains to a trusted issuer for the intended name
To measure the server's disk capacity
To check that every response is malware-free
To decrypt user passwords at rest
questions.explanation: Certificate validation helps ensure the client is communicating with the intended authenticated server.

questions.text: What is the security purpose of a cryptographic nonce in a protocol?
options: Help ensure freshness and prevent reuse of an old message in the intended context
Make the message shorter than its plaintext
Allow the same ciphertext to be safely replayed
questions.explanation: A nonce can bind a message to a unique session or operation and help detect replay.

questions.text: What should a system do with an unexpected authentication failure message in logs?
options: Record useful context without logging secrets such as passwords or tokens
Log the full submitted password for debugging
Disable the audit log to protect privacy
Store authentication tokens in a public dashboard
questions.explanation: Logs should aid detection while minimizing exposure of credentials and sensitive data.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of a backup that is isolated from ordinary administrator credentials?
options: Reduce the chance that ransomware or an intruder can alter both production data and its recovery copy
Speed up every live database query
Allow backups to be downloaded anonymously
questions.explanation: Isolated or immutable backups are harder for an attacker to destroy along with production systems.

questions.text: What does a digital signature verify when checked with the signer's trusted public key?
options: The signed data's integrity and that it was signed by the corresponding private key
That the data is confidential to every recipient
That the signer is legally trustworthy
That the signed software contains no vulnerabilities
questions.explanation: A valid signature authenticates the signing key and detects changes to the signed data.

questions.text: Why should an organization revoke a compromised API key?
options: To stop that credential from authorizing future requests
To delete every public copy of the API documentation
To rotate the database's primary key automatically
To make requests use a weaker cipher
questions.explanation: Revocation invalidates a credential known or suspected to be exposed.

questions.text: What does a vulnerability scanner generally identify?
options: Potential known weaknesses or misconfigurations that need investigation
Every possible future attack with certainty
The business impact of a flaw without human review
questions.explanation: Scanners detect indicators of known issues but findings need validation and prioritization.

questions.text: Why add a unique salt before hashing each password?
options: To make precomputed hash attacks less reusable
To send the password to the browser
To guarantee the hash is short
questions.explanation: Unique salts prevent identical passwords from producing identical stored hashes and frustrate rainbow tables.

questions.text: In STRIDE threat modeling, which threat category describes an attacker pretending to be another user or system?
questions.explanation: Spoofing is impersonation of an identity.

questions.text: A web server fetches URLs supplied by users. Which control most directly reduces server-side request forgery risk?
options: Allowlist destinations and block access to internal or metadata address ranges
Trust every URL that uses HTTPS
Escape HTML characters in the URL
questions.explanation: Strict destination validation and network egress restrictions limit requests to sensitive internal services.

questions.text: Why does a synchronizer-token defense help protect a state-changing web request from CSRF?
options: An attacker on another site cannot normally read the unpredictable token tied to the user's session
It encrypts the whole browser memory
It prevents the user from opening multiple tabs
questions.explanation: A secret unpredictable token required by the server is difficult for a cross-site attacker to obtain.

questions.text: What security property does mutual TLS add compared with ordinary server-authenticated TLS?
options: The server also authenticates a client certificate
All application data becomes end-to-end encrypted beyond the server
Every request is signed by the browser vendor
Certificate validation is no longer required
questions.explanation: In mutual TLS, both parties present certificates to authenticate each other.

questions.text: A password database is exposed. Why is a memory-hard password hashing function such as Argon2id preferable to a fast general-purpose hash?
options: It makes large-scale password guessing more costly in time and memory
It allows the server to recover the original password
It eliminates the need for per-password salts
It prevents users from choosing weak passwords
questions.explanation: Memory-hard password hashing raises the resource cost of offline guessing.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a Content Security Policy nonce on an inline script?
options: Authorize specifically marked script elements while blocking unapproved inline scripts
Encrypt the script source before the browser parses it
Grant the script database administrator privileges
Prevent all external stylesheets from loading
questions.explanation: A unpredictable per-response nonce can allow trusted scripts under a restrictive CSP.

questions.text: Why should a high-risk service check authorization on every object access rather than relying only on a user's role at login?
options: A valid role does not prove that the user may access each specific object
Roles are always stored in the browser
Login credentials expire before every object request
questions.explanation: Object-level authorization prevents insecure direct-object references and cross-tenant access.

questions.text: During incident response, what is a sound reason to preserve a forensic image before rebuilding a compromised host?
options: Preserve evidence and volatile investigation context needed to determine scope and cause
Guarantee that the attacker cannot access any other host
Make the host's software patches install faster
questions.explanation: Evidence preservation supports investigation before remediation changes the system state.

questions.text: What is the main advantage of using a hardware-backed key store for a sensitive signing key?
options: The private key can remain non-exportable while cryptographic operations occur in protected hardware
The key becomes public and easier to rotate
The key no longer needs access control
The application can recover the key from source code
questions.explanation: Hardware protection can prevent extraction of private key material and constrain its use.

questions.text: How does certificate pinning differ from ordinary public-key infrastructure validation?
options: It additionally restricts accepted certificates or keys to an expected set
It accepts any self-signed certificate without checks
It removes expiration dates from certificates
It verifies only the HTTP response body
questions.explanation: Pinning narrows trust to expected keys or certificates, though it requires careful rotation planning.

questions.text: A vulnerability has no available patch and is actively exploited. What is a useful immediate risk-reduction measure?
options: Apply a tested compensating control such as disabling the exposed feature or restricting access
Ignore it until the next annual audit
Publish the system's credentials to warn users
Remove all monitoring to prevent false alarms
questions.explanation: A compensating control can reduce exposure while a safe permanent fix is prepared.

questions.text: What does a replay attack exploit in a protocol that accepts a previously valid authenticated message?
options: The receiver fails to distinguish a repeated message from a fresh one
The message uses a valid encryption algorithm
The client sends the message over a reliable transport
questions.explanation: Freshness checks such as nonces or sequence numbers help reject previously captured messages.

questions.text: Why should a security-sensitive random token come from a cryptographically secure random number generator?
options: Unpredictability prevents attackers from feasibly guessing valid tokens
It guarantees the token is unique across all possible systems
It compresses the token before storage
questions.explanation: CSPRNG output is designed to be computationally unpredictable to an attacker.

questions.text: What is the security benefit of separating a build pipeline's signing credentials from its ordinary source-code repository?
options: A repository compromise alone is less likely to expose credentials that can sign trusted releases
The source code no longer needs review
The build becomes immune to malicious dependencies
Every build artifact is automatically reproducible
questions.explanation: Separating secrets and using constrained signing access limits what a source repository compromise can authorize.

questions.text: Which cloud service is commonly used to store files as objects?
questions.explanation: Object storage stores data objects with metadata in scalable buckets or containers.

questions.text: What does a cloud region usually represent?
options: A geographic area containing data centers
questions.explanation: Regions group cloud infrastructure in a geographic area.

questions.text: Which service model provides virtual machines for customers to manage?
questions.explanation: Infrastructure as a Service offers managed underlying compute resources.

questions.text: What is a cloud availability zone?
options: An isolated location within a region
questions.explanation: Zones are distinct locations designed to limit shared failures.

questions.text: Which cloud resource runs code in response to an event without managing servers?
questions.explanation: Serverless functions execute event-triggered code on provider-managed infrastructure.

questions.text: Autoscaling primarily adjusts capacity in response to:
questions.explanation: Autoscaling adds or removes resources as measured demand changes.

questions.text: A service needs persistent storage attached to one virtual machine. Which option fits best?
questions.explanation: Block storage presents persistent disk volumes to compute instances.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of a cloud load balancer?
options: Distribute incoming traffic among healthy targets
questions.explanation: Load balancers route traffic across targets to improve availability and capacity.

questions.text: Which practice best limits the blast radius of a compromised cloud credential?
questions.explanation: Least privilege restricts what a stolen credential can access.

questions.text: A team wants users worldwide to receive cached static images quickly. What should it use?
questions.explanation: A CDN caches content near users at distributed edge locations.

questions.text: What does infrastructure as code primarily enable?
options: Automatic removal of all security controls
Replacing application tests with billing reports
questions.explanation: IaC defines and provisions infrastructure consistently through code.

questions.text: Which cost model charges for measured resource consumption rather than fixed capacity?
questions.explanation: Usage-based billing ties charges to measured consumption.

questions.text: Why use a managed database service?
options: The provider handles tasks such as patching and backups
It guarantees every query is free
It removes the need to design a schema
It makes all data publicly accessible
questions.explanation: Managed services reduce operational work, though customers retain configuration responsibilities.

questions.text: An application must keep data available after a single zone outage. What design helps most?
options: Store the only copy on one instance
Use a larger instance in one zone
questions.explanation: Cross-zone redundancy avoids dependence on one failure domain.

questions.text: What does a private cloud typically mean?
options: Cloud infrastructure dedicated to one organization
Any cloud account with a private password
A public website with no advertisements
questions.explanation: A private cloud's resources are dedicated to a single organization.

questions.text: Why deploy a critical service across multiple availability zones?
options: To reduce the impact of a single-zone failure
To remove the need for backups
questions.explanation: Separate zones reduce correlated infrastructure failure risk within a region.

questions.text: A stateless service scales horizontally behind a load balancer. Where should session state usually go?
questions.explanation: External shared state remains accessible when requests reach different instances.

questions.text: A workload needs low-latency reads globally but accepts brief replication lag. Which design is appropriate?
options: Regional read replicas with asynchronous replication
One synchronous database in a distant region
A single local disk per client
questions.explanation: Asynchronous regional replicas improve read locality while allowing replication lag.

questions.text: Which metric best supports rightsizing a compute instance for a consistently CPU-bound workload?
questions.explanation: CPU utilization alongside delivered throughput reveals compute sizing needs.

questions.text: A company must recover from regional loss with an RTO of minutes. Which strategy best fits?
options: Maintain a tested warm standby in another region
Restore from monthly offline tapes only
Keep an untested copy in the same zone
Rely on DNS caching to recreate data
questions.explanation: A warm standby can be promoted quickly, unlike a cold restore.

questions.text: What is the key security benefit of a private endpoint to a cloud service?
options: Traffic can stay off the public internet
The endpoint removes the need for identity checks
It guarantees protection from compromised clients
questions.explanation: Private endpoints route service access through private network connectivity.

questions.text: A containerized service has variable demand and must start quickly. Which scaling signal is most useful?
questions.explanation: Queue depth or concurrency directly reflects pending service demand.

questions.text: How does a cloud control plane differ from a data plane?
options: It configures resources; the data plane carries workload traffic
It stores backups; the data plane creates accounts
It bills users; the data plane edits source code
It encrypts disks; the data plane grants policies
questions.explanation: Control-plane APIs manage configuration while data-plane paths handle actual workloads.

questions.text: Which approach best protects encryption keys from being embedded in application code?
options: Use a managed key service with scoped access
Store keys in a public source repository
questions.explanation: Managed key services centralize protected key custody and access policies.

questions.text: A cloud service's autoscaler reacts too slowly to sharp bursts. What change most directly reduces delay?
options: Use predictive scaling or maintain a warm capacity buffer
Move all services into one subnet
questions.explanation: Prediction or spare warm capacity can meet bursts before reactive scaling finishes.

questions.text: Which technique reduces egress cost when multiple services repeatedly consume the same large dataset?
options: Keep consumers and data in the same region
Copy the dataset to every client device
questions.explanation: Co-locating data and consumers can avoid inter-region transfer charges.

questions.text: What is a major trade-off of active-active multi-region application deployment?
options: Higher resilience but more complex consistency and operations
questions.explanation: Active-active improves availability while complicating state consistency and operations.

questions.text: In a shared-responsibility model, who normally secures cloud account identities and permissions?
questions.explanation: Customers remain responsible for their identities, access policies, and configurations.

questions.text: A database must meet a point-in-time recovery objective. Which feature is essential?
options: Continuous transaction-log or change capture retention
A weekly screenshot of the dashboard
questions.explanation: Retained logs or changes allow restoration to a specific time.

questions.text: How can immutable infrastructure reduce configuration drift?
options: Replace instances from versioned images instead of changing them in place
Permit ad hoc edits on every server
questions.explanation: Recreating systems from controlled images avoids accumulated manual changes.

questions.text: What is 18 + 27?
questions.explanation: Adding tens and ones gives 18 + 27 = 45.

questions.text: What is 56 minus 19?
What is 8 multiplied by 7?
questions.explanation: Eight groups of seven make 56.

questions.text: What is 3.6 plus 2.45?
questions.explanation: Aligning decimal places gives 3.60 + 2.45 = 6.05.

questions.text: What is 42 divided by 6?
questions.explanation: Since 6 × 7 = 42, the quotient is 7.

questions.text: What is 3/4 of 64?
questions.explanation: One quarter of 64 is 16, and three quarters is 48.

questions.text: What is 35% of 240?
Evaluate 18 ÷ 3 + 4 × 2 using order of operations.
questions.explanation: Division and multiplication first give 6 + 8 = 14.

questions.text: What is the least common multiple of 12 and 18?
questions.explanation: 36 is the smallest positive number divisible by both 12 and 18.

questions.text: A 2.4 kg bag is divided equally into 8 portions. How many grams is each portion?
Simplify the ratio 42:56.
questions.explanation: Dividing both terms by 14 gives 3:4.

questions.text: A jacket costs $120 before a 25% discount. What is its sale price?
questions.explanation: The discount is $30, leaving $120 − $30 = $90.

questions.text: What is 5/6 − 1/4?
questions.explanation: With denominator 12, 10/12 − 3/12 = 7/12.

questions.text: A car travels 150 km in 2.5 hours. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Average speed is 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h.

questions.text: Round 18.746 to the nearest hundredth.
questions.explanation: The thousandths digit is 6, so the hundredths digit rounds up.

questions.text: A price of $80 is discounted by 15%. What is the sale price?
questions.explanation: Fifteen percent of $80 is $12, so the sale price is $68.

questions.text: Evaluate 3/5 ÷ 9/10.
questions.explanation: Divide by multiplying by the reciprocal: 3/5 × 10/9 = 2/3.

questions.text: A value rises from 80 to 100, then falls by 20%. What is the final value?
questions.explanation: The increase gives 100; a 20% decrease leaves 80% of it, or 80.

questions.text: A mixture has 3 parts concentrate to 7 parts water. How much concentrate is in 2.5 L of mixture?
questions.explanation: Concentrate is 3/10 of the mixture: 3/10 × 2.5 = 0.75 L.

questions.text: What is the remainder when 1,347 is divided by 11?
questions.explanation: 11 × 122 = 1,342, leaving remainder 5.

questions.text: A price includes 8% tax and totals $216. What was the pre-tax price?
questions.explanation: The total is 1.08 times the original; 216 ÷ 1.08 = 200.

questions.text: Compute 2.5 × 0.048.
questions.explanation: 25 × 48 = 1,200 with four decimal places, giving 0.120.

questions.text: What is the greatest common divisor of 252 and 198?
questions.explanation: The Euclidean algorithm gives gcd(252,198) = gcd(198,54) = 18.

questions.text: A worker completes 3/8 of a task per day. How many days are needed for 1 1/2 tasks?
If 40% of a number is 86, what is the number?
A tank is 5/8 full. After adding 18 L it is 7/8 full. What is the tank's capacity?
questions.explanation: 18 L represents 2/8 = 1/4 of capacity, so capacity is 72 L.

questions.text: What is 17² − 13²?
questions.explanation: Use the difference of squares: (17 − 13)(17 + 13) = 4 × 30 = 120.

questions.text: A recipe for 8 uses 350 g of flour. How much flour is needed for 14 servings?
What is the smallest positive integer divisible by 15, 20, and 28?
questions.explanation: Their least common multiple is 2² × 3 × 5 × 7 = 420.

questions.text: Solve x + 7 = 12.
questions.explanation: Subtract 7 from both sides to get x = 5.

questions.text: If a = 3, what is 4a + 2?
questions.explanation: Substitute 3: 4(3) + 2 = 14.

questions.text: Simplify 6x + 2x.

questions.explanation: Distribute 3 to get 3n + 15.

questions.explanation: Subtract 3 and divide by 5 to obtain x = 5.

questions.text: Factor x² + 7x + 12.

questions.explanation: When multiplying powers with the same base, add exponents.

questions.explanation: 2x − 8 = 3x + 1 leads to x = −9.

questions.explanation: Slope-intercept form is y = mx + b.

questions.text: Solve x² = 49 over the real numbers.
questions.explanation: Both 7 and −7 square to 49.

questions.text: What are the roots of x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0?
questions.explanation: The quadratic factors as (x - 2)(x - 3).

questions.text: Solve 2x² − 5x − 3 = 0.
questions.explanation: Factor as (2x + 1)(x − 3) = 0.

questions.text: Find the vertex of y = x² − 6x + 11.
questions.explanation: The vertex x-coordinate is 6/2 = 3; substituting gives y = 2.

questions.text: For what x-value is the denominator of (x + 1)/(x² − 9) zero?
questions.explanation: x² − 9 factors to (x − 3)(x + 3).

questions.text: A geometric sequence has first term 5 and ratio 3. What is its sixth term?
questions.explanation: The sixth term is 5 × 3⁵ = 1,215.

questions.text: If f(x)=x² and g(x)=2x−1, what is f(g(2))?
Solve |2x − 5| = 7.
questions.explanation: Set 2x−5 equal to 7 and −7, yielding 6 and −1.

questions.text: What is the discriminant of 2x² + 3x + 5 = 0?
Solve the system 2x + 3y = 13 and x − y = 1.
questions.explanation: Substitute x=y+1: 2y+2+3y=13, so y=3 and x=4.

questions.text: Simplify (x² − 9)/(x − 3), for x ≠ 3.
questions.explanation: Factor the numerator as (x−3)(x+3) and cancel x−3.

questions.text: A quantity grows by 6% annually from 500. Which expression gives its value after t years?
questions.explanation: Compound growth multiplies the initial value by 1.06 for each year.

questions.text: Find the inverse of f(x)=3x−8.
questions.explanation: Set y=3x−8, swap variables, and solve x=(y+8)/3.

questions.text: What is the remainder when x³ + 2x² − x + 4 is divided by x − 2?
questions.explanation: The remainder theorem gives f(2)=8+8−2+4=18.

questions.text: For x² + kx + 16 to have equal real roots, what value can k take?
questions.explanation: Equal roots require discriminant k²−64=0, so k=±8.

questions.text: How many sides does a hexagon have?
questions.explanation: A hexagon has six sides.

questions.text: How many degrees are in a right angle?
questions.explanation: A right angle measures exactly 90 degrees.

questions.text: What is the perimeter of a rectangle 7 cm long and 3 cm wide?
questions.explanation: Perimeter is 2(7 + 3) = 20 cm.

questions.text: How many vertices does a triangular prism have?
questions.explanation: It has two triangular ends with three vertices each.

questions.text: Two angles of a triangle are 50° and 60°. What is the third angle?
questions.explanation: Triangle angles sum to 180°, leaving 70°.

questions.text: What is the area of a triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm?
questions.explanation: Triangle area is one half times base times height: 30 cm2.

questions.text: A right triangle has legs 9 and 12. What is its hypotenuse?
questions.explanation: By Pythagoras, √(9²+12²)=√225=15.

questions.text: What is the area of a circle with diameter 10?
questions.explanation: The radius is 5, so area is πr² = 25π.

questions.text: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 30°. How many sides does it have?
questions.explanation: Exterior angles total 360°, and 360 ÷ 30 = 12.

questions.text: A parallelogram has base 13 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area is base times perpendicular height: 13 × 6 = 78 cm².

questions.text: What is the distance between points (1, 2) and (4, 6)?
An isosceles triangle has vertex angle 40°. What is each base angle?
questions.explanation: The remaining 140° is split equally between the base angles.

questions.text: What is the volume of a rectangular prism measuring 4 by 5 by 8 cm?
questions.explanation: Volume is length × width × height: 4 × 5 × 8 = 160 cm³.

questions.text: A scale drawing uses 1 cm for 5 m. How long should a 20 m wall appear?
questions.explanation: At 5 m per centimeter, 20 m corresponds to 4 cm.

questions.text: What is the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon?
questions.explanation: For six sides, the sum is (6−2) × 180° = 720°.

questions.text: A circle has radius 5. What is its circumference?
questions.explanation: Circumference equals 2 pi r, so it is 10 pi.

questions.text: A chord is 5 units from a circle's center; the radius is 13. What is the chord length?
questions.explanation: The perpendicular bisects the chord: half-length is √(13²−5²)=12.

questions.text: What is the area of a sector with radius 6 and central angle 120°?
questions.explanation: The sector is one third of π(6²), giving 12π.

questions.text: A cone has radius 3 and height 4. What is its volume?

questions.explanation: Average coordinates: ((−3+5)/2,(7−1)/2)=(1,3).

questions.text: A triangle has side lengths 7, 24, and 25. What is its area?
questions.explanation: It is right-angled since 7²+24²=25²; area is 7×24/2=84.

questions.text: What is the inradius of an equilateral triangle with side length 6?
questions.explanation: Its inradius is s√3/6 = √3.

questions.text: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides 4 and 10. If the smaller area is 24, what is the larger area?
questions.explanation: The linear scale factor is 2.5, so area scales by 2.5²; 24×6.25=150.

questions.text: A regular octagon has side length 3. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: Eight equal sides give perimeter 8 × 3 = 24.

questions.text: A sphere has radius 3. What is its surface area?
questions.explanation: Surface area is 4πr² = 4π·9 = 36π.

questions.text: What is the slope of a line perpendicular to y = (2/3)x + 4?
questions.explanation: Perpendicular nonvertical slopes are negative reciprocals.

questions.text: A trapezoid has parallel sides 8 and 14 and height 5. What is its area?
What is the diagonal length of a rectangle with sides 7 and 24?
questions.explanation: The diagonal is √(7²+24²)=√625=25.

questions.text: A central angle subtends an arc measuring 80°. What is the corresponding inscribed angle?
questions.explanation: An inscribed angle is half the central angle subtending the same arc.

questions.text: What is the total surface area of a cube with edge length 4?
questions.explanation: Six square faces each have area 16, totaling 96 square units.

questions.text: What is the probability of getting heads on a fair coin toss?
questions.explanation: A fair coin has two equally likely outcomes.

questions.text: A fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability of rolling a 5?
questions.explanation: One of the six equally likely faces shows 5.

questions.text: A box contains 4 green and 6 yellow balls. What is the probability of choosing green?
questions.explanation: There are 4 favorable balls out of 10: 4/10 = 2/5.

questions.text: What is the probability of an impossible event?
questions.explanation: An impossible event has probability zero.

questions.text: A letter is selected at random from the word MATH. What is the probability it is a vowel?
questions.explanation: Only A is a vowel among the four letters.

questions.text: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. What is the probability of drawing red?
questions.explanation: There are 3 favorable outcomes among 5 counters.

questions.text: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of exactly one head?
questions.explanation: HT and TH are two of the four equally likely outcomes.

questions.text: A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability it is a heart?
questions.explanation: There are 13 hearts among 52 cards.

questions.text: A fair die is rolled twice. What is the probability both rolls are even?
questions.explanation: Each roll is even with probability 1/2; independent probabilities multiply.

questions.text: A bag has 5 black and 3 white tokens. Two are drawn without replacement. What is P(both black)?
A number is chosen uniformly from 1 through 12. What is the probability it is divisible by 3 or 4?
questions.explanation: Multiples are 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12: six of 12.

questions.text: If P(A)=0.35, what is P(not A)?
questions.explanation: Complementary probabilities sum to 1, so 1−0.35=0.65.

questions.text: A spinner has 8 equal sections, 3 blue. What is the probability of not landing blue?
questions.explanation: Five of the eight sections are not blue.

questions.text: Events A and B are independent, with probabilities 0.4 and 0.5. What is P(A and B)?
questions.explanation: For independent events, multiply: 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2.

questions.text: A raffle has 200 tickets and one winning ticket. What is the chance one ticket wins?
Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability their sum is 7?
questions.explanation: Six of the 36 equally likely ordered rolls sum to 7.

questions.text: Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard deck. What is the probability both are aces?
A disease affects 1% of people. A test is 90% sensitive and has 95% specificity. Given a positive result, approximately what is P(disease)?
A fair coin is tossed 5 times. What is the probability of exactly 3 heads?
questions.explanation: There are C(5,3)=10 sequences among 2⁵=32.

questions.text: A box has 4 red and 6 blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Given the first is red, what is P(second red)?
questions.explanation: After a red is removed, 3 of the remaining 9 are red.

questions.text: A fair die is rolled until a 6 appears. What is the probability the first 6 occurs on the third roll?
questions.explanation: The sequence is non-6, non-6, then 6: (5/6)²(1/6)=25/216.

questions.text: For events A and B, P(A)=0.6, P(B)=0.5, and P(A∩B)=0.3. What is P(A∪B)?
A committee of 3 is selected from 5 women and 4 men. What is the probability it has exactly 2 women?
questions.explanation: Choose 2 of 5 and 1 of 4: 40/84=10/21.

questions.text: A binomial experiment has n=4 and success probability 1/3. What is the probability of zero successes?
questions.explanation: The probability is (2/3)⁴ = 16/81.

questions.text: A fair die is rolled. Given that the result is greater than 2, what is the probability it is even?
questions.explanation: Among {3,4,5,6}, two of four outcomes are even, so the probability is 1/2.

questions.text: A family has 3 children. Assuming each birth is independently equally likely boy or girl, what is the chance of exactly 2 girls?
questions.explanation: Three of the eight equally likely sequences contain exactly two girls.

questions.text: A continuous random variable is uniform on [2,10]. What is P(X>7)?
questions.explanation: The interval above 7 has length 3 of total length 8.

questions.text: A fair coin is tossed 4 times. What is the probability of at least one tail?
questions.explanation: Use the complement: 1−P(all heads)=1−1/16=15/16.

questions.text: Events A and B are mutually exclusive, with P(A)=0.25 and P(B)=0.4. What is P(A∪B)?
questions.explanation: Disjoint event probabilities add: 0.25 + 0.4 = 0.65.

questions.text: A password is a uniformly chosen 4-digit string, allowing leading zeros. What is the probability all digits differ?
Which measure is the middle value in an ordered list?
questions.explanation: The median is the central value after sorting.

questions.text: What is the range of 4, 9, 11, and 15?
questions.explanation: Range is maximum minus minimum: 15−4=11.

questions.text: Which graph is commonly used to show categories and their frequencies?
questions.explanation: Bar charts compare counts or other summaries across categories.

questions.text: What is the mode of 2, 5, 5, 7, 9?
questions.explanation: Five occurs more often than any other value.

questions.text: A survey asks people their favorite color. What type of data is recorded?
questions.explanation: Favorite colors are labels rather than numerical measurements.

questions.text: What is the mean of 4, 6, 8, and 10?
questions.explanation: The sum is 28 and dividing by 4 gives 7.

questions.text: Find the median of 3, 8, 10, 12, 20, 25.
questions.explanation: The middle two are 10 and 12; their average is 11.

questions.text: A dataset has mean 12 across 5 values. What is the sum of its values?
questions.explanation: Mean = sum/count, so the sum is 12 × 5 = 60.

questions.text: If every observation is increased by 4, what happens to the mean?
questions.explanation: Adding a constant to each value shifts the mean by that constant.

questions.text: A sample standard deviation is 0. What must be true of its observations?
questions.explanation: Zero spread means every observed value equals the mean.

questions.text: Which measure is generally resistant to a single extreme outlier?
questions.explanation: The median depends on rank and is less affected by extreme values.

questions.text: A scatterplot shows points rising from left to right. What association is indicated?
questions.explanation: As one variable increases, the other tends to increase.

questions.text: In a roughly symmetric bell-shaped distribution, approximately what share lies within one standard deviation of the mean?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule places about 68% within one standard deviation.

questions.text: A poll samples only people leaving a gym to estimate all adults' exercise habits. What is the main issue?
questions.explanation: Gym visitors are not representative of all adults for this question.

questions.text: What does the interquartile range measure?
options: Spread of the middle half of the data
questions.explanation: IQR is Q3−Q1 and spans the central 50%.

questions.text: A large standard deviation usually indicates that data values are:
options: More spread out from the mean
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures spread around the mean.

questions.text: A sample mean is 50, standard deviation 10, and n=100. What is the standard error of the mean?
questions.explanation: Standard error is s/√n = 10/10 = 1.

questions.text: A 95% confidence interval for a population mean is (12, 18). Which interpretation is correct?
options: The method captures the true mean in 95% of repeated samples
95% of individual observations lie from 12 to 18
The mean has 95% probability of changing
Every sample mean lies in this interval
questions.explanation: Confidence describes long-run coverage of the interval procedure.

questions.text: A test yields p=0.03 at significance level 0.05. What is the decision?
options: Accept the null as certainly true
questions.explanation: Since p < 0.05, the result is statistically significant under this test.

questions.text: For a normal distribution with mean 100 and standard deviation 15, what z-score corresponds to 130?
A correlation of r=−0.9 between two variables establishes that:
options: They have a strong negative linear association
questions.explanation: Correlation describes strong negative linear association, not causation.

questions.text: Which condition is important for a one-sample t interval to be reliable with a small sample?
options: The population is approximately normal with no severe outliers
The sample mean must be zero
The population variance is known exactly
The sample includes every population member
questions.explanation: Small-sample t inference is sensitive to strong non-normality and outliers.

questions.text: In linear regression, residuals are defined as:
options: Predicted y divided by observed y
questions.explanation: A residual is the vertical prediction error, observed minus fitted response.

questions.text: A study reports a 95% confidence interval for a difference as (−2, 5). At a two-sided 5% level, what follows?
options: The difference is not statistically significant
The first group is significantly higher
questions.explanation: The interval includes zero, so it does not reject a zero difference.

questions.text: A dataset has Q1=14 and Q3=26. What is its interquartile range?
A two-sided test's significance level is reduced from 0.05 to 0.01, with sample size unchanged. What generally happens to power?
options: It is unchanged for every alternative
questions.explanation: A stricter rejection threshold generally makes detecting an effect less likely.

questions.text: If X and Y are independent with variances 4 and 9, what is Var(X+Y)?
questions.explanation: For independent variables, variances add: 4 + 9 = 13.

questions.text: In a multiple regression, a coefficient for x is 2.5. What does it represent, holding other predictors fixed?
options: A 2.5-unit predicted response increase per one-unit x increase
The correlation between x and the response
questions.explanation: A regression coefficient is the conditional change in predicted response per x unit.

questions.text: A sample proportion is 0.4 from n=100. What is its approximate standard error?
A variable is strongly right-skewed with several high outliers. Which pair best summarizes its center and spread?
questions.explanation: Median and IQR resist skewness and extreme observations.

questions.text: What is the derivative of x^2?
questions.explanation: The power rule gives d(x^2)/dx = 2x.

questions.text: What is the derivative of 5x?
questions.explanation: The derivative of ax is the constant a.

questions.text: What is the derivative of the constant function f(x)=9?
questions.explanation: A constant does not change as x varies, so its derivative is zero.

questions.text: What is the slope of y=x² at x=3?
questions.explanation: The derivative is 2x, which equals 6 at x=3.

questions.text: Evaluate the definite integral ∫₀² 1 dx.
questions.explanation: The constant function 1 accumulates area 1×2 = 2.

questions.text: What does a definite integral commonly represent geometrically?
questions.explanation: A definite integral accumulates signed area over an interval.

questions.text: Differentiate f(x)=3x⁴−2x².
questions.explanation: Apply the power rule to each term.

questions.text: Find ∫(6x²+4) dx.
questions.explanation: Antidifferentiate each term: 6x² gives 2x³, and 4 gives 4x.

questions.text: What is the derivative of sin(2x)?
questions.explanation: The chain rule multiplies cos(2x) by the inner derivative 2.

questions.text: Where does f(x)=x²−4x have a horizontal tangent?
Evaluate lim as x approaches 3 of (x²−9)/(x−3).
questions.explanation: Factor and cancel x−3; the remaining expression approaches 6.

questions.text: If f′(x)>0 throughout an interval, what is true of f on that interval?
questions.explanation: A positive derivative means the function increases.

questions.text: Find the average value of f(x)=x on [0,4].
questions.explanation: Average value is (1/4)∫₀⁴x dx = 2.

questions.text: A particle's position is s(t)=t³−3t. What is its velocity at t=2?
questions.explanation: Velocity is s′(t)=3t²−3; at 2 it equals 9.

questions.text: What is ∫₁³ 2x dx?
questions.explanation: An antiderivative is x²; 3²−1²=8.

questions.text: What is the derivative of sin(x)?
questions.explanation: The derivative of sine is cosine.

questions.text: Differentiate y=e^(3x²).
questions.explanation: By the chain rule, derivative is e^(3x²) times 6x.

questions.text: Find d/dx of x² ln(x), for x>0.
questions.explanation: Product rule gives 2x ln(x)+x²(1/x).

questions.text: Evaluate ∫₀¹ 3x² dx.
questions.explanation: An antiderivative is x³; its change from 0 to 1 is 1.

questions.text: A differentiable function has f′(x)=x(x−4). On which intervals is it decreasing?
questions.explanation: The derivative is negative between its roots 0 and 4.

questions.text: Find the local maximum value of f(x)=−x²+6x−5.
questions.explanation: The vertex is at x=3, where f(3)=4.

questions.text: Use implicit differentiation on x²+y²=25. What is dy/dx?
questions.explanation: Differentiating gives 2x+2y y′=0, so y′=−x/y.

questions.text: A 10-unit ladder leans against a wall. Its foot moves away at 2 units/s when 6 units from the wall. How fast does the top descend?
questions.explanation: x²+y²=100 gives yy′=−xx′; at x=6,y=8, y′=−1.5, so it descends at 1.5 units/s.

questions.text: Evaluate lim as x approaches 0 of (e^x−1)/x.
questions.explanation: This is the derivative of e^x at zero, equal to 1.

questions.text: Find the area enclosed by y=x and y=x² from x=0 to x=1.
questions.explanation: The area is ∫₀¹(x−x²)dx = 1/2−1/3 = 1/6.

questions.text: For f(x)=x³−3x, what is f″(2)?
Evaluate ∫ x cos(x²) dx.
questions.explanation: Substitute u=x², so du=2x dx.

questions.text: A function is concave down where its second derivative is:
questions.explanation: A negative second derivative indicates downward curvature.

questions.text: Use one Newton step for √10, starting with x₀=3.
What is the radius of convergence of Σ from n=0 to ∞ of (x−2)^n/5^n?
questions.explanation: The geometric series converges when |x−2|/5<1, giving radius 5.

questions.text: Which ancient civilization built the pyramids at Giza?
questions.explanation: The Giza pyramids were built in ancient Egypt during the Old Kingdom.

questions.text: Which river was central to farming in ancient Egypt?
questions.explanation: The Nile's annual floods supported Egyptian agriculture.

questions.text: Which ancient Greek city-state is especially associated with military training and discipline?
questions.explanation: Spartan society emphasized military training and service.

questions.text: What writing system did ancient Egyptians use for monumental inscriptions?
questions.explanation: Egyptian hieroglyphs were used on temples and monuments.

questions.text: Which sea did Phoenician traders navigate extensively?
questions.explanation: Phoenician cities traded widely around the Mediterranean.

questions.text: The Code of Hammurabi is associated with which civilization?
questions.explanation: Hammurabi ruled the Babylonian Empire in the 18th century BCE.

questions.text: Which city was the capital of the Assyrian Empire under Ashurbanipal?
questions.explanation: Ashurbanipal ruled from Nineveh, which held his famous library.

questions.text: What was the primary purpose of the Athenian ostracism procedure?
options: Exile a citizen seen as a political threat
Select a new archon by inheritance
questions.explanation: Ostracism could banish a citizen for ten years without a criminal conviction.

questions.text: The Punic Wars were fought mainly between Rome and which power?
questions.explanation: Rome and Carthage contested control of the western Mediterranean.

questions.text: Which ruler unified much of China and standardized script and measurements in the 3rd century BCE?
questions.explanation: The Qin emperor centralized administration and standardized systems.

questions.text: What was the main role of the Silk Road in antiquity?
options: Linking long-distance trade networks across Eurasia
Serving only as a Roman military road
questions.explanation: Overland routes connected traders and societies across Eurasia.

questions.text: Which ancient kingdom was ruled by the Meroitic civilization south of Egypt?
questions.explanation: Kush, with a major center at Meroë, flourished south of Egypt.

questions.text: What was the function of the Roman cursus honorum?
options: A sequence of elected public offices
questions.explanation: The cursus honorum outlined the customary progression through magistracies.

questions.text: Which ancient Indian text is a collection of hymns composed in Vedic Sanskrit?
questions.explanation: The Rigveda is among the oldest Vedic collections of hymns.

questions.text: What was the main purpose of the Achaemenid Royal Road?
options: Facilitate communication and movement across the Persian Empire
Mark the boundary of every Greek polis
questions.explanation: The road and courier system helped the Persian state communicate across distances.

questions.text: Which feature most distinguished the Athenian democracy of the 5th century BCE?
options: Eligible citizens voted directly in assemblies
questions.explanation: Eligible male citizens participated directly, though most residents were excluded.

questions.text: Which feature most clearly distinguished the Hellenistic kingdoms after Alexander's death?
options: Restoration of a unified Persian monarchy
Exclusion of Greek language from administration
questions.explanation: Successor kingdoms combined Macedonian dynasties with culturally diverse territories.

questions.text: What was the significance of the Rosetta Stone for Egyptology?
options: Its parallel texts helped decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs
It recorded the construction of the Great Pyramid
It proved the location of Troy
It was the first papyrus legal code
questions.explanation: The same decree in multiple scripts enabled comparison and decipherment.

questions.text: Which conflict ended with the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE?
options: Octavian's war against Antony and Cleopatra
questions.explanation: Octavian's victory at Actium cleared his path to sole rule.

questions.text: In ancient Mesopotamia, what did a ziggurat primarily serve as?
questions.explanation: Ziggurats were stepped temple structures associated with urban cults.

questions.text: Which reform is associated with Solon in early sixth-century BCE Athens?
options: Canceling certain debts and restructuring civic participation
questions.explanation: Solon's reforms addressed debt bondage and reorganized political rights.

questions.text: The Battle of Kadesh was fought between Egypt and which empire?
questions.explanation: Ramesses II's Egypt fought the Hittites at Kadesh in the 13th century BCE.

questions.text: Which evidence most strongly indicates that the Indus cities had planned urban infrastructure?
options: Gridded streets and standardized drainage systems
questions.explanation: Excavated cities such as Mohenjo-daro show planned streets and drainage.

questions.text: What was the Roman policy of extending citizenship to many free inhabitants of the empire in 212 CE?
questions.explanation: Caracalla's Constitutio Antoniniana granted citizenship to most free subjects.

questions.text: Which factor helped the Mauryan Empire administer a large territory under Ashoka?
options: Provincial officials and an extensive communication network
A purely nomadic army with no cities
questions.explanation: Mauryan administration used officials, roads, and inscriptions to project authority.

questions.text: What was the outcome of the Greco-Persian Wars at the Battle of Salamis in 480 BCE?
options: A Greek naval victory over Xerxes' fleet
The end of the Roman Republic
questions.explanation: The Greek fleet defeated the Persian navy in the narrow straits.

questions.text: Which ancient source is a major account of the Peloponnesian War by a contemporary participant?
options: Thucydides' History of the Peloponnesian War
questions.explanation: Thucydides wrote an analytical history of the war he experienced.

questions.text: What was the primary economic basis of the classical Maya city-states?
options: Agriculture, supplemented by tribute and trade
questions.explanation: Maya economies relied on intensive agriculture and linked exchange networks.

questions.text: Why did the Roman Republic's expansion contribute to social conflict in the second century BCE?
options: Conquests concentrated land and wealth while displacing small farmers
questions.explanation: Elite land accumulation and slave labor worsened pressures on smallholders.

questions.text: Which political change followed the Zhou dynasty's decline in China?
options: Competing states eventually unified under Qin rule
The Shang restored a unified empire
questions.explanation: Warring States competition preceded Qin's unification in 221 BCE.

questions.text: What was a common fortified residence of a medieval lord?
questions.explanation: Castles served as fortified residences and centers of local power.

questions.text: Which city was the capital of the Byzantine Empire?
questions.explanation: Constantinople served as the Byzantine imperial capital.

questions.text: What was a scriptorium in a medieval monastery?
options: A room where manuscripts were copied
questions.explanation: Monastic scribes copied and preserved manuscripts in scriptoria.

questions.text: Which religion spread across much of North Africa and the Middle East from the seventh century onward?
questions.explanation: Islam expanded rapidly from Arabia in the seventh century.

questions.text: What was a common medieval craft association called?
questions.explanation: Guilds organized craftspeople or merchants and regulated their trade.

questions.text: The Magna Carta was sealed in England in which year?
questions.explanation: King John sealed Magna Carta in 1215.

questions.text: Which ruler was crowned emperor in Rome by Pope Leo III in 800?
questions.explanation: Charlemagne's coronation revived the western imperial title.

questions.text: What was the main purpose of the medieval Hanseatic League?
options: Coordinate trade among northern European towns
questions.explanation: The league protected and promoted merchants' trade across northern Europe.

questions.text: The Black Death reached Europe in the mid-fourteenth century through which broad network?
options: Trade routes linking Asia and the Mediterranean
Roman roads still under imperial control
questions.explanation: Trade and shipping routes helped plague spread westward into Europe.

questions.text: Which language was widely used for scholarship and administration in the medieval Islamic world?
questions.explanation: Arabic served as a major language of learning and governance.

questions.text: What was the principal aim of the First Crusade, called in 1095?
options: Capture Jerusalem and aid the Byzantine Empire
Overthrow the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad
questions.explanation: The expedition aimed to aid Byzantium and seize Jerusalem.

questions.text: Which West African empire prospered from trans-Saharan gold and salt trade under Mansa Musa?
