questions.explanation: A stanza is a grouped unit of lines in a poem.

questions.text: Which character is the young wizard protagonist of J. K. Rowling's novels?
questions.explanation: Harry Potter is the central character in Rowling's fantasy series.

questions.text: What is the main character in a story usually called?
questions.explanation: The protagonist is the central character in a narrative.

questions.text: A story told by a narrator using “I” is written in which point of view?
questions.explanation: First-person narrators refer to themselves as “I” or “we”.

questions.text: Which novel begins with the line “Call me Ishmael”?
questions.explanation: Herman Melville's Moby-Dick opens with this famous first-person line.

questions.text: In tragedy, what does “hamartia” traditionally refer to?
options: A protagonist's error or flaw contributing to downfall
The final song of a chorus
questions.explanation: Hamartia is a consequential error or failing in classical tragic theory.

questions.text: Which poet wrote “The Raven”?
questions.explanation: Poe published the narrative poem in 1845.

questions.text: Which literary form typically uses fourteen lines and a patterned rhyme scheme?
questions.explanation: A sonnet is traditionally a fourteen-line poem, often in iambic pentameter.

questions.text: Who wrote the novel “Things Fall Apart”?
questions.explanation: Achebe's 1958 novel depicts Igbo society and colonial disruption.

questions.text: In drama, what is a soliloquy?
options: A speech in which a character speaks thoughts aloud, often alone
questions.explanation: A soliloquy reveals a character's thoughts directly to the audience.

questions.text: Which novel features the character Elizabeth Bennet?
questions.explanation: Elizabeth Bennet is the protagonist of Jane Austen's novel.

questions.text: What is an elegy primarily associated with?
options: Lament for the dead or reflection on loss
questions.explanation: An elegy is a poem of mourning or serious reflection, often on death.

questions.text: Which poet is traditionally credited with composing the ancient Greek epic “The Odyssey”?
questions.explanation: The Odyssey is an ancient Greek epic traditionally attributed to Homer.

questions.text: A recurring image or idea that develops a literary work is commonly called a:
questions.explanation: A motif is a recurring element that contributes to a work’s themes.

questions.text: Which narrative technique presents a character's thoughts in a continuous, often associative flow?
questions.explanation: Stream of consciousness attempts to represent the ongoing movement of thought.

questions.text: In “The Waste Land,” which ancient fertility figure is invoked in the poem's notes as a source for its title?
questions.explanation: T. S. Eliot's notes point to the Fisher King legend and Jessie Weston's study.

questions.text: Which term describes a story embedded within another story?
questions.explanation: A frame narrative encloses one or more inner narratives within an outer one.

questions.text: Who narrates Emily Brontë's “Wuthering Heights” through a layered frame structure?
questions.explanation: Lockwood records Nelly Dean's account, creating nested narration.

questions.text: Which movement is most associated with fragmented form and experimentation in early twentieth-century literature?
questions.explanation: Modernist writers often used fragmentation and formal innovation to represent modern experience.

questions.text: In literary analysis, “free indirect discourse” combines third-person narration with what?
options: A character's idiom or viewpoint without a reporting tag
A direct quotation in first person
A narrator addressing the reader as “you”
A stage direction spoken by the chorus
questions.explanation: It blends third-person narration with the vocabulary and perspective of a character.

questions.text: Which poet wrote “The Second Coming,” with its image of the “rough beast”?
questions.explanation: Yeats published “The Second Coming” in 1920.

questions.text: Which term names a brief reference to a person, event, or text outside the immediate work?
questions.explanation: An allusion invokes external material without fully narrating or explaining it.

questions.text: Who wrote the Bengali novel “Pather Panchali”?
questions.explanation: Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyay published Pather Panchali in 1929.

questions.text: In classical dramatic structure, which term refers to the reversal of a protagonist's fortune?
questions.explanation: Peripeteia is the reversal or turning point in a tragic plot.

questions.text: Which novelist created the fictional Yoknapatawpha County?
questions.explanation: Faulkner set many works in his imagined Mississippi county.

questions.text: What is “enjambment” in poetry?
options: Continuation of a sentence beyond the end of a line
A pause within a metrical line
A stanza of exactly four lines
questions.explanation: Enjambment carries syntax and sense across a line break without terminal punctuation.

questions.text: Which author wrote the Sanskrit play “Abhijnanashakuntalam”?
questions.explanation: Kalidasa's drama retells the story of Shakuntala and King Dushyanta.

questions.text: Which term refers to a narrator whose account cannot be fully trusted because of bias, limited knowledge, or distortion?
questions.explanation: An unreliable narrator's version of events invites doubt or reinterpretation.

questions.text: What is the main idea of a passage?
options: A detail from the final line
questions.explanation: The main idea summarizes what the passage is chiefly about.

questions.text: Passage: Lena put the wet umbrella by the door and shook raindrops from her coat. What is directly supported?
options: Lena came in from rainy weather
questions.explanation: The wet umbrella and coat indicate rain.

questions.text: Passage: Omar planted three bean seeds. A week later, two had sprouted. How many had not sprouted?
questions.explanation: Three planted minus two sprouted leaves one.

questions.text: Passage: The library closes at six. At 5:45, Jo still had to return a book. What should Jo do soon?
questions.explanation: The library closes in fifteen minutes.

questions.text: Passage: Nia chose the shaded path because the afternoon sun was hot. Why did she choose it?
questions.explanation: The passage gives the heat as her reason.

questions.text: If a passage says a character “gripped the umbrella as the wind howled,” what is most reasonable to infer?
questions.explanation: The wording supports an inference of windy conditions, but not snow or damage.

questions.text: Passage: The town added a bus every 15 minutes. Six months later, weekday car counts downtown were lower, though weekend counts were unchanged. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Weekday car counts fell after bus service increased
The buses caused every traffic change
questions.explanation: The comparison supports a weekday decline, not sole causation.

questions.text: Passage: Mara's first two paper bridges sagged under five coins. She folded the third into an accordion shape; it held twelve. What most likely helped?
options: The folded structure increased its strength
The bridge was shorter by definition
questions.explanation: The new fold is the changed feature and supports the load.

questions.text: Passage: A museum welcomed 400 visitors Saturday and 300 Sunday. The report says weekend attendance was 100 above forecast. What was forecast?
questions.explanation: Actual attendance was 700; subtracting 100 gives 600.

questions.text: Passage: Lee called the proposal “promising,” but asked for a larger trial before adoption. What is Lee's position?
options: Cautiously positive, with more evidence needed
questions.explanation: Praise is qualified by a request for further testing.

questions.text: Passage: The path was dry near the gate but muddy beneath the trees, where the canopy blocked sunlight. Why might the shaded part stay muddy longer?
options: It receives less sunlight to dry it
It is closer to the gate
The path is made of sunlight
questions.explanation: Reduced sunlight can slow evaporation.

questions.text: Passage: A school surveyed only students at the chess club and found that most preferred chess. What is the main limitation?
options: The sample may not represent all students
The club has too many games
questions.explanation: Club members are a selected group, not the whole school.

questions.text: Passage: The notice says the pool is closed Tuesday for repairs and will reopen Wednesday. When can visitors next expect it open?
questions.explanation: The notice names Wednesday as the reopening day.

questions.text: Passage: Noor's draft was shorter after editing, yet it included every required point. What did the editing most likely achieve?
questions.explanation: Shorter text with all points suggests concision.

questions.text: Passage: A plant beside the window grew toward the glass. Which explanation is most reasonable without further evidence?
options: It responded to light from the window
It was pulled by gravity sideways
It knew the glass was nearby
questions.explanation: Plants commonly grow toward a light source.

questions.text: Which detail best supports a claim that a town reduced traffic pollution?
options: Measured roadside nitrogen dioxide fell after bus service expanded
The town planted flowers in a park
A nearby shop changed its sign
questions.explanation: A measured pollutant change tied to the transport change directly supports the claim.

questions.text: Passage: In a trial, 40 seedlings received compost and 40 received none. Both groups got equal light and water; composted plants averaged 18 cm, controls 14 cm. Which inference is strongest?
options: Compost was associated with greater average height in this trial
Compost guarantees every plant grows taller
Light had no effect on either group
The result proves all soils need compost
questions.explanation: The controlled comparison supports an average difference in this trial only.

questions.text: Passage: The archive's oldest map is dated 1840, but its paper was reused from a document dated 1822. What does the earlier date establish?
options: The paper existed by 1822, not that the map did
The map predates every archive item
The map's author was born in 1822
questions.explanation: The reused paper dates the material, not the map's creation.

questions.text: Passage: Rainfall was below average for three months. Reservoir levels also fell, while household use rose slightly. Which statement best distinguishes evidence from cause?
options: Both low rainfall and increased use may have contributed
Rising use alone caused the fall
questions.explanation: The passage offers two plausible contributing factors, not a single proven cause.

questions.text: Passage: A report says a clinic's wait fell from 50 to 35 minutes after appointments were staggered. It gives no comparison clinic. Which claim is warranted?
options: Waits fell after the change at that clinic
Staggering alone caused the entire reduction
Every clinic would see the same result
Patients received faster treatment in every respect
questions.explanation: The before-and-after result is reported, but causal attribution is limited.

questions.text: Passage: Although the north field produced less grain, its yield per hectare was higher because it was much smaller. What does this contrast show?
options: Total output and yield rate measure different things
The north field produced more grain overall
questions.explanation: A smaller total can coexist with a larger area-adjusted rate.

questions.text: Passage: A witness says the hall was empty at 9:00. A camera shows one person entering at 9:05. Which conclusion follows?
options: The hall was empty at 9:00; someone entered later
The camera proves who was in the hall all day
questions.explanation: The observations refer to different times and are compatible.

questions.text: Passage: A survey reports 72% approval among respondents; 18% of those contacted replied. What key qualification should accompany the result?
options: The approval is exactly 72% of all residents
The response rate makes every response false
questions.explanation: A low response rate can introduce nonresponse bias.

questions.text: Passage: The writer calls a policy “costly,” then reports that it saved $2 million while costing $1.2 million. What is its net financial result?
questions.explanation: Savings exceed costs by $0.8 million.

questions.text: Passage: A historical letter says the bridge was “finished before the first frost.” Local records place the first frost between October 10 and 20. What date range can be inferred?
options: The bridge was finished before the first frost in that interval
The letter gives an exact day
questions.explanation: The wording establishes only a relative deadline.

questions.text: Passage: In a study, volunteers chose whether to use a study app; app users scored higher. Why is a causal conclusion uncertain?
options: Motivated students may have been more likely to choose the app
The app users were randomly assigned
questions.explanation: Self-selection leaves motivation as a possible confounder.

questions.text: Passage: A town's population rose 10% while its water use rose 8%. What happened to water use per resident, approximately?
questions.explanation: Use per person is 1.08 divided by 1.10, about 0.982.

questions.text: Passage: A narrator says, “I knew then that the locked room was empty,” but earlier admits never entering it. What should a careful reader note?
options: The narrator's certainty exceeds the evidence described
The narrator directly observed the empty room
The narrator is omniscient by definition
questions.explanation: The account gives no direct basis for knowing the room was empty.

questions.text: Passage: In a 100-person trial, 12 treated participants improved versus 8 controls. The report gives no uncertainty interval. What is the best reading?
options: The observed difference is four people; its precision is unclear
The control group improved by 12 people
questions.explanation: The raw difference is clear, but uncertainty cannot be assessed.

questions.text: Passage: A river was clearer downstream after a factory closed, but heavy rain had also ended that week. What additional comparison would best test the factory explanation?
options: Measure comparable upstream and downstream sites across similar conditions
Ask one visitor whether the water looks clean
Compare unrelated rivers from different years
questions.explanation: Matched sites and conditions help separate possible causes.

questions.text: How many legal deliveries are in a standard over?
questions.explanation: A standard over contains six legal deliveries.

questions.text: How many stumps form one wicket?
questions.explanation: A wicket has three stumps topped by two bails.

questions.text: Which player delivers the ball to the batter?
questions.explanation: The bowler delivers each ball from the bowling end.

questions.text: How many runs are awarded when a batter hits the ball over the boundary without it bouncing?
questions.explanation: A clean hit over the boundary earns six runs.

questions.text: Which player stands behind the stumps at the striker's end?
questions.explanation: The wicketkeeper fields behind the striker's wicket.

questions.text: What is a batter’s score of 100 runs in an innings called?
questions.explanation: A century is an individual score of at least 100 runs.

questions.text: A bowler delivers six legal balls with no runs conceded. What is the over called?
questions.explanation: A maiden over concedes no runs from the bowler's over.

questions.text: A delivery passes the striker untouched, is not called wide, and reaches the boundary. What is scored?
options: No runs because it missed the bat
questions.explanation: An untouched, non-wide ball reaching the boundary scores byes.

questions.text: What is a no-ball in cricket?
options: An illegal delivery carrying an extra to the batting side
A legal ball that earns no runs
A ball the batter chooses not to hit
A delivery that ends an innings
questions.explanation: A no-ball is an illegal delivery and normally gives an extra.

questions.text: A batter is out of their ground and the fielding side breaks the wicket while the batter is running. What dismissal may apply?
questions.explanation: A batter short of the ground may be run out.

questions.text: In a limited-overs match, what is the main purpose of the powerplay fielding restriction?
options: Limit fielders outside the inner circle for specified overs
Give the batting side extra wickets
Require every ball to be a yorker
Stop the match after a boundary
questions.explanation: Powerplay rules restrict boundary fielders to encourage scoring.

questions.text: What does LBW stand for?
questions.explanation: LBW means leg before wicket, a mode of dismissal.

questions.text: A batter hits the ball and the wicketkeeper catches it after it touches the ground. Is the batter caught out?
options: No, a catch must be completed before the ball touches ground
Yes, any keeper collection is a catch
Yes, but only in a Test
questions.explanation: A caught dismissal requires a fair catch before ground contact.

questions.text: How many runs are usually scored for a completed run when batters cross and make their grounds?
questions.explanation: Each completed run between the wickets adds one.

questions.text: When does the ball become live after a goal kick under the current Laws?
options: When it is kicked and clearly moves
Only after it leaves the penalty area
questions.explanation: A goal kick is in play once kicked and clearly moved.

questions.text: In Test cricket, what is a follow-on?
options: An option for the side batting second after a large first-innings deficit
A compulsory change of ball every over
questions.explanation: The follow-on allows the leading side to make the opponent bat again immediately, subject to the margin and rules.

questions.text: In a 50-over innings, a bowler has bowled 8 overs. What is the maximum additional overs that bowler may deliver under the usual limit?
questions.explanation: The usual maximum is one fifth of 50, or 10 overs.

questions.text: A no-ball is hit to the boundary without touching the ground first. What is the normal total credited for the boundary and no-ball?
questions.explanation: Six boundary runs plus the no-ball extra make seven.

questions.text: At the instant a fielder catches a shot, the fielder has a foot touching the boundary rope. What is the ruling?
options: Six, because the fielder is grounded beyond the boundary
Caught out, since the ball was held
questions.explanation: A fielder in contact with the boundary is beyond it for this catch.

questions.text: A batter is hit on the pad by a fair delivery. Which condition is essential for an LBW decision?
options: The ball would have hit the stumps, subject to LBW rules
The ball must first hit the bat
The batter must be inside the crease
questions.explanation: The projected path must strike the wicket and other LBW conditions apply.

questions.text: A bowler bowls a wide that passes the striker, and the keeper misses it; batters run two. How many runs are normally added?
questions.explanation: The wide extra plus two completed runs gives three.

questions.text: When can a batter be stumped?
options: They leave their ground playing or leaving a ball and the wicketkeeper puts the wicket down without a run attempt
They are inside the crease when a fielder catches the ball
A bowler oversteps the popping crease
The ball crosses the boundary after bouncing
questions.explanation: Stumping applies when the striker is out of ground and not attempting a run.

questions.text: In a tied limited-overs match, what does a Super Over provide?
options: A short additional contest to determine a winner under competition rules
A replay of the whole match automatically
A run penalty to the team batting second
An extra 50 overs for each side
questions.explanation: A Super Over is a tie-break procedure, where competition regulations use it.

questions.text: What is the key difference between a bowler's no-ball and wide?
options: A no-ball is an illegal delivery for specified infringements; a wide is too far from the batter to play reasonably
A wide is always a legal delivery with no extra
A no-ball can only occur after a boundary
There is no difference in the Laws
questions.explanation: They are distinct illegal-delivery calls with different grounds.

questions.text: A batter is caught off a no-ball. What is the usual dismissal result?
options: Not out caught, because a no-ball generally prevents that dismissal
Out caught as on any delivery
questions.explanation: A no-ball bars most dismissals, including caught, with limited exceptions.

questions.text: What does a declaration allow a captain to do in a multi-innings match?
options: Replace the ball with a new one each over
questions.explanation: A declaration closes the batting side's innings by choice.

questions.text: A team scores 320 in its first innings; its opponent makes 150. In a five-day Test, what first-innings lead does the first team hold?
questions.explanation: Subtract 150 from 320 to get a 170-run lead.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a ball's seam for a bowler?
options: It can assist grip and movement through the air or off the pitch
It determines the number of overs
questions.explanation: Seam position and condition can influence movement and control.

questions.text: A batter hits the ball twice deliberately to protect the wicket, without consent or an allowed exception. Which dismissal can apply?
options: Obstructing the field / handled-ball-related offence under current Laws
questions.explanation: Deliberately striking the ball again to protect the wicket is prohibited.

questions.text: A fielder deliberately stops the ball with a helmet left on the ground. What is the usual penalty?
options: Five penalty runs to the batting side
Five runs deducted from the batting side
questions.explanation: Contact with a protective helmet placed on the ground brings five penalty runs.

questions.text: How many players from one team start on the field in association football?
questions.explanation: Each team begins with eleven players, including the goalkeeper.

questions.text: How many goals is a standard goal worth in association football?
questions.explanation: Each goal counts as one goal.

questions.text: Which player may handle the ball inside their own penalty area, subject to the Laws?
questions.explanation: The goalkeeper has a limited handball privilege in their own area.

questions.text: What restarts play after the ball wholly crosses a touchline?
questions.explanation: A throw-in restarts play after the ball crosses the touchline.

questions.text: What colour card means a player is sent off?
questions.explanation: A red card indicates dismissal.

questions.text: What is awarded when a defending player commits a direct-free-kick foul in their own penalty area?
questions.explanation: A direct-free-kick offence in the defender’s penalty area results in a penalty kick.

questions.text: When is an attacker penalized for offside position?
options: When involved in active play from an offside position at a teammate's touch
Whenever standing beyond the halfway line
questions.explanation: Offside position alone is not an offence; involvement is required.

questions.text: What does the referee's advantage signal allow after a foul?
options: Play to continue when the non-offending team would benefit
The fouled team to add a goal
The offender to avoid a card automatically
questions.explanation: Advantage avoids stopping play when continuation benefits the fouled team.

questions.text: What does the referee signal by raising one arm for an indirect free kick?
options: The ball cannot score directly without touching another player
The kick must be taken by the goalkeeper
questions.explanation: An indirect free kick requires another player's touch before a goal.

questions.text: What is added time intended to compensate for?
options: Time lost to substitutions, injuries, and other stoppages
questions.explanation: The referee accounts for time lost during each half.

questions.text: Can a goal be scored directly from a throw-in?
options: No; a goal cannot be scored directly from a throw-in
Yes, but only for the throwing team
questions.explanation: The ball must touch another player before a goal can count.

questions.text: An attacker receives the ball directly from a goal kick. Is offside called solely for that reception?
options: No, a player cannot be offside directly from a goal kick
Yes, whenever beyond the last defender
Yes, if the goalkeeper kicked it
questions.explanation: Offside is not called directly from a goal kick.

questions.text: What is the minimum number of players a team must generally have for a match to continue under the Laws?
questions.explanation: A team with fewer than seven players cannot continue.

questions.text: What does a substitution replace?
options: One player leaving the field with an eligible substitute entering under procedure
The ball with a second ball
questions.explanation: A substitute takes the place of a player with referee permission.

questions.text: When does the goalkeeper generally lose the privilege of handling the ball?
options: When outside their own penalty area, subject to the Laws
Whenever the ball is inside the goal area
questions.explanation: The goalkeeper is subject to field-player handling restrictions outside the area.

questions.text: How far is the penalty mark from the goal line in association football?
questions.explanation: The penalty mark is 11 metres from the midpoint between the goalposts.

questions.text: At a teammate's touch, an attacker is level with the second-last opponent and later plays the ball. Is the attacker offside by position?
options: No; level with the second-last opponent is onside
Yes; only the goalkeeper may be level
Yes, unless the ball came from a corner
No, because offside never applies in the penalty area
questions.explanation: A player level with the second-last opponent is not in an offside position.

questions.text: A defender deliberately plays the ball, but it rebounds unpredictably to an attacker who had been offside. What matters in judging offside?
options: Whether the defender's action was a deliberate play, not a deflection or deliberate save
Whether the defender is inside the centre circle
questions.explanation: A deliberate play can reset the offside phase; deflections and saves do not.

questions.text: A player commits a careless trip outside the penalty area. What disciplinary action is required solely for carelessness?
options: A direct free kick, without a required card solely for carelessness
questions.explanation: Careless contact is a direct-free-kick offence; carelessness alone is not a card.

questions.text: A goalkeeper throws the ball directly into the opponents' goal from their own penalty area. What is the restart?
options: Goal kick to the opposing team
Corner kick to the goalkeeper's team
questions.explanation: A goal cannot be scored directly by throwing the ball into the opponents' goal.

questions.text: A defending player holds an opponent inside the defender's penalty area, away from the ball, while it is in play. What is normally awarded?
options: Indirect free kick outside the area
questions.explanation: Holding is a direct-free-kick offence, so inside the area it yields a penalty.

questions.text: A player is in an offside position but blocks the goalkeeper's line of vision without touching the ball. What may be called?
options: Offside for interfering with an opponent
No offence because there was no touch
questions.explanation: Blocking an opponent's line of vision can constitute offside involvement.

questions.text: A goal is scored after the ball touches the referee and possession changes to the opposing team. What is the correct restart under the Laws?
options: A dropped ball to the team that would have kept or gained possession
Indirect free kick to the defending team
questions.explanation: A referee touch that changes possession leads to a dropped ball.

questions.text: A player commits serious foul play while challenging for the ball. What is the expected sanction?
options: Red card for serious foul play
No card if the ball was touched
A yellow card in every case
questions.explanation: Serious foul play is a sending-off offence.

questions.text: A penalty taker kicks the ball backward at a penalty kick. What is the ruling?
options: Award an indirect free kick to the defending team
Count a goal if it enters
Award a corner to the attacking team
questions.explanation: The ball must be kicked forward; a backward kick is penalized with an indirect free kick.

questions.text: A player is in an offside position and receives the ball directly from an opponent's deliberate play, not a deliberate save. What is the usual offside ruling?
options: No offside offence from that deliberate play
Always offside based on the earlier position
questions.explanation: An opponent's deliberate play generally resets the offside phase.

questions.text: A goalkeeper handles a deliberate kick from a teammate inside the penalty area. What restart is awarded?
questions.explanation: Handling a deliberate kick from a teammate is an indirect-free-kick offence.

questions.text: A player enters the field without the referee's permission and interferes with play. What is the likely restart?
options: Direct free kick where the interference occurred, with discipline as appropriate
No restart because the player is a substitute
questions.explanation: Unauthorized entry with interference is penalized at the interference location.

questions.text: A defender trips an attacker to deny an obvious goal-scoring opportunity inside the penalty area, and the referee awards a penalty. If the defender was attempting to play or challenge for the ball, what sanction generally applies?
options: An automatic red card in every case
questions.explanation: A penalty for a DOGSO foul during an attempt to play the ball generally reduces the sanction to a caution.

questions.text: A player kicks a dropped ball directly into the opponents' goal before anyone else touches it. What is the restart?
questions.explanation: A goal cannot be scored directly from a dropped ball.

questions.text: How many points is a successful free throw worth?
questions.explanation: A free throw is worth one point.

questions.text: How many players from one team are on court during ordinary play?
questions.explanation: Each team fields five players.

questions.text: How many points is a made shot from behind the three-point line worth?
questions.explanation: A successful shot beyond the arc earns three points.

questions.text: What is the action of bouncing the ball while moving called?
questions.explanation: Dribbling advances the ball by bouncing it.

questions.text: Which basketball position is traditionally most associated with playing near the basket?
questions.explanation: Centers commonly operate close to the rim.

questions.text: How long is the NBA shot clock?
questions.explanation: The NBA shot clock is 24 seconds, with specific reset rules.

questions.text: How many periods are played in a regulation NBA game?
questions.explanation: NBA regulation consists of four 12-minute quarters.

questions.text: What is a double dribble?
options: Starting to dribble again after ending a dribble, or dribbling with both hands simultaneously
Bouncing the ball twice before a pass
questions.explanation: A player may not resume a dribble after ending it.

questions.text: What triggers a backcourt violation after a team establishes frontcourt control?
options: The offense causes the ball to return to its backcourt and touches it there first
A defender touches the ball in the frontcourt
questions.explanation: The offense cannot be first to touch its returned ball in backcourt.

questions.text: What is a screen intended to do?
options: Legally impede a defender's path to free a teammate
questions.explanation: A legal screen obstructs a defender without illegal contact.

questions.text: A defender touches the ball after it is on its downward flight toward the basket and it may score. What violation may occur?
questions.explanation: Interfering with a qualifying descending shot is goaltending.

questions.text: What is a turnover?
options: A possession lost to the opponent without a made basket
questions.explanation: A turnover transfers possession through an error or violation.

questions.text: After an offensive rebound in the NBA, what shot-clock time is generally set?
questions.explanation: An offensive rebound generally resets the NBA clock to 14 seconds.

questions.text: In a standard NBA possession, what happens after the ball touches the rim and the offense retains it?
options: The shot clock generally resets to 14 seconds
The clock resets to 24 in every case
The ball is awarded to defense
questions.explanation: An offensive rebound after a rim contact generally gives 14 seconds.

questions.text: What does a technical foul generally penalize?
options: Unsporting conduct or certain non-contact rule violations
questions.explanation: Technical fouls address conduct and specified administrative violations.

questions.text: What is the result of a defensive player committing six personal fouls in an NBA game?
questions.explanation: NBA players are disqualified after six personal fouls.

questions.text: An NBA team has possession in the frontcourt with 18 seconds on the shot clock when a defender commits a qualifying personal foul. What is the usual shot-clock reset?
questions.explanation: A qualifying foul with 14 or more remaining generally retains the existing time.

questions.text: A shot is released before the shot clock expires, hits the rim, and the shooting team recovers it. What is the NBA shot-clock setting?
questions.explanation: An offensive rebound after a rim hit gives 14 seconds.

questions.text: A player jumps from the frontcourt, catches the ball in the air, and lands in the backcourt. What is the likely ruling if the player was the first to touch it after the team established frontcourt control?
options: Legal play because the player was airborne
questions.explanation: The player is treated as having frontcourt status when jumping from there.

questions.text: A defender establishes legal guarding position, then moves laterally while maintaining it before contact. What is key to judging a charging/blocking call?
options: Whether the defender obtained legal position and whether contact was initiated illegally
Whether the contact made a sound
questions.explanation: Position, timing, and the nature of contact govern the call.

questions.text: A shot is still above the cylinder and within the imaginary cylinder when a defender touches it. What violation may apply?
questions.explanation: Touching the ball in the protected cylinder can be basket interference.

questions.text: A team has used its final team-foul allowance in a quarter under NBA rules. What generally follows a non-shooting defensive personal foul?
options: Free throws for the offended player
questions.explanation: Team-foul penalties award free throws after the limit, with rule exceptions.

questions.text: A player catches a pass while moving, comes to a legal one-foot stop, and then pivots. What determines whether the movement is traveling?
options: The established pivot foot may not be illegally lifted or returned before release
Only the number of dribbles matters
The player must remain motionless forever
questions.explanation: Traveling depends on legal footwork and pivot-foot rules.

questions.text: Why might a coach use a pick-and-roll?
options: The screener can roll toward the basket after screening the ball handler's defender
questions.explanation: The roll creates a passing or finishing option after the screen.

questions.text: What is the strategic purpose of switching on a screen?
options: Defenders exchange assignments to cover the two offensive players
The offense exchanges the ball for a timeout
questions.explanation: Switching can prevent the ball handler from gaining separation.

questions.text: A player is fouled while shooting a successful three-pointer. Under standard rules, what is the possible award?
options: The basket counts and one free throw
The basket is erased and three free throws
Two points and two free throws
questions.explanation: A made field goal plus a shooting foul can produce an and-one.

questions.text: In FIBA play, how long is the shot clock after an offensive rebound following a shot that touches the ring?
questions.explanation: FIBA resets the shot clock to 14 after the offense regains such a rebound.

questions.text: What is the main risk of trapping a ball handler near the sideline?
options: It can force a difficult pass but may leave other attackers open
It automatically creates a traveling violation
It guarantees the offense loses possession
questions.explanation: A trap pressures the ball but creates potential passing outlets.

questions.text: A defender tips a pass, and the offensive team retrieves it in its own backcourt after previously establishing frontcourt control. What must be considered?
options: Whether the defense caused the ball to return, which can exempt the offense from backcourt violation
A backcourt violation is automatic on every retreat
A basket is awarded to defense
The ball is dead whenever tipped
questions.explanation: A defensive touch that sends the ball back changes the backcourt analysis.

questions.text: Why does a team intentionally foul late in a close game?
options: To stop the clock and make opponents earn points at the line
To add a point to its own score automatically
To reset the game to the opening tip
To remove the shot clock from the rules
questions.explanation: A foul stops time, trading a possible free-throw attempt for possession opportunity.

questions.text: What score comes after 30 in a standard tennis game?
questions.explanation: The standard sequence is love, 15, 30, 40, then game, subject to deuce.

questions.text: What is the name for a score of zero in tennis?
questions.explanation: Tennis calls a score of zero love.

questions.text: How many serves does a player normally get to start a point?
questions.explanation: A player has a first and second serve.

questions.text: Which surface is used at Wimbledon?
questions.explanation: Wimbledon is played on grass courts.

questions.text: What piece of equipment is used to strike the ball?
questions.explanation: Tennis players strike the ball with a racket.

questions.text: At deuce in a standard game, a player generally needs:
questions.explanation: A player must win advantage and then the next point.

questions.text: Where must a legal tennis return land during a rally?
options: Inside the opponent's court, including its boundary lines
questions.explanation: A returned ball is in if it lands within the opponent's court.

questions.text: What happens after a first serve fault?
options: The server gets a second serve
questions.explanation: A second fault on that point would be a double fault.

questions.text: A serve clips the net and lands in the correct service box. What is the call?
questions.explanation: A net-cord serve landing in the correct box is replayed.

questions.text: What is a double fault?
options: Two service faults on one point, awarding the point to the receiver
questions.explanation: Failing both serve attempts loses the point.

questions.text: Which Grand Slam is played on hard courts in Melbourne?
questions.explanation: The Australian Open is played in Melbourne on hard courts.

questions.text: What does a break of serve mean?
options: The receiver wins a game in which the opponent served
The server wins a game at love
A player takes a medical timeout
questions.explanation: Breaking serve means winning the opponent's service game.

questions.text: In doubles, which court area is added compared with singles?
questions.explanation: Doubles uses the wider alleys during rallies.

questions.text: A ball lands exactly on a singles sideline. Is it in?
options: Yes; lines are part of the court
No; the ball must miss every line
Only if called by the server
questions.explanation: A ball touching a boundary line is in.

questions.text: What is a groundstroke?
options: A forehand or backhand hit after the ball bounces
A serve that hits the ground twice
A shot struck only from the net
A ball hit outside the court
questions.explanation: Groundstrokes are forehands or backhands after a bounce.

questions.text: Which Grand Slam tournament is played on clay courts?
questions.explanation: The French Open is played on clay at Roland-Garros.

questions.text: At 6-6 in a set using a standard tiebreak, players change ends after which points?
questions.explanation: Players switch ends after each six points in a standard tiebreak.

questions.text: In a 10-point match tiebreak, when does the change of ends normally occur?
questions.explanation: Players change ends after each six points in a match tiebreak.

questions.text: A server's foot touches the baseline before the racket strikes the serve. What is the call?
questions.explanation: The server must not touch the baseline before contact.

questions.text: A returner is not ready and makes no attempt to return a serve. What is the usual ruling if the serve is otherwise good?
options: The point is replayed if the receiver was not ready
questions.explanation: A receiver who is not ready is not penalized for failing to return.

questions.text: A player touches the net while the ball is in play. What is the usual consequence?
options: The opponent receives a let serve
No consequence if the ball is still moving
questions.explanation: Touching the net during play loses the point.

questions.text: What is the standard order of service in a doubles tiebreak?
options: The player due to serve serves the first point; thereafter service rotates every two points
Each player serves six points in turn
The same server serves the whole tiebreak
The receiving team chooses each point
questions.explanation: After the initial point, players serve in two-point turns.

questions.text: A ball in play strikes a player's body before bouncing. What is the ruling?
options: The player wins if it was a volley
questions.explanation: A player touched by the ball loses the point.

questions.text: A doubles serve touches the net and lands in the correct service court. What is the call under standard rules?
questions.explanation: A valid net-cord serve is replayed as a let.

questions.text: What is the effect of a foot fault on a second serve?
options: It is a double fault and the receiver wins the point
The server receives a warning only
questions.explanation: A fault on the second serve completes a double fault.

questions.text: In a no-ad scoring game, what happens at deuce?
options: The next point decides the game, with receiver choosing the court side
Players must win two points consecutively
The server gets an extra serve
questions.explanation: No-ad scoring uses one deciding point at deuce.

questions.text: What is the main tactical benefit of hitting a deep, high topspin shot?
options: It can push the opponent back while adding bounce and margin over the net
It stops the ball before it crosses the net
questions.explanation: Topspin permits a higher trajectory and a heavy, deep bounce.

questions.text: A player serves to the wrong service court, and the error is noticed after the point. What is generally done with that point under the rules?
options: The point stands; correct the serving side or court for the next point
Replay every point in the game
Ignore the error for the rest of the match
questions.explanation: Points played before discovery generally stand.

questions.text: A ball hits a singles net post and lands inside the correct court during a rally. What is the result?
options: The striker loses the point because the post is out of bounds
questions.explanation: In singles, the doubles posts and area outside them are out.

questions.text: A player reaches over the net to hit a ball that has not crossed to their side. Is that normally legal?
options: No; the player must wait for the ball to cross, except permitted follow-through
Yes, whenever the player can reach it
Yes, if the shot is a volley
questions.explanation: A player cannot strike the ball before it crosses the net.

questions.text: How often are the Summer Olympic Games usually held?
questions.explanation: The Summer Olympics are normally held every four years.

questions.text: What does the Olympic oath traditionally ask participants to uphold?
options: Fair play and respect for the rules
A pledge to host the next Games
questions.explanation: The oath emphasizes fair competition and respect.

questions.text: What flame is lit as part of the Olympic tradition?
questions.explanation: The Olympic flame is carried to the host city.

questions.text: What is an Olympic mascot?
options: A character representing a particular edition of the Games
An official who times every race
A medal awarded to the host
questions.explanation: Mascots are characters created to represent a Games edition.

questions.text: What is the Olympic medal ceremony for?
options: Recognizing the leading athletes in an event
questions.explanation: Medal ceremonies honor athletes' event results.

questions.text: The Olympic rings represent how many continents in the traditional symbolism?
questions.explanation: The five interlocking rings symbolize the union of the inhabited continents.

questions.text: What does a host city's Olympic emblem primarily identify?
questions.explanation: Each edition uses a distinct emblem for its identity.

questions.text: Which city hosted the 2008 Summer Olympic Games?
questions.explanation: Beijing was host city in 2008.

questions.text: What is the Olympic Truce intended to promote?
options: A period of peace and safe participation around the Games
questions.explanation: The ancient-inspired truce calls for peace and safe passage.

questions.text: How are the Summer and Winter Olympics generally scheduled in the modern cycle?
options: They occur in the same city every year
Winter precedes Summer by one month
They share one Games every four years
questions.explanation: The events alternate, leaving two years between editions.

questions.text: What determines whether a sport is included in an Olympic programme?
options: IOC processes and the applicable programme decisions
A vote by the winning athlete
questions.explanation: Inclusion follows Olympic governance and programme procedures.

questions.text: Why were the Tokyo 2020 Olympics held in 2021?
options: They were postponed because of the COVID-19 pandemic
The host city changed at the last minute
The Winter Games took their dates
The event was converted to a youth festival
questions.explanation: The pandemic forced a one-year postponement.

questions.text: What is the role of a host city during the Olympic Games?
options: Stage the events using venues and services under host arrangements
questions.explanation: The host organizes and stages the event with Olympic partners.

questions.text: Which is the correct order of Olympic podium medals from first to third?
questions.explanation: Gold denotes first, silver second, and bronze third.

questions.text: What does a Paralympic Games primarily showcase?
options: Elite sport for athletes with eligible impairments
questions.explanation: The Paralympics are an international multi-sport event for athletes with disabilities.

questions.text: Which city hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896?
questions.explanation: Athens hosted the first modern Olympics in 1896.

questions.text: The Olympic Charter's motto was updated in 2021. What word was added to the Latin motto?
questions.explanation: The motto became Citius, Altius, Fortius – Communiter.

questions.text: Which edition was the first Summer Olympics to include women competitors?
questions.explanation: Women competed for the first time at Paris 1900.

questions.text: Why was the 1940 Summer Olympics not held in its originally selected host city, Tokyo?
options: The Games were cancelled because of World War II
Tokyo changed the venue to a winter resort
The IOC moved it to Paris and held it
It was postponed by a pandemic
questions.explanation: The 1940 Games were cancelled during the war.

questions.text: Which city hosted the first Winter Games held separately from the Summer Olympics?
questions.explanation: Chamonix hosted the inaugural Winter Olympics.

questions.text: What does the Olympic Charter establish?
options: Fundamental principles and rules governing the Olympic Movement
Only the schedule of one host city's events
The results of the most recent Games
questions.explanation: The Charter is the codification of Olympic principles and governance.

questions.text: Which city was the first to host the Summer Olympics three times, after its 2012 Games?
questions.explanation: London hosted in 1908, 1948, and 2012.

questions.text: What was distinctive about the 1956 Melbourne Olympics for equestrian events?
options: Equestrian events were held in Stockholm due to quarantine restrictions
The events were replaced by motor racing
They were moved to London due to weather
questions.explanation: Quarantine rules prevented horses from entering Australia, so events took place in Stockholm.

questions.text: Which city hosted the 1980 Summer Olympics?
questions.explanation: Moscow hosted the 1980 Games.

questions.text: Which edition is notable as the first Summer Olympics held in South America?
questions.explanation: Rio 2016 was the first Summer Games in South America.

questions.text: What distinguishes the Youth Olympic Games from the main Olympic Games?
options: They are designed for young athletes and include sport plus education/culture
They are exclusively for retired Olympians
They award medals only in winter sports
They are held every year in one city
questions.explanation: The youth event combines competition with educational and cultural activities.

questions.text: How many rings are in the Olympic symbol, and what do their colours imply?
options: Five rings; the colours with the white background include every national flag's colours
Six rings; each stands for a medal
Five rings; each is a host city
Seven rings; each represents a continent
questions.explanation: At least one colour from every national flag appears in the symbol's palette.

questions.text: Which two consecutive Summer Games were boycotted by major groups during the Cold War?
questions.explanation: The US-led boycott affected Moscow; the Soviet-led boycott followed in Los Angeles.

questions.text: What is the IOC's role in selecting a host for the Olympic Games?
options: Its members elect the host through the established candidature process
The previous host appoints the next city unilaterally
The UN assigns a city by lottery
The winning athlete selects the venue
questions.explanation: Host election is an IOC responsibility under its procedures.

questions.text: Why are Olympic records distinct from world records?
options: Olympic records are performances achieved at the Olympic Games; world records span eligible competitions
Olympic records are always faster than world records
They are different names for medal counts
Only host nations may hold Olympic records
questions.explanation: The records differ by the competitions in which the performances occurred.

questions.text: In a marathon, what is the official race distance?
questions.explanation: The marathon distance is 42.195 kilometres.

questions.text: What does a personal best describe?
options: An athlete's own top performance to date
The best result in world history
questions.explanation: A personal best is the athlete's highest or fastest mark.

questions.text: What does a shared sports record indicate?
options: More than one competitor has achieved the same recognized mark
A team won by sharing its points
questions.explanation: A tie can leave multiple athletes credited with the record.

questions.text: What does a basketball single-game scoring record measure?
options: The most points scored by one player in one game
questions.explanation: It records an individual's points in a single game.

questions.text: Which event result is recorded in a high-jump record?
questions.explanation: High-jump marks record the bar height successfully cleared.

questions.text: A hat-trick in many team sports generally means a player has:
options: Scored three times in one game
questions.explanation: A hat-trick commonly means three scoring achievements by one player in a match.

questions.text: Why must a track world record usually be ratified by the governing body?
options: To verify rules, timing, conditions, and evidence
To select the athlete's next event
To decide who received the most applause
questions.explanation: Ratification checks that the performance meets record requirements.

questions.text: A runner improves a 10.20-second record to 10.15 seconds. By how much did the time improve?
questions.explanation: 10.20 minus 10.15 equals 0.05 seconds.

questions.text: Why can a wind-assisted sprint time fail to qualify as an outdoor world record?
options: Wind may exceed the legal limit
The runner must use a different lane
questions.explanation: Rules limit aiding wind for record eligibility.

questions.text: Which performance is higher in the long jump?
questions.explanation: The longest measured distance is the best jump.

questions.text: A basketball player has 30 points, 10 rebounds, and 10 assists in one game. What is this achievement called?
questions.explanation: Double digits in three statistical categories make a triple-double.

questions.text: What does a season record of 20-10 usually mean in a league listing?
options: Twenty home games and ten away
questions.explanation: The common win-loss format lists wins first.

questions.text: Two athletes tie a record height in high jump. What breaks the tie under standard competition rules?
options: Countback using misses at the tied and earlier heights
questions.explanation: Countback considers failures at heights, with a jump-off possible by rules.

questions.text: A team wins 12 matches in a row, draws the next, then wins again. What is its longest winning streak in that sequence?
questions.explanation: A draw ends the consecutive-win run.

questions.text: Why are records in different sports not directly comparable by their raw numbers?
options: Events use different rules, units, and performance demands
All records use the same unit
A larger number always means better
questions.explanation: Context and measurement determine what a record means.

questions.text: Which athletics event combines ten track-and-field disciplines?
questions.explanation: The decathlon consists of ten events.

questions.text: In athletics, why can a record be wind-legal in the 200 m but not the 100 m under the common +2.0 m/s limit?
options: Record eligibility considers the wind reading in the specific event and round
The 200 m has no wind limit
Wind is measured only for field events
questions.explanation: Each performance's measured wind must satisfy the event's ratification rule.

questions.text: A runner's official 100 m time is 9.58 seconds and a later wind-assisted mark is 9.52. Which is the legal record if the latter wind exceeds the limit?
options: Neither because lower time is invalid
questions.explanation: An over-limit wind mark is not eligible as an official record.

questions.text: How does the decathlon scoring system compare performances across its ten events?
options: Event-specific tables convert marks into points, which are summed
The longest event distance alone decides
Every event gives one point per metre
questions.explanation: Each discipline's performance earns points from standardized tables.

questions.text: In a record progression, an athlete lowers a time from 44.90 to 44.72 seconds. What is the improvement in milliseconds?
questions.explanation: 0.18 seconds equals 180 milliseconds.

questions.text: Why can a swimming world record be listed separately for a short-course and long-course pool?
options: The pool lengths and turn frequency differ, affecting performance conditions
Short course is a different sport with no records
Long-course times are always slower by exactly one second
Records count only the number of turns
questions.explanation: Course length changes the race layout and number of turns.

questions.text: A batter scores 100 runs in 80 balls and another scores 100 in 60 balls. Which statistic captures their scoring pace?
questions.explanation: Strike rate measures runs scored per 100 balls faced.

questions.text: A pitcher records 20 wins in a baseball season but has a higher earned-run average than a teammate with 15 wins. What does this illustrate?
options: Win totals and run prevention measure different aspects
The pitcher with more wins must have the lower ERA
questions.explanation: Team support and run prevention can make records diverge.

questions.text: In tennis, why is a Grand Slam title count not always equivalent to a calendar-year Grand Slam?
options: A calendar-year Grand Slam requires winning all four majors in the same year
Any four career majors count as one calendar slam
A calendar year has three majors
questions.explanation: The calendar-year condition requires all four in one season.

questions.text: A cyclist's fastest time is set on a course with a substantial downhill, while another record is on a flat certified course. What is the key comparison issue?
options: Course profile and record category must be comparable
The downhill time is automatically the official record
Times cannot be measured on hills
questions.explanation: Course conditions strongly affect performance and record validity.

questions.text: Which method best distinguishes a genuine all-time record from a promotional claim?
options: Check the sport governing body's ratification and event conditions
Accept the largest number on a poster
questions.explanation: Official ratification provides the relevant verification.

questions.text: In baseball, what is a perfect game?
options: A pitcher or pitching staff retires every batter faced with no one reaching base
A team wins by ten runs
A pitcher strikes out every batter
A game ends after nine pitches
questions.explanation: No opposing batter may reach base during a perfect game.

questions.text: A record is set in a race with a following wind of +2.4 m/s where the applicable limit is +2.0 m/s. What is the proper status?
options: Excellent performance but wind-assisted and ineligible for that record
Legal record because it is under 3.0
questions.explanation: The wind exceeds the record-eligibility threshold.

questions.text: How is a points-based record in a multi-event competition different from a single-event record?
options: It aggregates scored performances across multiple disciplines
It is based solely on elapsed time
questions.explanation: A combined-events total sums points from several events.

questions.text: When comparing a national record with a world record, what must be checked first?
options: The governing body's recognition, event rules, and eligible conditions
Whether the athlete has a gold medal
questions.explanation: Recognition and conditions define the record category.

questions.text: What does a film director primarily guide?
options: The creative and dramatic realization of a film
questions.explanation: The director leads the film’s artistic and dramatic execution.

questions.text: What does a film premiere refer to?
options: An early public showing of a film
questions.explanation: A premiere is an initial public screening.

questions.text: What information is commonly listed in a film's end credits?
questions.explanation: Credits acknowledge performers and crew.

questions.text: What is a movie's written dialogue and action plan called?
questions.explanation: A screenplay contains a film's scenes and dialogue.

questions.text: What does a film editor primarily do?
options: Select and assemble shots into a sequence
questions.explanation: Editing shapes the film from recorded footage.

questions.text: Which award is presented by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences?
questions.explanation: The Academy Awards are commonly called the Oscars.

questions.text: What does a film's production design establish?
options: The visual look of settings, props, and physical environments
questions.explanation: Production design creates the story's physical visual world.

questions.text: What is a cameo in a movie?
options: A brief appearance by a notable performer
A scene filmed in one take
questions.explanation: A cameo is a small, often recognizable role.

questions.text: What is diegetic sound?
options: Sound that exists within the story world
questions.explanation: Characters could hear diegetic sounds in the scene.

questions.text: What does a cinematographer chiefly oversee?
questions.explanation: Cinematography shapes framing, lighting, and camera images.

questions.text: What is a sequel?
options: A film continuing a story from an earlier film
A remake of an unrelated story
questions.explanation: A sequel follows events or characters from an earlier work.

questions.text: What does a film's aspect ratio describe?
options: The proportional width and height of the image
The ratio of actors to crew
questions.explanation: Aspect ratio expresses frame width relative to height.

questions.text: What is a practical effect?
options: An effect created physically on set rather than solely digitally
An effect added only in subtitles
questions.explanation: Practical effects are produced physically during filming.

questions.text: What is a documentary film primarily intended to do?
options: Tell only an invented fantasy story
Record a live music track only
questions.explanation: Documentaries address real-world subjects, though methods vary.

questions.text: What does a film's theatrical release refer to?
options: Its distribution to cinemas for public exhibition
questions.explanation: A theatrical release makes a film available in cinemas.

questions.text: In filmmaking, a “long take” is a shot that:
options: Continues for an extended duration without a cut
Shows the entire film in one frame
questions.explanation: A long take maintains a shot for an extended time before editing.

questions.text: What is an establishing shot usually used to do?
options: Orient viewers to a location or setting
questions.explanation: It establishes spatial or contextual information for a scene.

questions.text: In continuity editing, what does the 180-degree rule help preserve?
options: Consistent screen direction and spatial relationships
questions.explanation: The axis rule keeps characters' positions intelligible across cuts.

questions.text: What is a match cut?
options: A cut linking shots through visual or conceptual similarity
A cut that removes all sound
A shot filmed by two cameras only
A fade to black at the end
questions.explanation: A match cut creates a transition through a shared element.

questions.text: What does an unreliable narrator in a film do?
options: Provides an account viewers have reason to question
questions.explanation: The film signals that the narrator's version may be misleading.

questions.text: What is cross-cutting commonly used to suggest?
options: Parallel actions occurring in different places, often at the same time
questions.explanation: Alternating edits connect simultaneous or related action.

questions.text: In film sound, what is a leitmotif?
options: A recurring musical idea associated with a character or concept
questions.explanation: A recurring motif helps link music to story elements.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a sound bridge across a cut?
options: To carry sound from one scene into another and smooth the transition
To repair a physical bridge on set
questions.explanation: Sound continuing across an edit links adjacent scenes.

questions.text: What is a film's blocking?
options: Planned movement and positioning of performers in a scene
questions.explanation: Blocking organizes actors' positions and movement.

questions.text: What does a shallow depth of field typically do?
options: Keeps a limited range of distance in focus
questions.explanation: A shallow focus plane separates a subject from blurred surroundings.

questions.text: What is ADR in film post-production?
options: Re-recording dialogue in a studio to replace or improve production audio
A camera movement toward an actor
A method of choosing a film rating
questions.explanation: Automated dialogue replacement records dialogue after filming.

questions.text: What is a location scout seeking?
options: Suitable real-world places for filming scenes
questions.explanation: Scouting identifies locations that meet production needs.

questions.text: What distinguishes a remake from a sequel?
options: A remake retells an earlier film; a sequel continues its story
questions.explanation: Remakes revisit a prior work; sequels extend it.

questions.text: Why might a director use a wide shot before a close-up?
options: To establish the setting before emphasizing a subject or detail
To remove the need for editing
questions.explanation: The wide shot gives context; the close-up directs attention.

questions.text: What does color grading do in post-production?
options: Adjusts the image's color and tonal appearance
questions.explanation: Color grading shapes the finished film's visual palette.

questions.text: Anime is animation most strongly associated with which country?
questions.explanation: Anime is a broad term for animation associated with Japan.

questions.text: What is an anime key visual commonly used for?
options: Promoting a series with a representative illustration
questions.explanation: A key visual is promotional art representing a title.

questions.text: Which role is credited with directing an anime episode?
questions.explanation: The episode director oversees that episode's staging and execution.

questions.text: What are in-between drawings for?
options: Creating motion between the major key poses
questions.explanation: In-betweens fill the movement between key frames.

questions.text: Which role voices an animated character in the Japanese production industry?
questions.explanation: Seiyuu is the Japanese term for a voice actor.

questions.text: In anime production, a storyboard mainly helps plan:
options: The sequence and composition of scenes
questions.explanation: Storyboards map shots and action before full animation.

questions.text: What does an anime episode's key animation primarily define?
questions.explanation: Key animators create major poses that guide in-between work.

questions.text: What is an anime cour?
options: A roughly three-month broadcast block, often about 11–13 episodes
questions.explanation: Cour describes a seasonal broadcast segment.

questions.text: What does a sakuga sequence commonly refer to among anime fans?
options: A notably expressive or fluidly animated passage
A recap with no new footage
questions.explanation: The term often praises standout animation.

questions.text: What is an opening theme in an anime series?
options: The song and sequence introducing an episode
A music track heard only in cinemas
questions.explanation: An opening theme accompanies the episode's opening sequence.

questions.text: What is an OVA traditionally distributed as?
options: An original video animation released directly to video
questions.explanation: OVA means original video animation, traditionally video-first.

questions.text: What is an in-between animator responsible for?
options: Drawing intermediate frames between key poses
questions.explanation: In-betweens create motion between key animation drawings.

questions.text: What does a character designer establish for an anime?
options: The character's visual appearance and model references
questions.explanation: Designs guide consistent character depiction.

questions.text: What is a recap episode?
options: An episode that revisits previously shown story material
The first episode of a new franchise
questions.explanation: Recaps summarize earlier events, sometimes with new framing.

questions.text: What is a light novel?
options: A Japanese prose-fiction format often illustrated
questions.explanation: Light novels are prose books often featuring illustrations.

questions.text: What does “manga” generally refer to?
questions.explanation: Manga refers to Japanese comics and graphic novels.

questions.text: What does a key animator contribute to a traditionally produced anime scene?
options: Major poses and movement keys that define the action
questions.explanation: Key animation establishes essential poses and timing.

questions.text: Why can limited animation still create a strong impression of motion?
options: Composition, held poses, camera movement, and selective motion direct attention
Every frame must be fully redrawn
It replaces sound with still images
The frame rate is always higher
questions.explanation: Selective movement and staging make limited drawings expressive.

questions.text: What is a layout artist's role in an anime sequence?
options: Plan shot composition, staging, and spatial relationships
questions.explanation: Layouts bridge storyboards and detailed animation by defining each shot.

questions.text: What is compositing in digital anime production?
options: Combining animated layers, backgrounds, effects, and camera treatments into shots
questions.explanation: Compositing integrates separate visual elements into the final image.

questions.text: What is the function of an animation director on an episode?
options: Maintain drawing consistency and correct key animation
Choose the TV network's advertising rates
questions.explanation: The role supervises character drawing and animation consistency.

questions.text: How does a storyboard differ from a finished animation layout?
options: It sketches sequence and beats; layouts specify shot composition in greater detail
A storyboard is always a soundtrack
A layout lists only the cast
They are interchangeable with no production distinction
questions.explanation: Storyboards plan scene flow; layouts refine individual shot staging.

questions.text: What is a sakuga-focused cut often notable for?
options: Distinctive, carefully animated movement or expressive drawing
questions.explanation: The term highlights standout animation craftsmanship.

questions.text: What is the source material in an anime adaptation?
options: The earlier work being adapted, such as manga, a novel, or a game
questions.explanation: Source material is the pre-existing narrative or work.

questions.text: Why might an anime adaptation use an anime-original ending?
options: The source may be unfinished or the production may choose a different resolution
Every manga ends without a story
It is required by all broadcasters
questions.explanation: Production timing or creative choices can lead to an original ending.

questions.text: What is a split-cour anime season?
options: A season broadcast in separate blocks with a break between them
One episode divided into two screens
A series shown simultaneously in two languages
A theatrical film released in two countries
questions.explanation: A split cour separates broadcast blocks by a hiatus.

questions.text: In Japanese animation credits, what does the term seiyuu identify?
questions.explanation: Seiyuu refers to voice performers.

questions.text: What is the role of a production committee in many anime projects?
options: A group of companies sharing financing, rights, and commercial interests
A panel that draws every frame
A government body that writes scripts
A team of episode reviewers only
questions.explanation: Committees coordinate investment and associated rights among partners.

questions.text: What distinction does a key frame set provide over in-between drawings?
options: It defines major poses and timing points for the motion
It is always the episode's first image
It adds spoken dialogue to silent footage
It is used only for subtitles
questions.explanation: Key frames establish the motion's principal poses.

questions.text: Why can a manga chapter count and anime episode count differ substantially?
options: Adaptation may condense, expand, reorder, or add material
Each chapter must equal exactly one episode
questions.explanation: Adaptation pacing and production choices alter the amount covered.

questions.text: What is a pilot episode?
options: An initial episode made to introduce or sell a series
The final episode of every series
A show broadcast only on aircraft
questions.explanation: A pilot introduces a series concept and is often used to evaluate it.

questions.text: What is a television season?
options: A group of episodes released as one planned run
questions.explanation: A season groups a series' episodes into a release run.

questions.text: What is a TV show's theme song?
options: A recurring musical piece associated with the program
A summary of the final episode
questions.explanation: A theme song identifies or introduces a program.

questions.text: What is a series premiere?
options: The first episode broadcast for a series
questions.explanation: The premiere introduces a show's first episode.

questions.text: What does a sitcom usually mean?
questions.explanation: Sitcom abbreviates situation comedy.

questions.text: A season finale is usually:
options: The closing episode of a season
The first episode of a season
questions.explanation: A season finale closes a season’s episode run.

questions.text: What is a cliffhanger ending?
options: A suspenseful unresolved moment that encourages viewers to continue
A final scene explaining every mystery
questions.explanation: A cliffhanger leaves an important question unresolved.

questions.text: What does serialized storytelling mean in television?
options: Story developments continue across multiple episodes
Episodes are aired in reverse order
A show has no recurring plot
questions.explanation: Serialized plots unfold over several episodes.

questions.text: What is syndication in television distribution?
options: Licensing a program to broadcasters or stations beyond its original network
questions.explanation: Syndication distributes a program to additional outlets.

questions.text: What is a bottle episode?
options: An episode produced with a limited set, cast, or locations
questions.explanation: Bottle episodes use constrained production resources.

questions.text: What is a cold open?
options: A scene before the opening credits or title sequence
A preview shown a week earlier
questions.explanation: A cold open starts the episode before its titles.

questions.text: What does a showrunner typically do?
options: Lead the creative and production direction of a television series
questions.explanation: Showrunners oversee a series' writing and production.

questions.text: What is a midseason finale?
options: An episode marking a pause in a season's broadcast run
The last episode of the entire series
questions.explanation: It provides a break point before later episodes return.

questions.text: What is a spin-off series?
options: A new show centered on a character or world from an existing show
A remake of a foreign film only
questions.explanation: Spin-offs develop an element of a prior series into its own show.

questions.text: What does a laugh track provide in some sitcoms?
options: Recorded audience laughter mixed into the episode
questions.explanation: A laugh track is prerecorded audience laughter.

questions.text: A show released with every episode available at once is commonly described as:
questions.explanation: A binge release makes a full season or batch available together.

questions.text: What does a television writers' room do?
options: Develops episode stories, outlines, and scripts collaboratively
questions.explanation: Writers collaborate on story and script development.

questions.text: What is a story arc in a television series?
options: A narrative thread that develops across multiple episodes
The curve of an episode's ratings
questions.explanation: Story arcs progress over time rather than resolving in one scene.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a continuity supervisor on a TV production?
options: Track details across shots and episodes to maintain consistency
questions.explanation: Continuity tracking catches mismatched props, costumes, and story details.

questions.text: What does a teaser do in a television episode structure?
options: Previews a hook or conflict, often before the main titles
Summarizes the entire series after the finale
questions.explanation: A teaser opens with an attention-grabbing scene.

questions.text: What is a procedural drama typically structured around?
options: A case or problem resolved in each episode, often with ongoing character plots
A single plot that never advances
A contest with no recurring characters
questions.explanation: Procedurals feature recurring processes or cases.

questions.text: How does a serialized drama differ from a mostly episodic series?
options: Its central plot depends more on developments across episodes
Every episode begins with a new unrelated setting
It cannot have a season finale
questions.explanation: Serialized narratives rely on cumulative story progression.

questions.text: What does a network's pilot commitment generally concern?
options: An agreement to produce or evaluate a pilot under specified terms
An order for the series finale
questions.explanation: Pilot commitments specify development or production obligations.

questions.text: Why might a show use a bottle episode during a season?
options: To focus on character and story while using fewer sets or resources
To introduce an entirely new cast each week
questions.explanation: Constrained production can support character-driven storytelling.

questions.text: What is a backdoor pilot?
options: An episode of an existing show designed to introduce a potential spin-off
A pilot broadcast without a title
A series finale aired out of order
questions.explanation: It tests a spin-off concept within another program.

questions.text: What does a table read allow a TV production to assess?
options: How the script's dialogue and scenes play aloud with the cast
questions.explanation: A cast reading reveals pacing and dialogue issues.

questions.text: What is a production order of a season?
options: The commissioned episode count, which may differ from the number aired
A list of characters by screen time
questions.explanation: Production order indicates how many episodes are commissioned.

questions.text: What is a narrative A-plot commonly?
options: The primary story thread of an episode
A scene filmed with camera A
questions.explanation: The A-plot is usually the episode's main storyline.

questions.text: Why can broadcast order differ from production order?
options: Networks may schedule completed episodes differently for programming reasons
Episodes must air in alphabetical title order
questions.explanation: Scheduling decisions can change the sequence audiences see.

questions.text: What is a show's canon?
options: The events and facts treated as officially part of its story continuity
A camera lens used in each episode
questions.explanation: Canon denotes accepted story-world continuity.

questions.text: How many notes are in a standard major scale?
