questions.explanation: A major scale has seven distinct scale degrees before the octave.

questions.text: What does the dynamic marking forte ask a performer to do?
questions.explanation: Forte indicates a loud dynamic.

questions.text: What does a sharp sign do to a written note?
questions.explanation: A sharp raises the pitch by a semitone.

questions.text: What is a musical interval?
options: The pitch distance between two notes
The length of a song title
questions.explanation: Intervals describe the distance between pitches.

questions.text: What is the written collection of musical notes called?
questions.explanation: A musical score notates a composition.

questions.text: What does tempo describe in music?
questions.explanation: Tempo is the pace of the underlying beat.

questions.text: What does a time signature tell a musician?
options: How beats are grouped in each measure
questions.explanation: The signature indicates beats per measure and their note value.

questions.text: What does a crescendo instruct a performer to do?
questions.explanation: Crescendo means a gradual increase in dynamics.

questions.text: What is syncopation?
options: Emphasis on unexpected or weak beats
A melody played only in unison
questions.explanation: Syncopation shifts accents away from expected strong beats.

questions.text: What is a chord?
questions.explanation: A chord combines two or more pitches.

questions.text: What does a key signature indicate?
options: The sharps or flats that define a piece's tonal framework
The number of musicians on stage
questions.explanation: Key signatures mark the tonal collection's recurring alterations.

questions.text: What is a melody?
options: A sequence of pitches perceived as a musical line
The speed of the beat only
questions.explanation: Melody is an organized succession of notes.

questions.text: What does legato mean in performance?
options: Notes are played smoothly and connected
questions.explanation: Legato calls for connected, smooth articulation.

questions.text: What does a rest in written music indicate?
options: A period of silence for the specified duration
questions.explanation: Rests notate silence lasting a defined rhythmic value.

questions.text: Which interval spans three semitones in common Western equal temperament?
questions.explanation: A minor third spans three semitones.

questions.text: In equal temperament, how many semitones make an octave?
questions.explanation: A standard octave spans twelve semitones.

questions.text: In a major key, what is the usual quality of the triad built on scale degree five?
questions.explanation: The dominant triad in a major key is major.

questions.text: What is a tritone in equal temperament?
questions.explanation: The tritone spans six semitones.

questions.text: What is counterpoint?
options: The combination of independent melodic lines
questions.explanation: Counterpoint organizes multiple distinct melodic voices.

questions.text: In common-practice harmony, what is a modulation?
options: A change from one tonal center or key to another
A sudden stop in the beat
A repeat of the same chord only
A shift from piano to forte
questions.explanation: Modulation establishes a new key area.

questions.text: What distinguishes a natural minor scale from a major scale in scale degrees?
options: Its third, sixth, and seventh are lowered
Its second and fifth are raised
questions.explanation: The natural minor pattern lowers degrees 3, 6, and 7 relative to major.

questions.text: What is a suspension in tonal harmony?
options: A prepared note held into a new chord before resolving by step
A chord played only on the first beat
An unplanned pause in the performance
A note doubled at the octave
questions.explanation: A suspension delays a chord tone's resolution.

questions.text: What does a 6/8 time signature commonly imply about beat grouping?
options: One beat divided into six measures
questions.explanation: Compound duple 6/8 is commonly felt in two groups of three eighth notes.

questions.text: What is an enharmonic equivalent?
options: Different note spellings that sound the same in equal temperament
Two notes with different sound and spelling
questions.explanation: For example, C-sharp and D-flat share a pitch in equal temperament.

questions.text: How does a dominant seventh chord commonly resolve in functional harmony?
options: Its tendency tones move toward the tonic harmony
It always moves to the subdominant
questions.explanation: The dominant seventh typically resolves to tonic.

questions.text: What is the overtone series above a fundamental?
options: A sequence of partial frequencies related to the fundamental
questions.explanation: Overtones occur at frequency multiples of a fundamental.

questions.text: What is equal temperament designed to do across keys?
options: Distribute tuning compromises so intervals permit playing in all keys
Tune all instruments to one note only
questions.explanation: Equal temperament balances interval sizes for flexible modulation.

questions.text: In orchestration, what is a transposing instrument?
options: An instrument whose written pitch differs from its sounding pitch
An instrument that cannot play melodies
A keyboard tuned to one key
A percussion instrument without a pitch
questions.explanation: Its notation sounds at a different pitch, such as a B-flat clarinet.

questions.text: What does a fugue exposition establish?
options: The subject entering successively in different voices
The tempo change at the end
questions.explanation: The exposition presents the fugue subject in its voices.

questions.text: What is a polyrhythm?
options: Two or more contrasting rhythmic patterns sounding simultaneously
A chord progression in many keys
questions.explanation: Polyrhythm layers distinct rhythmic divisions at once.

questions.text: What does “NPC” commonly stand for in a video game?
questions.explanation: An NPC is a character not controlled directly by a player.

questions.text: What does a game's tutorial usually teach?
questions.explanation: Tutorials introduce core play mechanics.

questions.text: Which device is commonly used to control a character on a console?
questions.explanation: A controller sends player inputs to the console.

questions.text: In a game, what is a level?
options: A stage or area of play
questions.explanation: Levels divide play into stages or spaces.

questions.text: What does a health bar commonly represent?
questions.explanation: It visualizes health remaining before defeat.

questions.text: In a multiplayer game, latency most directly refers to:
options: Delay between an action and its network response
questions.explanation: Latency is the time delay in communication between systems.

questions.text: In a role-playing game, what does a skill tree let players do?
options: Unlock abilities through chosen progression paths
questions.explanation: Skill trees structure character ability progression.

questions.text: What is a hitbox?
options: An invisible region used to detect collisions or attacks
A box containing a game's retail disc
A menu for selecting audio tracks
A device that measures frame rate
questions.explanation: Hitboxes determine when game objects interact.

questions.text: Why might a game use checkpoints?
options: To let play resume from a saved progress point
To verify a player's real-world identity
To improve a monitor's color range
To increase the size of a game map
questions.explanation: Checkpoints reduce repeated play after failure.

questions.text: What does matchmaking typically use to form competitive teams?
options: Player or team criteria such as skill and availability
The alphabetical order of game titles
questions.explanation: Matchmaking pairs participants using relevant criteria.

questions.text: A game patch is generally released to:
options: Fix issues or change game content
Turn a digital game into a board game
questions.explanation: Patches update software after release.

questions.text: What does a cooldown prevent a player from doing immediately?
questions.explanation: Cooldowns impose a wait before reuse.

questions.text: What is a game engine primarily responsible for?
options: Providing systems for graphics, physics, and game logic
Assigning game ratings in every country
questions.explanation: Engines provide reusable game-development tools.

questions.text: In a strategy game, fog of war usually hides:
options: Unseen portions of the map or enemy activity
All sound effects during a match
questions.explanation: Fog of war limits information about unexplored areas.

questions.text: What does cross-play allow in multiplayer gaming?
options: Players on different platforms to play together
One player to use two game titles at once
A game to run without any software
A controller to work as a monitor
questions.explanation: Cross-play connects supported gaming platforms.

questions.text: A game’s frame rate is measured in:
questions.explanation: Frame rate is the number of frames rendered each second.

questions.text: A game simulation runs at a fixed timestep while rendering varies. What is the main benefit?
options: More consistent physics updates across frame rates
Automatic balancing of every multiplayer match
questions.explanation: Fixed simulation steps improve determinism.

questions.text: Why can client-side prediction improve a responsive online game?
options: It displays likely movement before server confirmation
It removes the need for authoritative servers
It prevents every form of cheating
questions.explanation: Prediction masks network delay for players.

questions.text: What is the purpose of rollback netcode?
options: Revising briefly predicted game states when delayed inputs arrive
Restoring deleted save files from a publisher
questions.explanation: Rollback corrects predicted states using late inputs.

questions.text: In game AI, what does a behavior tree organize?
options: Conditional actions and decisions for an agent
questions.explanation: Behavior trees structure agent decision logic.

questions.text: Why use level-of-detail models in a 3D game?
options: To render distant objects with less geometric detail
To give every object a unique control scheme
To prevent players from changing camera views
To store more dialogue in each texture
questions.explanation: Simpler distant models reduce rendering work.

questions.text: What is occlusion culling intended to avoid?
options: Rendering objects hidden behind other geometry
questions.explanation: Hidden objects need not be drawn.

questions.text: A game's deterministic lockstep model requires peers to:
options: Advance the same simulation from synchronized inputs
Render identical pixels on different hardware
Use the same display refresh rate
Store all assets on one computer
questions.explanation: Shared inputs drive a synchronized deterministic simulation.

questions.text: Why can nondeterministic physics complicate replay synchronization?
options: Identical inputs may produce divergent states
It makes every frame render at once
It removes collision detection from gameplay
questions.explanation: State divergence breaks input-based replay.

questions.text: What is an entity-component-system architecture designed to separate?
options: Entities, data components, and processing systems
Game ratings, reviews, and release dates
questions.explanation: ECS separates identity, data, and behavior.

questions.text: Why might a game stream world assets as the player travels?
options: To limit memory use and loading pauses
To increase the number of controller buttons
questions.explanation: Streaming loads relevant assets progressively.

questions.text: What does input buffering commonly allow?
options: A button press just before an opportunity to register when it opens
A game to store unlimited video recordings
A network packet to skip authentication
A player to see hidden map regions
questions.explanation: Buffered input preserves timely player commands.

questions.text: In game design, why tune an economy's resource sinks?
options: To remove currency or resources and control accumulation
To connect an offline game to a server
To increase a character's animation rate
questions.explanation: Sinks counter resource creation and inflation.

questions.text: What problem can server-authoritative movement help mitigate?
questions.explanation: The server validates movement against game rules.

questions.text: What does procedural generation use to create game content?
options: Algorithms and rules rather than only hand-authored layouts
A player's microphone to build maps
A publisher's sales figures as textures
questions.explanation: Rules and algorithms construct generated content.

questions.text: Which organization publishes the annual Human Development Report?
options: International Union for Conservation of Nature
questions.explanation: The UN Development Programme publishes the Human Development Report.

questions.text: Which UN body includes all member states and debates global issues?
questions.explanation: The General Assembly includes all UN members.

questions.text: What is the main role of an election commission?
options: Administering or overseeing elections under applicable law
Negotiating international treaties for all states
questions.explanation: Election bodies oversee electoral processes.

questions.text: Which agreement is the founding treaty of the European Union?
questions.explanation: The Maastricht Treaty established the EU framework.

questions.text: What does a parliamentary opposition primarily do?
options: Scrutinize and challenge the government's actions
questions.explanation: Opposition parties hold government to account.

questions.text: The Paris Agreement is an international agreement focused on:
questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement sets a framework for addressing climate change.

questions.text: Which UN organ can authorize binding measures under the Charter's enforcement provisions?
questions.explanation: The Security Council has primary peace-and-security responsibility.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of a parliamentary question period?
options: Allow legislators to question ministers about government business
Conduct judicial trials in the legislature
Set exchange rates by public vote
questions.explanation: Question periods enable legislative scrutiny.

questions.text: What is a treaty ratification?
options: A state's formal confirmation of consent to be bound, under its procedures
A court's informal opinion on a proposal
A news outlet's translation of a treaty
A temporary suspension of diplomatic relations
questions.explanation: Ratification expresses formal treaty consent.

questions.text: Which institution proposes most EU legislation before the Parliament and Council consider it?
questions.explanation: The Commission generally holds the EU legislative initiative.

questions.text: What does proportional representation seek to link?
options: A party's seat share with its vote share
A country's population with its coastline
Tax revenue with the number of ministries
Court cases with the length of a constitution
questions.explanation: Proportional systems translate votes into seats proportionally.

questions.text: What is an observer mission's typical role during an election?
options: Assessing whether the process follows stated standards
Announcing a winner before ballots are counted
questions.explanation: Observers assess process integrity and report findings.

questions.text: What does a ceasefire agreement ordinarily establish?
options: Terms for halting or reducing hostilities
A permanent border in every case
Automatic membership in the United Nations
questions.explanation: Ceasefires set terms for stopping fighting.

questions.text: Under the UN system, what is the role of the Secretary-General?
options: Chief administrative officer and diplomatic representative
President of the International Court of Justice
Commander of every member state's forces
Head of the World Trade Organization
questions.explanation: The Charter designates the Secretary-General as chief administrative officer.

questions.text: What is a coalition government?
options: A government formed by multiple parties sharing support or office
A government composed only of judges
An international court ruling on elections
A temporary alliance of central banks
questions.explanation: Coalitions combine parties to govern.

questions.text: Which institution sets monetary policy for the euro area?
questions.explanation: The European Central Bank is responsible for monetary policy in the euro area.

questions.text: Which UN Charter article describes the Security Council's primary responsibility for international peace and security?
questions.explanation: Article 24 assigns that primary responsibility.

questions.text: What distinguishes the International Court of Justice from the International Criminal Court?
options: The ICJ hears disputes between states; the ICC prosecutes individuals for specified crimes
The ICJ prosecutes individuals; the ICC hears only state disputes
Both courts are UN General Assembly committees
The ICC is a regional trade tribunal
questions.explanation: Their jurisdictions and parties differ.

questions.text: What does the principle of subsidiarity generally mean in EU governance?
options: Decisions should be taken at the lowest effective level, where EU action is not more effective
EU institutions must decide every local matter
Member states cannot adopt policies in shared fields
Only courts may propose EU legislation
questions.explanation: Subsidiarity guides the appropriate level of action.

questions.text: What is the function of a national human rights institution accredited under the Paris Principles?
options: Promoting and protecting human rights independently at the national level
Replacing the UN Human Rights Council
Negotiating trade tariffs for member states
questions.explanation: NHRIs have national human-rights mandates and independence standards.

questions.text: What does the International Law Commission primarily do?
options: Promotes progressive development and codification of international law
Runs elections in UN member states
questions.explanation: The ILC assists with international-law development and codification.

questions.text: Under the WTO, what is the most-favoured-nation principle generally intended to prevent?
options: Discriminating among trading partners absent an applicable exception
All customs duties in every circumstance
questions.explanation: MFN generally requires equal treatment of trading partners.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of a UN Security Council resolution imposing sanctions?
options: Restricting specified activities or dealings to address a threat to peace
questions.explanation: Sanctions are measures directed at specified conduct or actors.

questions.text: What is the principle of non-refoulement in refugee protection?
options: Not returning a person to a place where they face specified serious threats
Requiring every refugee claim to be heard by the ICJ
questions.explanation: It bars return to defined danger in applicable law.

questions.text: What is the role of the UN Human Rights Council's Universal Periodic Review?
options: Reviewing each UN member state's human-rights record periodically
Appealing criminal convictions from national courts
Selecting members of the Security Council
questions.explanation: UPR is a peer review of every state's human-rights record.

questions.text: What does the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations principally codify?
options: Rules and immunities governing diplomatic missions and agents
The law of armed conflict at sea
The creation of the European Union
questions.explanation: The convention governs diplomatic relations.

questions.text: What is a common reason for an international organization to use weighted voting?
options: To reflect agreed differences such as members' financial contributions
To ensure every member has an identical vote count
To remove member states from decision-making
To replace treaty-based authority with custom
questions.explanation: Some organizations allocate influence by agreed criteria.

questions.text: In international relations, what does a confidence-building measure aim to do?
options: Reduce misperception and the risk of escalation through transparency or contact
questions.explanation: CBMs increase predictability and reduce tension.

questions.text: What is the legal significance of a UN General Assembly resolution in most cases?
options: It is generally recommendatory, though it may have other legal relevance
It automatically overrides every national constitution
It is always a binding Security Council decision
It creates criminal liability without a treaty
questions.explanation: General Assembly resolutions are usually recommendations.

questions.text: What does the principle of universal jurisdiction allow a state to do in certain cases?
options: Exercise jurisdiction over specified grave crimes regardless of ordinary territorial links
Set policy for every other state
Ignore all immunities and fair-trial rules
Review the validity of every UN resolution
questions.explanation: Some grave crimes may be prosecuted without usual territorial links.

questions.text: Who is widely credited with developing the practical incandescent light bulb?
questions.explanation: Edison and his team developed a commercially practical incandescent lamp.

questions.text: Which invention made it possible to capture and reproduce still images using light?
questions.explanation: Cameras record images formed by light.

questions.text: What does a refrigerator do to food storage conditions?
options: Keeps contents cool to slow spoilage
questions.explanation: Cooling slows many spoilage processes.

questions.text: Which device converts sound into an electrical signal for recording or transmission?
questions.explanation: Microphones transduce sound into electrical signals.

questions.text: Which invention helps a person see very small objects more clearly?
questions.explanation: Microscopes magnify small structures.

questions.text: The movable-type printing press associated with Johannes Gutenberg developed in:
questions.explanation: Gutenberg’s press transformed printing in 15th-century Europe.

questions.text: What key component made early radio communication practical over distance?
options: A transmitter and receiver using electromagnetic waves
questions.explanation: Radio systems transmit and receive electromagnetic signals.

questions.text: What does a semiconductor transistor principally do in electronic circuits?
questions.explanation: Transistors control current as switches or amplifiers.

questions.text: What was the original purpose of the Jacquard loom's punched cards?
questions.explanation: Punched cards directed the loom's pattern selection.

questions.text: Which technology enables a photocopier to form an image using charged regions on a drum?
questions.explanation: Electrophotography uses charge and toner to reproduce images.

questions.text: What innovation made the first practical steam locomotive possible?
options: Using steam power to drive wheels on rails
Using solar cells to charge a battery
Using radio signals to control horses
Using compressed air to print books
questions.explanation: Steam engines supplied locomotive motive power.

questions.text: What is the main function of a catalytic converter in a car?
options: Measuring the vehicle's speed by GPS
questions.explanation: Catalysts help transform pollutants in exhaust.

questions.text: What does an optical fiber carry in a telecommunications system?
options: Electrical charge through a copper core
questions.explanation: Fiber carries data as guided light.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a safety interlock in a machine?
options: Preventing operation when a hazardous condition exists
questions.explanation: Interlocks prevent unsafe machine operation.

questions.text: Which invention allowed powered flight to be controlled through coordinated pilot inputs?
options: Control surfaces such as rudder and elevators
questions.explanation: Control surfaces change an aircraft's orientation.

questions.text: Who is commonly credited with inventing the World Wide Web?
questions.explanation: Tim Berners-Lee proposed and implemented the World Wide Web at CERN.

questions.text: Why did the integrated circuit represent a major advance over assembling many discrete components?
options: It placed multiple electronic components together on a semiconductor substrate
It replaced electrical circuits with mechanical gears
It stored software on paper tape only
It allowed all devices to run without power
questions.explanation: Integration reduced size and interconnection complexity.

questions.text: What is the operating principle of a liquid-crystal display pixel?
options: Electric fields alter liquid-crystal light modulation between polarizers
A heated filament directly emits each color
Sound waves engrave images into glass
Magnetic ink changes a paper's reflectivity
questions.explanation: Liquid crystals modulate light under electrical control.

questions.text: What does a phase-locked loop do in electronic systems?
options: Locks an oscillator's phase to a reference signal
Converts a digital image into a paper watermark
Measures force using a hydraulic piston
questions.explanation: A PLL synchronizes oscillator phase and frequency.

questions.text: Why is the Bessemer process historically important in steelmaking?
options: It enabled efficient conversion of molten iron into steel by blowing air through it
It created aluminum by electrolysis of seawater
It printed steel patterns with movable type
It powered furnaces using nuclear fission
questions.explanation: Air blowing oxidized impurities in molten iron.

questions.text: What is the key idea behind regenerative braking in an electric vehicle?
options: The motor operates as a generator to recover some kinetic energy
The brakes route exhaust into the fuel tank
The wheels store energy as compressed steam
The battery powers the engine while parked
questions.explanation: A motor-generator returns some braking energy to storage.

questions.text: How does a charge-coupled device sensor capture an image?
options: Collecting photo-generated charge in pixels and transferring it for readout
Using a chemical film to develop without light
Reflecting radio waves from each pixel
Measuring sound pressure across the lens
questions.explanation: CCDs move light-generated pixel charges for readout.

questions.text: What does a memristor theoretically relate in circuit behavior?
options: Electric charge and magnetic flux linkage
questions.explanation: Memristance links charge and flux.

questions.text: Why are feedback control systems used in inventions such as thermostats?
options: They compare output with a target and correct deviations
They prevent measurements from being taken
They guarantee the sensor never drifts
They remove the need for a controlled process
questions.explanation: Feedback uses measured error to adjust system output.

questions.text: What makes a Hall-effect sensor useful for detecting rotation?
options: A magnetic field change can indicate the passage of a rotating magnet
It reads printed serial numbers on a shaft
It detects rotation by cooling the bearings
It converts wheel color into radio frequency
questions.explanation: Changing magnetic fields provide rotation signals.

questions.text: What is the core principle of additive manufacturing?
options: Building an object layer by layer from a digital design
Removing all material with a cutting tool
Casting only one fixed shape in sand
questions.explanation: Additive processes form objects through successive layers.

questions.text: How does a photovoltaic cell generate electricity?
options: Absorbed photons create charge carriers separated by an internal electric field
A turbine compresses sunlight into current
A heated coil magnetizes the panel
questions.explanation: The photovoltaic effect separates light-generated charges.

questions.text: What problem does error-correcting memory address?
options: Detecting or correcting certain data bit errors
Increasing a processor's clock speed without limit
questions.explanation: Redundant information supports error detection or correction.

questions.text: What does a gyroscope provide to an inertial navigation system?
options: Angular-motion information for estimating orientation changes
A satellite's exact position without sensors
questions.explanation: Gyroscopes measure rotation for orientation estimation.

questions.text: Why did the invention of the Haber–Bosch process affect agriculture?
options: It enabled large-scale synthesis of ammonia fertilizer from nitrogen and hydrogen
It replaced irrigation with artificial rainfall
It created seeds using radiation imaging
It converted soil minerals directly into sunlight
questions.explanation: Synthetic ammonia made nitrogen fertilizer widely available.

questions.text: Who wrote the play “Hamlet”?
questions.explanation: Hamlet is a tragedy by William Shakespeare.

questions.text: Which artist painted the Mona Lisa?
questions.explanation: Leonardo da Vinci painted the portrait.

questions.text: Who wrote the novel Pride and Prejudice?
questions.explanation: Jane Austen published the novel in 1813.

questions.text: Which scientist is associated with the laws of motion and universal gravitation?
questions.explanation: Newton formulated influential laws of motion and gravitation.

questions.text: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
questions.explanation: Armstrong stepped onto the Moon in 1969.

questions.text: Who became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize?
questions.explanation: Marie Curie received the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.text: Which architect designed the Sagrada Família in Barcelona?
questions.explanation: Gaudí led the basilica's design.

questions.text: Which scientist developed the theory of natural selection independently of Darwin?
questions.explanation: Wallace independently formulated natural selection.

questions.text: Who composed the opera The Magic Flute?
questions.explanation: Mozart composed the opera.

questions.text: Which leader is closely associated with India's nonviolent independence movement?
questions.explanation: Gandhi led campaigns of nonviolent resistance.

questions.text: Who wrote the political treatise The Prince?
questions.explanation: Machiavelli wrote The Prince in the 16th century.

questions.text: Which painter is known for the series of water lilies paintings?
questions.explanation: Monet repeatedly painted water lilies.

questions.text: Which mathematician's work helped establish modern computing theory through the concept of a universal machine?
questions.explanation: Turing formalized computation with an abstract machine.

questions.text: Who was the South African anti-apartheid leader imprisoned for many years before becoming president?
questions.explanation: Mandela became South Africa's president in 1994.

questions.text: Which novelist created the fictional detective Hercule Poirot?
questions.explanation: Christie created Poirot and Miss Marple.

questions.text: Which Indian mathematician is known for major contributions to number theory and infinite series?
questions.explanation: Ramanujan made influential contributions to number theory and series.

questions.text: Which mathematician introduced the concept of a group in the study of algebraic equations?
questions.explanation: Galois connected groups with polynomial solvability.

questions.text: Which ancient historian wrote The History of the Peloponnesian War?
questions.explanation: Thucydides chronicled the Peloponnesian War.

questions.text: Who formulated the uncertainty principle in quantum mechanics?
questions.explanation: Heisenberg stated the uncertainty principle.

questions.text: Which writer used the pen name George Eliot?
questions.explanation: Mary Ann Evans wrote under that name.

questions.text: Which composer wrote the ballet The Rite of Spring?
questions.explanation: Stravinsky composed the 1913 ballet.

questions.text: Who led the first successful expedition to reach the South Pole in 1911?
questions.explanation: Amundsen's team reached the Pole first.

questions.text: Which economist wrote The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money?
questions.explanation: Keynes published the influential work in 1936.

questions.text: Which philosopher wrote Being and Time?
questions.explanation: Heidegger published Being and Time in 1927.

questions.text: Which chemist proposed the periodic table and predicted properties of undiscovered elements?
questions.explanation: Mendeleev organized elements and predicted gaps.

questions.text: Who became the first woman to serve as prime minister of the United Kingdom?
questions.explanation: Thatcher became prime minister in 1979.

questions.text: Which African American mathematician's orbital calculations supported early U.S. crewed spaceflight?
questions.explanation: Johnson calculated trajectories for early missions.

questions.text: Which Spanish artist co-founded Cubism with Georges Braque?
questions.explanation: Picasso and Braque pioneered Cubism.

questions.text: Which scholar translated and interpreted ancient Greek texts, influencing medieval European learning?
questions.explanation: Averroes wrote influential Aristotelian commentaries.

questions.text: Which U.S. civil-rights leader delivered the 1963 'I Have a Dream' speech?
questions.explanation: King delivered the speech at the March on Washington.

questions.text: Where is the headquarters of the United Nations located?
questions.explanation: The UN headquarters is in New York City.

questions.text: Which organization sets international rules for civil aviation?
questions.explanation: ICAO develops standards for international aviation.

questions.text: Which organization is known for coordinating international postal services?
questions.explanation: The UPU coordinates international postal cooperation.

questions.text: Which organization works on global labor standards and workers' rights?
questions.explanation: The ILO develops labor standards and promotes decent work.

questions.text: Which organization administers the Nobel Peace Prize?
questions.explanation: The Norwegian Nobel Committee selects the Peace Prize laureate.

questions.text: Which organization coordinates international public health work?
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization is the UN agency for international public health.

questions.text: What is the main mandate of the International Atomic Energy Agency?
options: Promoting peaceful nuclear use and verifying safeguards
questions.explanation: The IAEA supports peaceful use and safeguards.

questions.text: Which organization maintains the international system of units through metrology coordination?
options: Bureau International des Poids et Mesures
questions.explanation: The BIPM coordinates global measurement standards.

questions.text: Which agency coordinates international cooperation on intellectual property protection?
questions.explanation: WIPO is the UN agency for intellectual property.

questions.text: Which organization develops standards for international shipping safety and pollution prevention?
questions.explanation: The IMO sets global shipping standards.

questions.text: What is the core purpose of the International Telecommunication Union?
options: Coordinating international telecommunications and radio spectrum
questions.explanation: ITU coordinates telecom standards and spectrum.

questions.text: Which organization provides concessional financing and expertise for development projects?
questions.explanation: IDA provides grants and low-interest development credits.

questions.text: Which organization coordinates global meteorological observations and standards?
questions.explanation: WMO coordinates international weather and climate services.

questions.text: What is the central purpose of the International Committee of the Red Cross?
options: Protecting and assisting victims of armed conflict under humanitarian law
questions.explanation: The ICRC protects conflict victims and promotes humanitarian law.

questions.text: Which organization is responsible for coordinating international police cooperation?
questions.explanation: INTERPOL facilitates police cooperation across borders.

questions.text: Which institution is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations?
questions.explanation: The International Court of Justice is the UN’s principal judicial organ.

questions.text: Which treaty established the World Trade Organization in 1995?
questions.explanation: The Marrakesh Agreement established the WTO.

questions.text: Which institution is the principal organ of the Council of Europe responsible for human-rights judgments?
questions.explanation: The ECHR applies the European Convention on Human Rights.

questions.text: What is the core purpose of the Financial Action Task Force?
options: Setting standards to combat money laundering and terrorist financing
Providing emergency loans to sovereign states
questions.explanation: FATF develops AML and counter-terrorist-financing standards.

questions.text: Which organization administers the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES)?
questions.explanation: The CITES Secretariat supports implementation of the convention.

questions.text: Which body oversees the implementation of the Chemical Weapons Convention?
options: Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons
Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
questions.explanation: The OPCW verifies compliance with the convention.

questions.text: What is the primary role of the International Organization for Standardization?
questions.explanation: ISO develops consensus-based standards.

questions.text: Which body is the main forum for global negotiations on climate change under the UN climate convention?
questions.explanation: The COP is the convention's decision-making conference.

questions.text: What is the mandate of the International Fund for Agricultural Development?
options: Financing rural development and poverty reduction
questions.explanation: IFAD invests in rural people and livelihoods.

questions.text: Which organization coordinates the global response to transboundary animal diseases through its standards and information systems?
questions.explanation: WOAH supports animal-health standards and reporting.

questions.text: What is the role of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision?
options: Developing supervisory standards and guidance for banks
Setting retail interest rates in each country
Auditing every commercial bank's annual accounts
questions.explanation: The Basel Committee develops prudential supervisory standards.

questions.text: Which organization provides a forum for governments to negotiate international rules on nuclear safeguards?
questions.explanation: The IAEA implements safeguards agreements and verification.

questions.text: What is the purpose of the International Civil Service Commission in the UN system?
options: Regulating and coordinating conditions of service for UN common-system staff
questions.explanation: ICSC supports common-system staff conditions.

questions.text: Which organization maintains the Codex Alimentarius food standards?
questions.explanation: FAO and WHO jointly established the Codex Commission.

questions.text: What function does the International Civil Aviation Organization's Council perform?
options: Governing the organization and adopting international aviation standards
Licensing pilots in each member state
questions.explanation: The Council governs ICAO and adopts standards.

questions.text: Which reference work is known for documenting record-breaking achievements worldwide?
questions.explanation: Guinness World Records documents notable record achievements.

questions.text: Why should a record attempt use a clearly defined measurement unit?
options: So the result can be compared consistently
So participants can change the result later
So different quantities can be added together
questions.explanation: Standard units make measurements comparable.

questions.text: Which evidence can help verify a timed record attempt?
options: A calibrated timer and independent witnesses
An unedited claim with no time marks
questions.explanation: Independent timing evidence supports verification.

questions.text: What does a record category define?
options: The specific achievement and rules being measured
The audience size for an event
questions.explanation: Categories specify what counts as an attempt.

questions.text: Why should a record attempt follow published rules?
options: To make attempts fair and comparable
To prevent anyone from checking the outcome
To change the measurement after the event
questions.explanation: Consistent rules enable fair comparisons.

questions.text: What should a fair record attempt generally provide?
options: An anonymous claim with no witnesses
A result that cannot be repeated or checked
questions.explanation: Clear criteria and evidence make a record claim verifiable.

questions.text: Why might an adjudicator require video from multiple angles?
options: To verify the attempt continuously and resolve visibility gaps
To improve the event's entertainment value only
To replace the attempt's written rules
questions.explanation: Multiple views can reveal whether criteria were met.

questions.text: What should an organizer do if a record rule is ambiguous before an attempt?
options: Request clarification from the record authority in advance
Ignore the ambiguity and alter the result
Ask spectators to vote on the rule
questions.explanation: Advance clarification protects fair adjudication.

questions.text: Why is calibration important for a distance record measurement?
options: It checks that the instrument measures against a known standard
It removes the need to identify endpoints
It guarantees the result will be accepted
questions.explanation: Calibration improves measurement reliability.

questions.text: What is the purpose of independent witnesses at a record attempt?
options: To corroborate that the attempt followed the rules
To adjust the equipment during measurement
To decide the participant's training plan
questions.explanation: Witnesses provide independent confirmation.

questions.text: A record is for the largest assembled mosaic. Which measure is most relevant?
options: Verified number of pieces meeting the stated assembly rules
Number of people who watched the assembly
questions.explanation: The category defines the relevant count.

questions.text: Why should evidence include a clear start and finish for a timed challenge?
options: To establish the interval being measured
To set the record holder's age
questions.explanation: Defined endpoints are essential for timing.

questions.text: What makes a record claim reproducible in principle?
options: Documented rules, methods, and verifiable evidence
A result kept secret from reviewers
A changing definition after each attempt
An unsupported statement on social media
questions.explanation: Documentation allows others to check the method.

questions.text: Why must a record category avoid rewarding dangerous behavior?
options: Safety is more important than achieving a measurement
Risk removes the need for evidence
questions.explanation: Record validation should not encourage serious harm.

questions.text: Which process best handles a disputed measurement at an event?
options: Review the stated method and evidence against the rules
Change the category after results are known
Let the competitor choose the final figure
questions.explanation: Adjudication should follow predetermined criteria.

questions.text: Why do record organizations update records over time?
options: New verified achievements can surpass previous marks
questions.explanation: Records can change when a new achievement is verified under the rules.

questions.text: A proposed record measures the most objects stacked. What rule best improves repeatability?
options: Specify qualifying objects, stable stacking criteria, and how the final count is verified
Let each entrant define an object differently
Count only objects visible in a publicity photo
Change the stability rule between attempts
questions.explanation: Operational criteria make attempts comparable.

questions.text: Why can an uncertainty budget matter when validating a precision record?
options: It accounts for sources of measurement error affecting the reported value
It predicts how much an entrant will spend
It permits rounding any result upward
questions.explanation: Uncertainty quantifies limits on measured precision.

questions.text: A record uses sensors sampled at 10 Hz. What is a key verification concern?
options: Whether the sampling rate can capture relevant peaks without aliasing
Whether the sensor casing matches the event logo
Whether readings are reported in alphabetical order
Whether the contestant chose the sensor color
questions.explanation: Sampling must adequately represent the signal.

questions.text: What is a fair way to handle equipment differences between competing attempts?
options: Define allowed equipment specifications and verify compliance consistently
Allow unrecorded modifications for favored entrants
Ignore equipment if results seem plausible
questions.explanation: Consistent equipment rules support comparability.

questions.text: Why should an adjudicator preserve raw measurement data as well as a summary?
options: Raw data permits independent review of processing and anomalies
Raw data guarantees an attempt succeeds
A summary cannot be checked under any circumstances
Raw data determines who may enter future attempts
questions.explanation: Original data enables transparent reanalysis.

questions.text: For a record based on a continuous performance, why define permitted pauses?
options: Pause rules affect the duration and continuity being measured
They eliminate the need for a clock
They make all performances equal length
questions.explanation: Pause definitions shape the measured performance.

questions.text: What is the risk of selecting a record threshold after reviewing the entrant's result?
options: It introduces outcome-driven bias into the category
It ensures equal treatment across attempts
It removes uncertainty from the measurement
questions.explanation: Post hoc thresholds undermine impartiality.

questions.text: Why might a record body exclude a category with no objective endpoint?
options: Different reviewers could not apply a consistent verification standard
Every record must involve a stopwatch
Subjective categories can never be documented
An endpoint is needed only for athletic events
questions.explanation: Objective criteria enable consistent decisions.

questions.text: A team claims a record for a synchronized action. What evidence best demonstrates synchrony?
options: Time-stamped continuous recordings with a stated tolerance and measurement method
A group photograph taken after the event
A list of participant names only
An estimate from an audience member
questions.explanation: Timestamped evidence can test the defined tolerance.

questions.text: How should a record authority handle a result whose measurement uncertainty crosses the prior record?
options: Apply its predeclared decision rule, accounting for uncertainty
Declare a new record based on the favorable endpoint only
Ask competitors to decide by majority vote
questions.explanation: Predefined rules prevent selective interpretation.

questions.text: Why document chain of custody for a physical record artifact?
options: To show the tested item remained identifiable and was not substituted
To establish the maker's advertising rights
To calculate the event's ticket sales
To prove the artifact is visually attractive
questions.explanation: Chain of custody supports sample integrity.

questions.text: What does blinding reviewers to entrant identity help reduce?
options: Bias in applying subjective parts of an evaluation
Measurement error in a calibrated ruler
The need to define category rules
The duration of a timed attempt
questions.explanation: Blinding can reduce identity-related bias.

questions.text: Why use a pre-registered protocol for a record measured through multiple trials?
options: It fixes methods and selection criteria before outcomes are known
It allows the best trial to be chosen without limits
It replaces verification with a public announcement
questions.explanation: Pre-registration limits result-driven choices.

questions.text: What is the purpose of an appeals process in record adjudication?
options: Reviewing a decision for procedural or evidentiary error
Allowing every claimant to rewrite the rules
Guaranteeing all rejected claims are accepted
questions.explanation: Appeals provide a structured review of decisions.

questions.text: What is inflation?
options: A general rise in prices over time
questions.explanation: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level.

questions.text: What does a consumer usually give up when choosing one product over another?
options: The alternatives they could have purchased instead
questions.explanation: Choices involve foregone alternatives.

questions.text: What is a market in economics?
options: An arrangement where buyers and sellers exchange
A measure of a country's land area
questions.explanation: Markets coordinate exchange between buyers and sellers.

questions.text: If a product becomes more popular while supply is unchanged, what may happen to its price?
questions.explanation: Greater demand can place upward pressure on price.

questions.text: What is a wage?
questions.explanation: Wages are compensation for work.

questions.text: If demand rises while supply stays constant, what commonly happens to the market price?
questions.explanation: Higher demand with unchanged supply tends to put upward pressure on price.

questions.text: What does a binding price ceiling set below equilibrium commonly cause?
questions.explanation: A below-equilibrium ceiling can create shortages.

questions.text: What does price elasticity of demand measure?
options: How responsive quantity demanded is to a price change
How much a firm spends on wages
The speed at which money circulates
The number of sellers in an industry
questions.explanation: Elasticity measures percentage responsiveness.

questions.text: What is a negative externality?
options: A cost imposed on others outside a transaction
A benefit received by a buyer
questions.explanation: External costs affect third parties.

questions.text: What does comparative advantage depend on?
options: Lower opportunity cost of producing a good
Higher total output in every activity
The absolute price of all imports
questions.explanation: Comparative advantage is based on opportunity cost.

questions.text: In a competitive market, what does equilibrium price tend to balance?
options: Quantity buyers want and quantity sellers offer
questions.explanation: Equilibrium equates quantity demanded and supplied.

questions.text: What is a public good in the standard economic sense?
options: Non-rival and difficult to exclude non-payers from using
Produced only by a public company
A good with a legally fixed price
questions.explanation: Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable.

questions.text: What does marginal cost describe?
options: The additional cost of producing one more unit
The average revenue from all customers
The total cost of a firm's first year
The price consumers pay after tax
questions.explanation: Marginal cost is the cost of an incremental unit.

questions.text: What is a progressive tax?
options: A tax whose average rate rises as the tax base increases
A tax paid only by exporters
A tax with one identical amount for every income
A tax that decreases whenever income rises
questions.explanation: Progressive systems apply higher average rates to higher bases.

questions.text: What does a production possibilities frontier illustrate?
options: Trade-offs between output combinations with given resources and technology
The relationship between a bank's assets and liabilities
How a firm advertises to different customers
questions.explanation: The frontier shows feasible production trade-offs.

questions.text: The opportunity cost of a choice is:
options: The value of the best alternative given up
The total money in a bank
A fee charged by every market
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost measures the next-best alternative forgone.

questions.text: In a two-good exchange economy, the contract curve identifies allocations that are:
questions.explanation: Contract-curve allocations are Pareto efficient.

questions.text: What does the Slutsky equation decompose after a price change?
options: Substitution and income effects on demand
Fixed and variable costs of supply
Imports and exports in the balance of payments
questions.explanation: It separates compensated substitution from income effects.

questions.text: In a standard adverse-selection model, why can a market unravel?
options: Hidden type information changes who is willing to transact at pooled prices
Buyers know every seller's quality perfectly
A tax makes supply perfectly elastic
questions.explanation: Information asymmetry can drive higher-quality types out.

questions.text: What is the Coase theorem's key prediction under its ideal assumptions?
options: Bargaining can reach an efficient allocation regardless of initial rights, if transaction costs are zero
Property rights cannot affect bargaining outcomes
Markets fail whenever two parties disagree
questions.explanation: With zero transaction costs, bargaining can internalize externalities.

questions.text: In a Cournot duopoly, firms choose what strategically?
options: Quantities simultaneously, taking rivals' quantities into account
Product quality after observing consumers' incomes
Wages fixed by a central planner
questions.explanation: Cournot competition is quantity competition.

questions.text: What is the welfare interpretation of a deadweight loss from a tax?
options: Mutually beneficial trades that no longer occur
All tax revenue collected by government
The transfer from buyers to sellers
questions.explanation: Deadweight loss is lost surplus from distorted decisions.

questions.text: What does a compensated demand curve hold constant by construction?
options: Utility or purchasing power sufficient to isolate a substitution response
Nominal income in every possible definition
All prices except the changed price
The consumer's quantity of every good
questions.explanation: Compensation isolates substitution from income effects.

questions.text: Why can a multiple-equilibrium coordination game make expectations economically important?
options: Beliefs can select among self-consistent outcomes
Prices must equal marginal cost in every outcome
Government spending uniquely determines every choice
questions.explanation: Expectations can coordinate behavior on different equilibria.

questions.text: What condition characterizes a first-best Pigouvian tax on a marginal external cost?
options: It equals marginal external damage at the efficient quantity
It is set to the firm's fixed cost
It makes private marginal benefit zero
questions.explanation: The tax internalizes marginal external damage.

questions.text: In a principal-agent problem with hidden action, what does incentive compatibility require?
options: The agent prefers the intended action under the offered contract
Every possible contract yields equal utility
questions.explanation: Incentives must make the desired action optimal.

questions.text: What does the natural rate of unemployment represent in standard macroeconomic models?
options: Unemployment consistent with labor-market equilibrium absent cyclical pressure
A legally mandated minimum unemployment level
The share of workers permanently out of the labor force
The unemployment rate during every recession
questions.explanation: It excludes cyclical deviations from equilibrium.

questions.text: What is the central implication of the Solow model's diminishing returns to capital?
options: Capital deepening alone cannot sustain permanent per-capita growth
Population growth has no effect on steady state
questions.explanation: Diminishing returns limit growth from capital accumulation alone.

questions.text: Why can an unanticipated inflation surprise redistribute wealth between borrowers and lenders?
options: It changes the real value of fixed nominal repayments
It changes every loan's contractual principal automatically
It eliminates default risk in nominal contracts
It fixes the real interest rate at zero
questions.explanation: Unexpected inflation lowers real fixed repayments.

questions.text: What does the first welfare theorem assume about externalities and information for its competitive-market conclusion?
options: No relevant market failures, including external effects or asymmetric information
questions.explanation: Market completeness and competition assumptions are essential.

questions.text: What is the principal of a loan?
questions.explanation: Principal is the original amount of money borrowed or invested.

questions.text: What is a stock in a corporation?
questions.explanation: Shares represent equity ownership.

questions.text: What does a budget help a household plan?
questions.explanation: Budgets organize expected income and expenses.

questions.text: What is a bank deposit?
options: Money placed with a financial institution
A fee charged by a stock exchange
questions.explanation: Deposits are funds held by a bank.

questions.text: What does insurance generally provide in exchange for a premium?
options: A promise that no loss can occur
questions.explanation: Insurance transfers specified financial risks.

questions.text: What does diversification aim to do in an investment portfolio?
questions.explanation: Diversification can reduce concentration risk but cannot eliminate all risk.

questions.text: What does a bond issuer promise under a typical fixed-rate bond?
options: Interest payments and repayment of principal under its terms
A share of ownership in the issuer
A guaranteed increase in market price
A deposit insured by every government
questions.explanation: Bonds are debt claims with contractual terms.

questions.text: What is a credit score commonly used to estimate?
options: A borrower's credit risk based on credit information
A company's future stock return exactly
The amount of cash in a bank vault
questions.explanation: Scores summarize creditworthiness indicators.

questions.text: Why might a bond's market price fall when market interest rates rise?
options: Its existing coupons become less attractive than new yields
Its maturity date moves closer automatically
Its coupon payments stop by definition
questions.explanation: Bond prices adjust inversely to yields, all else equal.

questions.text: What is a mutual fund?
options: A pooled investment vehicle holding assets for investors
A loan made only between relatives
questions.explanation: Funds pool investors' money into a portfolio.

questions.text: What does a balance sheet show at a point in time?
options: Cash receipts over a full year only
Every forecast sale for the next decade
A list of shareholders' tax returns
questions.explanation: The balance sheet reports financial position.

questions.text: What is liquidity in personal finance?
options: How readily an asset can be converted to spendable cash
The amount of profit on a single trade
The length of a loan contract
The risk that a company changes its name
questions.explanation: Liquidity concerns access to cash.

questions.text: What is a dividend?
options: A distribution of company earnings or assets to shareholders
A fee paid to a bond issuer
A deposit required to open a bank
questions.explanation: Companies may distribute value to shareholders.

questions.text: What does an annual percentage rate generally help borrowers compare?
options: The yearly cost of borrowing, subject to disclosed calculation rules
The resale value of a home
questions.explanation: APR expresses borrowing costs on an annualized basis.

questions.text: What is a mortgage?
options: A loan commonly secured by real property
A deposit account that pays no interest
A share in a housing cooperative only
A government bond backed by land
questions.explanation: A mortgage is secured borrowing, often for property.

questions.text: With compound interest, interest is calculated on:
questions.explanation: Compound interest earns interest on accumulated interest as well as principal.

questions.text: What does duration estimate for a bond portfolio?
options: Sensitivity of price to changes in yield
The issuer's probability of default exactly
The remaining life of every bond with no weighting
questions.explanation: Duration approximates interest-rate price sensitivity.

questions.text: Under CAPM, what does beta measure?
options: An asset's sensitivity to market portfolio returns
questions.explanation: Beta measures systematic market exposure.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a discounted cash-flow valuation?
options: Estimating present value by discounting expected future cash flows
Adding historical revenue without regard to timing
Predicting market price from trading volume alone
Calculating a bond's coupon without its face value
questions.explanation: DCF values expected cash flows in present terms.

questions.text: What does a credit spread generally compensate bond investors for beyond a benchmark rate?
options: Credit and liquidity risks, among other factors
questions.explanation: Spreads reflect risk and market conditions.

questions.text: What is convexity used for in fixed-income analysis?
options: Capturing curvature in the bond price-yield relationship
Estimating a stock's dividend growth exactly
questions.explanation: Convexity improves duration-based price estimates.

questions.text: How does a call option's payoff to its buyer at expiration depend on the underlying price?
options: It is max of underlying price minus strike and zero
It is always the strike price
It is max of strike minus underlying price and zero
It equals the option premium in every case
questions.explanation: A call gives upside above its strike.

questions.text: What is a currency forward contract?
options: An agreement to exchange currencies at a set future date and rate
A spot trade settled immediately by definition
A share issued by a central bank
A policy that fixes all exchange rates permanently
questions.explanation: Forwards lock a future exchange rate.

questions.text: What does value at risk (VaR) estimate under a specified model and confidence level?
options: A loss threshold over a stated horizon that should not be exceeded at that confidence
The maximum possible loss under all conditions
Expected profit on the next transaction
The probability a bond pays its coupon
questions.explanation: VaR is a quantile-based loss measure, not a worst-case bound.

questions.text: What does the Modigliani–Miller proposition imply in its frictionless setting?
options: Capital structure does not affect firm value under stated assumptions
Taxes and bankruptcy costs are unavoidable
questions.explanation: The irrelevance result depends on restrictive assumptions.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a swap in interest-rate risk management?
options: Exchanging cash flows with different rate bases under agreed terms
Insuring a portfolio against every loss
questions.explanation: Swaps exchange specified payment streams.

questions.text: What does a bank's net interest margin compare?
options: Net interest income with interest-earning assets
Gross loans with total employee count
Cash reserves with government tax revenue
questions.explanation: NIM relates net interest income to earning assets.

questions.text: In portfolio theory, what benefit can imperfectly correlated assets provide?
options: Lower portfolio variance for a given mix
A fixed rate of dividend growth
questions.explanation: Diversification can reduce total volatility.

questions.text: What does a put-call parity relation connect for European options on a non-dividend-paying stock?
options: Call, put, stock, bond, and strike values
A company's debt rating and earnings
Spot and forward commodity inventories only
questions.explanation: Parity follows from equivalent replicated payoffs.

questions.text: What is wrong-way risk in counterparty credit exposure?
options: Exposure tends to increase when the counterparty's credit quality worsens
Collateral always rises as default risk rises
Market risk is unrelated to counterparty credit
A counterparty has no contractual obligations
questions.explanation: Exposure and default likelihood become adversely correlated.

questions.text: What is a target market?
options: The specific group a product is intended to serve
questions.explanation: A target market is the audience a business aims to reach.

questions.text: What does a brand name help customers identify?
options: A product or organization and its source
questions.explanation: Names help distinguish a brand's offerings.

questions.text: What is market research used to learn about?
options: Only a firm's tax filing date
questions.explanation: Research informs decisions about markets and customers.

questions.text: What is a product advertisement intended to do?
options: Communicate an offering to a potential audience
questions.explanation: Advertising communicates messages to target audiences.

questions.text: What does customer feedback tell a marketer?
questions.explanation: Feedback provides insight into customer experience.

questions.text: In the traditional marketing mix, the “4 Ps” include product, price, place, and:
questions.explanation: The traditional 4 Ps are product, price, place, and promotion.

questions.text: What is market segmentation?
options: Dividing a broad market into groups with shared characteristics
Setting one price for all products
Combining a firm's departments into one unit
questions.explanation: Segmentation groups consumers with similar needs.

questions.text: What does brand positioning describe?
options: How a brand is intended to be perceived relative to alternatives
Where a firm's office furniture is located
The order in which products are manufactured
How a company selects its tax jurisdiction
questions.explanation: Positioning establishes a distinctive place in customers' minds.

questions.text: What is a conversion rate in digital marketing?
options: The share of users who complete a defined desired action
The percentage of advertisements written in another language
The change in exchange rate after a campaign
The share of products returned to a warehouse
questions.explanation: Conversion rate measures completion of a target action.

questions.text: What does customer lifetime value estimate?
options: The net value expected from a customer relationship over time
The cost to ship one order
The number of ads a customer views per hour
questions.explanation: CLV estimates relationship value, not a certainty.

questions.text: What is a marketing persona?
options: A research-informed profile representing a customer segment
A real customer required to approve every campaign
A legal entity that owns an advertising agency
A list of product inventory codes
questions.explanation: Personas summarize audience characteristics and needs.

questions.text: What does a call to action in an advertisement do?
options: Encourages the audience to take a specific next step
Explains how a company's taxes are calculated
Guarantees an increase in market share
questions.explanation: A CTA directs the audience toward an action.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of a marketing funnel?
options: Represent stages from awareness toward conversion or retention
Calculate the volume of a product container
Determine the firm's annual tax rate
questions.explanation: Funnels map customer progression through stages.

questions.text: What does earned media usually include?
options: Unpaid coverage or sharing by independent sources
Ads purchased directly from a publisher
questions.explanation: Earned media comes from third-party attention.

questions.text: Why should campaign metrics be tied to a defined objective?
options: To assess whether the activity advanced its intended outcome
To avoid deciding whom to target
questions.explanation: Relevant metrics connect performance to goals.

questions.text: A/B testing compares two versions primarily to:
options: Measure which performs better against a defined outcome
questions.explanation: A/B tests compare variants using measured outcomes.

questions.text: Why can last-click attribution overstate the importance of a final touchpoint?
options: It assigns all recorded conversion credit to that touchpoint
It counts every impression as a sale
questions.explanation: Last-click omits earlier interactions' contribution.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a randomized holdout in a marketing experiment?
options: Estimating incremental effect by comparing exposed and withheld groups
Increasing the campaign's reach without measurement
Replacing all customer research with modeling
questions.explanation: Holdouts provide a counterfactual comparison.

questions.text: What does customer acquisition cost typically measure?
options: Marketing and sales cost per newly acquired customer
Revenue generated by every existing customer
The retail price of the product
The cost to retain one employee
questions.explanation: CAC relates acquisition spend to new customers.

questions.text: Why might a brand track aided and unaided awareness separately?
options: Prompted recognition differs from spontaneous recall
One measure tracks revenue and the other cost
Aided awareness is always higher-quality sales
questions.explanation: The measures capture different kinds of brand recall.

questions.text: What is a conjoint study designed to estimate?
options: How consumers value product attributes and trade-offs
The number of products in a warehouse
The legal validity of a trademark
questions.explanation: Conjoint analysis estimates preferences across attribute combinations.

questions.text: What is cannibalization in product marketing?
options: A new offering taking sales from the firm's existing offerings
A retailer reducing shelf space for every brand
A customer purchasing a product repeatedly
questions.explanation: Cannibalization shifts demand within a firm's portfolio.

questions.text: Why can a high click-through rate be a misleading campaign success measure?
options: Clicks may not produce valuable downstream behavior
It accounts for every view without bias
questions.explanation: Engagement alone may not meet business objectives.

questions.text: What does a brand lift study seek to measure?
options: Change in brand outcomes attributable to advertising exposure
The physical weight of product packaging
The lifetime value of every buyer exactly
questions.explanation: Brand lift evaluates changes in awareness or perception.

questions.text: Why is a geographic holdout useful when individual-level tracking is limited?
options: It compares markets with and without a campaign using aggregate outcomes
It guarantees identical consumer behavior between regions
It replaces the need for an outcome metric
It reveals every customer's browsing history
questions.explanation: Geo experiments estimate lift using market-level comparisons.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a media mix model?
options: Estimating how channels and other factors relate to aggregate outcomes over time
Choosing a brand's color palette from customer photos
Tracking a single user's path across all devices
Setting retail prices by competitor vote
questions.explanation: MMM models aggregate sales and marketing drivers.

questions.text: What is a lookalike audience typically built to do?
options: Find prospects resembling a source audience on selected characteristics
Identify customers who have already unsubscribed
questions.explanation: Lookalikes extend reach to similar prospects.

questions.text: Why should marketers monitor frequency in a digital campaign?
options: Repeated exposure can lead to diminishing returns or ad fatigue
Higher frequency always guarantees a purchase
questions.explanation: Excessive repetition may reduce effectiveness.

questions.text: What is the role of a demand-side platform in programmatic advertising?
options: Automating media buying across available advertising inventory
questions.explanation: DSPs automate advertiser-side media purchasing.

questions.text: Why use a pre-specified primary metric in an A/B test?
options: To reduce selective interpretation after seeing results
questions.explanation: Pre-specification limits outcome switching.

questions.text: What is a business plan commonly used to communicate?
options: A venture’s goals and how it intends to reach them
questions.explanation: A business plan outlines goals, market, operations, and financial assumptions.

questions.text: What is a common reason an entrepreneur conducts customer interviews?
options: To understand a potential customer's needs and problems
To guarantee investors will fund the venture
questions.explanation: Interviews help explore customer problems.

questions.text: What is a startup founder?
options: A person who establishes a new venture
A customer who buys a company's stock
A regulator who approves every business
A supplier who sets market demand
questions.explanation: Founders create and organize new ventures.

questions.text: What does revenue represent for a business?
options: Income earned from sales or services before expenses
The money left after all costs in every case
The value of every company asset
questions.explanation: Revenue is earned income before costs.

questions.text: Why might a new venture create a prototype?
options: To demonstrate or test an early version of an idea
To file its annual tax return
To guarantee the product is profitable
To prevent customers from giving feedback
questions.explanation: Prototypes help test ideas and communicate design.

questions.text: A minimum viable product is best described as:
options: A simple version used to test key assumptions with users
A fully finished product with every planned feature
A product with no intended users
questions.explanation: An MVP tests a core value proposition with the least useful product scope.

questions.text: What is a value proposition?
options: The specific benefit an offering promises to a target customer
A list of company legal filings
The amount of cash in a bank account
questions.explanation: It explains why customers may choose the offering.

questions.text: What does a startup's burn rate measure?
options: The rate at which it spends cash over time
The number of products sold each day
The interest paid by its customers
questions.explanation: Burn rate tracks cash consumption.

questions.text: What is a cap table used to record?
questions.explanation: Capitalization tables track ownership stakes.

questions.text: What is bootstrapping a venture?
options: Building it primarily with founders' resources and operating revenue
Raising money only through a public stock offering
Buying a competitor before testing demand
Hiring a lender to own the company
questions.explanation: Bootstrapping relies on internal resources and revenue.

questions.text: What does a business incubator commonly provide to early ventures?
options: Support such as workspace, mentoring, or services
A legally binding valuation for every startup
An automatic patent for each idea
questions.explanation: Incubators offer resources to help ventures develop.

questions.text: What does customer discovery test first?
options: Whether a real customer problem and target segment exist
Whether the founder can avoid all competition
Whether an idea has a catchy name
Whether the company can scale globally immediately
questions.explanation: Discovery investigates customer problems and assumptions.

questions.text: What is a venture's runway?
options: How long available cash can fund operations at a given burn rate
The distance from its office to an airport
The time until a product patent expires
The number of months a customer remains
questions.explanation: Runway estimates time before cash is depleted.

questions.text: Why might a founder seek an angel investor?
options: To obtain early-stage capital and potentially advice or connections
questions.explanation: Angels may provide capital and experience.

questions.text: What does a pivot mean in startup practice?
options: Changing a significant venture assumption based on learning
Closing a company without reviewing its performance
Adding every requested feature at once
Changing the founder's title but not the strategy
questions.explanation: Pivots adjust direction in response to evidence.

questions.text: Product-market fit broadly means that:
options: A product meets a strong need for a defined market
A company has the largest office
Every customer pays the same amount
questions.explanation: Product-market fit describes meaningful demand from a target market.

questions.text: What is a liquidation preference in a venture financing term sheet?
options: A priority right to receive specified proceeds before common shareholders in a liquidity event
A right to liquidate customer inventory at any time
A guarantee that the company cannot fail
A clause requiring founders to repay all sales revenue
questions.explanation: Preferences govern payout priority in specified events.

questions.text: Why can a startup's gross margin differ from its contribution margin?
options: Contribution margin may subtract additional variable costs beyond cost of goods sold
Gross margin includes every fixed corporate expense
Contribution margin always excludes direct costs
The terms are identical in all accounting systems
questions.explanation: Contribution margin can include broader variable costs.

questions.text: What is a SAFE commonly used for in startup financing?
options: A contract for future equity conversion under specified events
A secured mortgage on a founder's home
A government license to sell securities
questions.explanation: A SAFE provides future equity rights under its terms.

questions.text: How does a priced equity round generally differ from a convertible note?
options: It establishes a share price and equity issuance at the financing
It must be repaid as debt at a fixed date
questions.explanation: Priced rounds sell shares at an agreed valuation.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a cohort analysis for a subscription startup?
options: Comparing behavior of customer groups acquired in similar periods
Estimating the color preferences of all website visitors
Tracking company ownership across funding rounds
questions.explanation: Cohorts reveal retention and revenue patterns over time.

questions.text: Why can negative unit economics make growth risky?
options: Each additional sale may increase losses before fixed costs
More customers automatically eliminate variable costs
It guarantees the company can raise capital
It means the product has no target market
questions.explanation: Scaling unprofitable transactions can deepen cash needs.

questions.text: What does a startup's net revenue retention rate typically measure?
options: Revenue retained and expanded from an existing customer cohort, including churn and expansion
New customers acquired divided by advertising clicks
